title: Stop. Rank the next hour.
body:
### Situation
The day has gone sideways and you still have energy to waste. Rank the next hour before you spend it.

### Do
1. Stop moving. Sit or kneel. Pack stays with you.
2. Name the failure in one line: lost, hurt, weather, no water, dark coming.
3. Check people first — bleeding, breathing, can they walk, are they cold.
4. Rank the next hour: stop a killer, then shelter, then water, then signal, then travel.
5. Fire is a tool, not a religion. Build it if you need heat, boil, or smoke. Skip it if you need to get below treeline before the storm.
6. Write the last sure point, the time, and the next action on paper or a phone note.
7. Reassess every 30 minutes or when the weather or a person changes.

### Cautions
- Walking while you “think it through” is still walking the error larger.
- Do not start a long bushwhack to “get out today” until you know direction and daylight.
- Phone maps die. A written last-sure-point survives the battery.
- **Rockies**: afternoon convection often wins. If it is already 11:00 and you are above treeline, shelter and descent beat a pretty camp.
summary: When the day fails, stop and rank people, shelter, water, signal, then travel.

title: You are not sure where you are.
body:
### Situation
The trail vanished, the junction did not match, or the group split. You cannot name your location on the map.

### Do
1. Stop. Mark the spot with a hat, stick, or rock cairn you can see from 50 yd (45 m).
2. Last sure point: name it, time you left it, direction of travel, time walking since.
3. Look back. The route you came from is still a route.
4. If you can reverse the last 10–15 minutes to a known feature, do that once. Do not reverse for an hour.
5. If reverse fails: stay put, make yourself big (color, sound, smoke), and wait for the search to work.
6. If you must move: move to a catching feature you can name — trail, road, creek, ridgeline — on a bearing, and stop when you hit it.
7. Night and weather raise the stay-put threshold. Shelter and signal beat a night march.

### Cautions
- “Just a little farther” is how people walk into the next drainage.
- Do not follow a random drainage downhill unless you already chose it as a catching feature.
- Splitting the group to “find the trail” creates two lost parties.
- **Rockies**: drainages braid in beetle-kill and blowdown. A creek is a handrail, not a trail.
summary: Stop, name the last sure point, reverse once if cheap, otherwise stay put and signal.

title: Someone is hurt. Scene first.
body:
### Situation
A fall, a slice, a twist, or a collapse. You are now running a scene, not a hike.

### Do
1. Stop the group. Nobody else falls off the same thing.
2. Scene: rockfall, water, fire, weather, animals. Move the person only if the scene will kill them.
3. Heavy bleeding first. Direct pressure. Pack the wound if it soaks.
4. Airway and breathing next. Talk to them. If they do not answer, open the airway.
5. Keep them warm from the ground up while you work. A pad or pack under the torso.
6. Decide walk-out vs stay-and-signal. If they cannot take weight, do not “try the trail.”
7. Write time of injury, what you did, and what changed. Hand that note to the next helper.

### Cautions
- Moving a person off a slope to “get comfortable” can finish a spine or bleeding problem.
- Pain is not a diagnosis. Treat the failure: bleed, breathe, cold, cannot walk.
- Do not give a bunch of pills you cannot name. Water and warmth are the field drugs you know.
- **Rockies**: a “simple sprain” at 11,000 ft (3350 m) with a storm cell is an overnight. Plan shelter the minute they cannot walk.
summary: Make the scene safe, stop bleeding, keep them warm, then decide walk-out versus stay-and-signal.

title: The sky is now the problem.
body:
### Situation
Wind, lightning, whiteout, or a temperature crash is arriving faster than your plan. Terrain choice is the decision.

### Do
1. Name the threat: lightning, wind, wet cold, snow, flood, or dark plus any of those.
2. Lightning: off peaks, off isolated trees, off ridgelines. Down and into a low spot that is not a creek.
3. Wind: get off the saddle and the ridge. Lee of timber or a boulder field. Stake or weight the tarp now.
4. Wet cold: dry layer on skin, wind layer on the outside, food and water in. Fire only if it does not delay shelter.
5. Flood: out of the slot, out of the wash, off the alluvial fan. Higher ground that is not a peak.
6. If you are above treeline and cells are building, descent is the shelter.
7. Reassess every 15 minutes while it is changing.

### Cautions
- A summit photo is not worth the first strike cell.
- Do not hide in a metal-framed tent on a knoll and call it cover.
- Hypothermia starts in 50 F (10 C) rain with wind. Summer does not cancel it.
- **Rockies**: Front Range summer cells often fire after noon. Turn around times exist because the physics does.
summary: Name the weather threat and change terrain: down from lightning, off the ridge for wind, out of the wash for flood.

title: You are behind on water.
body:
### Situation
Bottles are low or empty, the next known source is a guess, and the day is still working. Thirst is late information.

### Do
1. Stop sweating for free. Shade, slow the pace, mouth closed, pack weight off if you are stopped.
2. Inventory: every bottle, bladder, dirty bag, and melt option. Count hours of daylight left.
3. Drink what you have in small hits if you are already crashing. Hoarding the last cup while you stagger is not a plan.
4. Move toward a named source or a drainage you can defend on the map — not toward “maybe a seep.”
5. Treat before you drink still water. Clear is not clean.
6. If you cannot reach water before dark, make camp, reduce work, and signal. Walking all night thirsty is how people fall.
7. Watch the group for the quiet one who stopped peeing and started stumbling.

### Cautions
- Alcohol, extra salt, and a hard push at 9,000 ft (2740 m) empty the tank faster than the plains.
- Do not chug untreated ditch water because you are scared. A few hours thirsty beats days sick.
- Snow is not a full water ration until it is melted and in you. Eating cold snow drops core temp.
- **Rockies**: dry air and wind steal water you never see. Front Range west-facing slopes can run dry in August.
summary: Stop wasting sweat, count what you have, move to a named source, treat before you drink.

title: Night or weather will hit before you are home.
body:
### Situation
You will not make the trailhead before dark, a storm, or a person who cannot continue. Shelter is the task.

### Do
1. Pick the site before you pick the structure. Wind, water, dead trees, lightning, and the ground you will lie on.
2. Dry layer on skin now, while you can still work. Wet cotton against the body is a heat leak.
3. Ground insulation first: pack, boughs, a twig bed, a closed-cell pad. The dirt will take your heat.
4. Roof second: tarp, poncho, debris, snow. Stop the rain and the radiating sky.
5. Wind wall third. A beautiful roof that funnels a 30 mph (48 km/h) gust is a kite.
6. Keep the kit you still need — light, water, signal — inside the shelter, not 20 ft (6 m) away in the dark.
7. If a person is already shivering hard, shelter and calories beat a perfect lashing.

### Cautions
- Building until you are soaked and exhausted is how shelter becomes the injury.
- Dry creek beds and meadow bottoms collect cold air and, later, water.
- **Rockies**: beetle-kill snags come down in wind. Look up. A green thicket on a slight rise beats a dead lodgepole cathedral.
summary: Site first, then ground insulation, roof, and wind wall. Stop work before you are the casualty.

title: The terrain is trying to finish this.
body:
### Situation
Scree, dead trees, a fast creek, a cliff band, or a slope that will not hold you. The map said “go.” The ground says no.

### Do
1. Name the hazard out loud so the group shares it: rockfall, water, trees, exposure, animals, weather.
2. Look for the cheap bypass. Extra 20 minutes on dirt beats 20 seconds on a no-fall zone.
3. One person at a time in the danger band. The rest wait out of the fall line.
4. Creek: unbuckle the pack belt, face upstream, three points, downstream exit picked before you step in.
5. Scree and talus: test every hold, keep the group out of each other’s fall line, do not run it.
6. If you cannot reverse what you just did, you chose a one-way. Stop and rethink before the next move.
7. After a close call, sit. Adrenaline makes the next mistake.

### Cautions
- “The GPS line goes here” is not a field test of the slope.
- Crossing at the narrow whitewater because it looks short is a classic drowning site.
- **Rockies**: beetle-kill deadfall hides holes. Probe with a pole. Afternoon rockfall increases as ice melts on high faces.
summary: Name the terrain hazard, find the cheap bypass, and move one at a time out of the fall line.

title: You are losing heat faster than you make it.
body:
### Situation
Shivering, wet clothes, wind, or a temperature drop that will not wait for camp. Heat budget is now the mission.

### Do
1. Stop the heat leak: get out of the wind, off the snow or dirt, and out of wet next-to-skin layers.
2. Dry or change the base layer. Wring it if it is the only one. A damp dry-ish layer under a wind shell beats a soaked T-shirt in a breeze.
3. Hat, hood, dry socks. Head and feet are cheap wins.
4. Food and water. A cold dehydrated person cannot shiver forever.
5. Shelter and insulation from the ground. Fire if you can build it without getting wetter or burning the only tarp.
6. Buddy check: watch for the person who got quiet, clumsy, or “I’m fine” while fumbling zippers.
7. If shivering is violent or the person is confused, this is now a stay-and-signal medical problem, not a hike.

### Cautions
- Alcohol does not warm you. It opens the pipes and dumps heat.
- Cotton holds water against skin. Get it off the torso.
- **Rockies**: a 40 F (4 C) night after a 75 F (24 C) Front Range day is normal. Wet plus wind at 11,000 ft (3350 m) is a hypothermia factory.
summary: Stop wind and wet, get off the ground, add calories, then shelter. Confusion means stay and signal.

title: Heat is beating the group.
body:
### Situation
Someone is dizzy, nauseated, cramping, or stopped sweating on a hot climb. The sun and the grade are the load.

### Do
1. Shade now. Pack, tarp, boulder, tree. Get them off black rock and out of the full sun.
2. Loosen clothing. Cool the neck, armpits, and groin with water if you can spare it.
3. Sip water. Small and steady. A salt snack if they can keep it down.
4. Legs up if they are pale and faint and the scene is safe.
5. Do not send them back up the same slope “to finish the peak.” Descend to cooler air when they can walk.
6. Watch for the one who is hot, confused, and not sweating. That is a get-to-care problem. Cool and signal.
7. Slow the whole group. One casualty becomes three if you keep the original pace.

### Cautions
- Dumping a whole bottle on a person who is already dry on water may be the last water.
- Ibuprofen does not fix heat. Rest, shade, water, and descent do.
- **Rockies**: Denver at 5,280 ft (1609 m) plus a west-facing foothill in June will cook you. The high plains edge has almost no shade. Start earlier than you want.
summary: Shade, cool, sip, descend. Confusion plus a hot dry skin is a stay-and-signal problem.

title: Dark is here and you are not done.
body:
### Situation
You ran out of daylight still moving, or the light died. Night changes every other problem.

### Do
1. Decide: bivy here vs a short, known move to a better site. Unknown travel in the dark is a last resort.
2. Lights: one task light, one spare. Red or low white to save night vision and battery.
3. Make the camp findable: whistle, reflective, a small fire only if you already judged the site and the wind.
4. Count people. Night is when someone walks 40 ft (12 m) to pee and becomes a second incident.
5. Warmth: extra layer now, not when you wake up shaking. Eat and drink before you bag up.
6. If you must walk: slow, short legs, handrail feature, frequent stops. No cliff bands, no creek crossings you did not already like in daylight.
7. Write the plan for dawn so the 03:00 panic has something to read.

### Cautions
- Phone flashlight is a battery funeral. Headlamp or it stays off.
- Night “shortcuts” off trail are how ankles and cliffs happen.
- **Rockies**: timberline to parking lot can be a two-hour stumble in the dark, and the temperature will drop 20 F (11 C) without asking. Bivy high and walk at first light if the trail is not obvious.
summary: Default to a known bivy. Save light, count people, and save travel for a handrail you already trust.

title: Find water on the Front Range.
body:
### Situation
Bottles are low and you need a real source, not a rumor. You are in Front Range foothills, montane forest, or high alpine.

### Do
1. Read the map for blue lines, lakes, and the next drainage below you. Walk to a named feature, not a hope.
2. Descend a sidehill toward the sound of water. Canyons concentrate it. Ridges waste the walk.
3. Look for willows, darker green ribbons, and animal trails dropping into a fold. That is often a seep or creek.
4. Spring: take it at the rock face or the first clean pool, not after it has wandered through a cattle meadow.
5. High country: lingering snow on north aspects can be melted. Old dirty fans are last resort.
6. Plains-to-foothills edge: stock tanks and irrigation ditches exist. Treat them as dirty. Ask whether the walk to a known creek is cheaper.
7. Mark the source on the map and in a note so you can find it again at dusk.

### Cautions
- A green meadow is not always water. It can be a dry seep with thirsty mosquitoes.
- Do not drop into a slot canyon you cannot climb out of just because you heard a trickle.
- **Rockies**: west aspects and south-facing parks run dry in late summer. North-facing drainages hold snow and water later. August Front Range can fool Denver people who packed one bottle.
summary: Walk to a named drainage or spring. Willows and north aspects hold water later than south parks.

title: Clear is not clean.
body:
### Situation
You found water. It looks fine. You still have to decide how to make it drinkable enough to keep walking.

### Do
1. Prefer moving water over a warm pond. Prefer a spring over a lake outlet after a beaver meadow.
2. Prefilter the obvious: grass, grit, dead bugs, glacier flour. Cloth, bandana, or the filter’s own prefilter.
3. Then treat: boil, filter to the spec you packed, or chemical with the wait time the bottle actually needs.
4. Cold, silty, or tea-colored water makes chemicals slower and filters clog faster. Prefilter harder. Wait longer.
5. Keep dirty and clean containers from touching rims. One dirty cap on a clean bottle undoes the work.
6. If you have no treat method, weigh distance to a better source against a small sip and a later problem. Do not fill the whole day from a cattle puddle.
7. Label the bottle in your head: dirty, treating, clean.

### Cautions
- “Mountain water is clean” is a story. High lakes and clear creeks still carry gut bugs.
- Iodine and chlorine struggle with cloudy water. Boil or filter that, or wait much longer.
- **Rockies**: beaver ponds and popular 14er streams are not wilderness magic. Treat them.
summary: Prefilter grit, then boil, filter, or chemical. Clear creek water still gets treated.

title: Boil it. Watch the rolling.
body:
### Situation
You have a pot, a heat source, and questionable water. Boiling is the method that does not care about filter pores or chemical contact time.

### Do
1. Prefilter debris so you are not boiling soup. Cloth or a settle-and-pour.
2. Fill the pot. Lid on if you have one — you lose less water to steam and it boils sooner.
3. Bring it to a rolling boil: big bubbles, not a shy simmer.
4. At Front Range and 14er altitudes, keep the roll going a full minute. Time it. Thin air lowers the boiling temperature.
5. Let it cool with the lid on. Pour into the clean bottle. Do not dip the dirty scoop back in.
6. If fuel is short, boil the day’s drinking water in one batch, not six tiny cups.
7. Snowmelt: melt first, then bring to a boil. Do not scorch the pot dry.

### Cautions
- A bubble or two at 12,000 ft (3660 m) is not a rolling boil. Wait for the real roll, then a minute.
- Boiling does not remove chemical pollution, heavy metals, or livestock runoff taste. It is for living contaminants.
- Steam burns. Tilt the pot away from your hands and the shelter wall.
- **Rockies**: stoves and fires both starve for oxygen up high. Wind screens help. Open fire under a timberline wind will waste fuel.
summary: Prefilter, rolling boil, one extra minute at altitude, then cool in a clean bottle.

title: Run the filter like it can clog.
body:
### Situation
You packed a pump, squeeze, or gravity filter and you are at a silty creek or a lake with a floor of muck.

### Do
1. Scoop from mid-depth, not the stirred bottom. Let a pot settle 5–10 minutes if the water is gray.
2. Prefilter through cloth. Glacier flour and organic tea kill cartridges.
3. Keep dirty and clean hoses honest. The dirty end never touches the clean bottle mouth.
4. Filter into a clean container. If the flow dies, backflush or clean the prefilter before you force it.
5. If the cartridge froze, inspect it. A cracked hollow-fiber filter is a straw, not a filter. Switch to boil or chemical.
6. At day’s end, purge water out of the cartridge if tonight will freeze.
7. Carry a backup method. Filters fail. Boil and chemical do not need pores.

### Cautions
- Forcing a clogged filter can bypass the element or blow a seal. You will not see the bypass.
- Filters that claim bacteria spec may not handle viruses. Know what you packed.
- **Rockies**: spring runoff and glacial streams on 14ers are flour mills. Settle, cloth, then filter, or you will be boiling by supper.
summary: Settle and cloth-prefilter first. Protect dirty/clean ends. Freeze and silt kill cartridges.

title: Drops and tablets need time.
body:
### Situation
You are treating with chlorine dioxide, bleach-spec drops, or iodine tablets because the filter is down or you packed light.

### Do
1. Prefilter until the water is as clear as you can get it. Cloud hides the work.
2. Dose the real volume, not the bottle’s swagger marks. Read your own kit’s count.
3. Mix. Cap loose for a minute so treated water touches the threads, then tighten.
4. Wait the full contact time. Cold water needs longer. If the bottle is fridge-cold, give it extra.
5. Do not add drink mix until the wait is done. Sugar and flavor fight some chemicals.
6. If the water is still cold and cloudy after a standard wait, wait longer or boil.
7. Keep one untreated dirty bottle for fetching so you do not contaminate the treated one.

### Cautions
- The tablet is not done when it dissolves. The clock starts after it dissolves and is mixed.
- Chemicals are weaker against some cysts in cold dirty water. Time and clarity matter.
- Iodine is a poor long-term plan for some people. Use what you packed, then get to a better method.
- **Rockies**: 40 F (4 C) creek water in June is normal. Double the patience, not the dose, unless your kit says otherwise.
summary: Clear the water, dose, wet the threads, then wait the full cold-water contact time.

title: Snow is a slow, cold well.
body:
### Situation
Liquid water is gone or frozen and you are looking at snowfields, a lake crust, or last winter’s drift.

### Do
1. Choose clean snow: white, not yellow, not the trail’s edge, not the surface with goat tracks.
2. Melt it. Stove or fire with a little starter water in the pot so it does not scorch.
3. Bring melted water to a boil if the snow sat on dirt, heather, or a popular camp.
4. Ice from a moving creek is better than lake-edge slush. Still treat after melt.
5. Do not eat snow as your main intake. It costs core heat and gives little volume.
6. Dark pot, sun, and a black bag can melt a lunch ration in calm weather. It will not hydrate a hard march alone.
7. Keep the melt bottle inside the bag at night so it does not become a block.

### Cautions
- Pink or dirty snow is not a flavor. Skip it.
- Old avalanche debris is mixed with soil and branches. Treat it like dirty water.
- **Rockies**: June snow above treeline is normal on north faces. It is also a terrain trap. Melt from the edge, do not walk the middle of a hanging field.
summary: Melt clean snow with starter water, treat if it sat on dirt, and do not eat snow for hydration.

title: Carry it. Ration the work, not the kidneys.
body:
### Situation
The next source is hours away, or you are not sure it exists. You have what is on your back.

### Do
1. Count ounces (ml). Count hours. Count people. Heat and altitude raise the burn.
2. Sip on a schedule, not when your mouth panics. A swallow every 15–20 minutes on a climb.
3. Cut extra work: shade, slower pace, less talking, pack straps that do not saw.
4. Do not dump water on your head if that water is the day’s drinking. A wet bandana from a spare sip is cheaper.
5. Cache only what you can find again: obvious feature, mark, and a plan to pick it up. A bottle under a random spruce is gone.
6. Split the load so one person is not carrying everyone’s water and falling behind.
7. Turn around while you still have a walk-home reserve. Empty at the summit is a bet.

### Cautions
- Rationing to sips while you hammer a 14er is how people bonk and need a rescue they cannot talk for.
- Sharing one dirty bottle mouth shares more than water.
- **Rockies**: from Denver dry air to a Front Range west slope, two liters can vanish before the first saddle. Carry more than the plains habit.
summary: Count volume against hours, sip on a clock, cut extra sweat, keep a walk-home reserve.

title: Thirst is a late gauge.
body:
### Situation
Someone is fading, headache, cranky, dark urine, or stopped peeing. You need to treat this as a water and heat problem now.

### Do
1. Stop in shade. Pack off. Sit.
2. Sip. Do not chug a liter on a nauseated stomach. Small hits for 10 minutes.
3. Cool the person if they are overheating. See the heat card.
4. Salt snack if they can eat. Water alone on a long sweat day can cramp.
5. Check the rest of the group. The loud one reports it. The quiet one is further along.
6. If they are confused, fainting, or cannot keep water down, this is a get-to-care problem. Stop travel that is not toward help.
7. Restart walking only when urine is heading back toward pale and they can talk in full sentences.

### Cautions
- Headache at altitude can be water, sun, or altitude. Treat water and rest first, then see the altitude card.
- Dark urine after a long push is information. Ignore it and the next information is a stumble.
- **Rockies**: dry wind on the high plains edge pulls water off your tongue. You will not feel sweaty. Drink anyway.
summary: Shade, sip small, salt if they can eat. Confusion or no urine means stop and get to care.

title: Gut bug signs. Treat as if.
body:
### Situation
A day or more after suspect water, someone has gut cramps, rotten gas, or diarrhea that will not quit. You cannot name the bug in the field.

### Do
1. Treat it as a gut-bug problem, not a diagnosis. The name does not change the field work.
2. Hydrate. Small sips, often. If they cannot keep water down, that is the emergency, not the toilet.
3. Keep hands off group food. Separate cook spoon. Soap or sanitizer after toilet.
4. Do not dose mystery pills from a side pocket unless they are the person’s known meds.
5. Slow the mileage. A gut problem plus a 14er descent is a fall waiting.
6. Get to care when you can walk there. Persistent diarrhea, blood, fever, or a person who cannot drink needs real care.
7. Write what they drank and when. It helps the next provider. It does not prove the source.

### Cautions
- Do not announce that someone “has giardia.” You do not know. You know they are sick after water.
- Anti-diarrheal pills can be the wrong move if there is fever or blood. Get to care.
- **Rockies**: beaver meadows and busy Indian Peaks creeks are classic worry sites. Treat water on the way in so this card stays theoretical.
summary: Treat gut signs as a hydration and hygiene problem. Do not name the bug. Get to care if they cannot drink.

title: Some water is a last resort.
body:
### Situation
You have a choice of sources, or only a bad one. Rank them before you fill.

### Do
1. Skip water with a dead animal in it, obvious sewage, or a chemical sheen you can smell as fuel.
2. Skip bright green scum mats and water that stinks like rotten eggs if you have any other option.
3. Cattle ponds, irrigation returns, and trailhead ditches are dirty even when clear. Treat hard or walk.
4. Still warm ponds after beaver work are a gut-bug factory. Prefer the inlet trickle.
5. Below mines and heavy road cuts, prefer a side spring over the main stained channel if you can find one.
6. If the only water is bad, prefilter, boil, and use it for a short keep-walking ration while you move to a better source.
7. Mark bad sources so the next person in your group does not fill there.

### Cautions
- Boiling does not fix fuel, pesticides, or heavy metals. Walking to a different drainage might.
- Do not dig a “seep well” in a cow pasture and call it a spring.
- **Rockies**: Front Range foothills mix elk, cattle, and people. The pretty stock pond on the plains edge is a last resort, not a picnic.
summary: Skip carcass, fuel sheen, and scum if you can. Cattle and beaver ponds get treated hard or walked past.

title: Decide if fire is worth the time.
body:
### Situation
You want a fire. Want is not the test. Heat, boil, signal, and morale are the tests.

### Do
1. Ask: do I need heat, boiled water, a smoke signal, or a dry-out? If no, skip it.
2. Check the site: wind, bans in your head from the trailhead, dry grass, beetle-kill, overhead snags.
3. If a person is wet and going down, fire is in the top three with shelter and dry layers.
4. If you only need 2 cups (0.5 L) of water and you have a stove, stove wins.
5. If you need to be seen, a smoky fire at a clearing beats a hidden cooking ring in timber.
6. Time it. A wet fire can eat an hour. That hour might belong to shelter or descent.
7. Once you decide yes, commit: tinder, kindling, fuel, site, water to kill it later.

### Cautions
- A fire in dry beetle-kill is a way to become the incident.
- Night fires on a ridgeline look brave and throw sparks into wind.
- **Rockies**: fire bans are common on the Front Range by July. A stove still boils. Illegal fire plus wind is a different kind of lost.
summary: Build fire for heat, boil, or signal. Skip it when a stove or descent spends the hour better.

title: Site the fire so it cannot run.
body:
### Situation
You have decided to burn. The ground you pick is the difference between a tool and a wildfire.

### Do
1. Bare mineral soil if you can. Scrape duff down to dirt in a circle wider than the fuel pile.
2. Overhead: no dead branches, no snag, no low spruce skirt.
3. Wind: build on the lee of a boulder or bank. Face the fire so sparks go to dirt, not grass.
4. Distance from shelters, tarps, and hanging clothes: far enough that a gust is embarrassing, not catastrophic.
5. Keep water or dirt staged to kill it. A pot already full.
6. In snow, build on a platform of green sticks so the fire does not drown in its own melt.
7. Never in dry meadow grass, peat, or a bed of pine duff you only kicked aside.

### Cautions
- Old fire rings in a bad place are still a bad place.
- Roots in duff can smolder downhill and pop up later.
- **Rockies**: beetle-kill lodgepole drops black twigs that take a spark. Give yourself more dirt than you think. Wind on a Front Range saddle will throw coals.
summary: Mineral soil, no overhead snags, water staged, sparks aimed at dirt. Skip dry duff and grass.

title: Tinder that actually lives here.
body:
### Situation
You need the first flame and the kit is thin. You are in Front Range pine, spruce-fir, or aspen.

### Do
1. Look for resinous dead pine twigs, fatwood in old stumps, and the dry inner bark of dead standing trees.
2. Birch bark if you are in an aspen-birch mix — take from deadfall, not a living strip around a trunk.
3. Dry grass, seed heads, and the fuzzy fireweed leftover in late season. Keep it dead-dry in a pocket.
4. Pitch blobs on wounded pines. A dab on a feather stick is a cheat code.
5. Split wet wood to the dry heart. The outside can be soaked; the inside often is not.
6. Carry a thumb of dry tinder in a film of plastic or a tin. The forest is not dry just because the sky is.
7. Make more tinder than the fire looks like it needs. The first flame is greedy.

### Cautions
- Stripping live bark off a green tree wastes time and does not burn.
- Juniper bark is stringy and useful. Juniper country is also fire country. Site still matters.
- **Rockies**: ponderosa whiskers and lodgepole twigs light well when dead and dry. Green aspen is a liar. Beetle-kill wood can be dry as a kiln — great tinder, terrible wildfire neighbor.
summary: Resin twigs, fatwood, dead inner bark, and pocket-dry grass. Split wet sticks to the dry heart.

title: Build a fire that feeds itself.
body:
### Situation
Tinder is ready and you still need a fire that lasts. Structure is the skill, not the spark.

### Do
1. Stage three piles: tinder, pencil-thick kindling, then thumb-to-wrist fuel. Do not start until all three exist.
2. Lay a small teepee or lean-to of kindling with a cave for the tinder. Air has to get in.
3. Light the tinder. Feed pencil sticks one at a time. Do not dump the pile and smother it.
4. When the kindling takes, add the next size. Wait for flame to wrap a piece before the next.
5. Build a coal bed. Coals boil water and bank overnight. Flames just look good.
6. Keep spare dry fuel inside the shelter mouth or under a log. Weather will not wait.
7. If it dies, rebuild from dry heartwood. Blowing on wet smoke is theater.

### Cautions
- Huge logs on a baby flame crush it.
- Tight rock rings with no air gap starve the fire. Leave a mouth to the wind.
- **Rockies**: thin dry air makes flame look eager and then die when you skip kindling sizes. Do not jump from tinder to a wrist-thick lodgepole.
summary: Stage tinder, kindling, and fuel first. Grow sizes. Coals are the product.

title: Wet wood still has a dry heart.
body:
### Situation
Everything is raining and you still need heat or a boil. The forest is wet on the outside.

### Do
1. Hunt standing dead, not ground soggy. Split it. The heart is the bet.
2. Make a roof first: tarp, poncho, or a dense spruce. You cannot dry tinder in a shower.
3. Feather sticks from the dry heart. Shave a pile. More than you want to make.
4. Use the ferro or a long-burn starter on that pile, not on bark that has been in the mud.
5. Build small under the roof, then move to a scraped site if sparks threaten the tarp.
6. Keep a dry kindling bundle on your body or in a bag. Body heat is a dryer.
7. Once you have coals, lay wet fuel around the edge to dry before it goes on, not in the middle to quench.

### Cautions
- Gasoline, alcohol from a flask, and spray cans are how people become the burn patient.
- A tarp dripping into the fire makes steam and then a hole in the tarp.
- **Rockies**: summer monsoon cells soak a sidehill in twenty minutes. Start the dry bundle before the cell, not after you are already hypothermic.
summary: Split standing dead, shave the heart, light under a roof, dry the next sticks on the edge.

title: Thin air makes fire hungry.
body:
### Situation
You are near or above treeline and the stove or fire is lazy. Less oxygen, more wind, wetter fuel on snow.

### Do
1. Wind screen the stove. A foil wrap or rock U. Leave air at the base.
2. For wood: smaller pieces, more air, closer attention. Big logs will not make up for thin air.
3. Sit the pot tight to the flame. Lid on. You are fighting a lower boil temperature and a stronger wind.
4. Melt snow in batches. Do not bury the flame in a heap of snow.
5. If wood is all krummholz and wet, stop wasting matches. Use the stove you carried for this reason.
6. Time boils with a watch. Guessing at 12,000 ft (3660 m) leaves you short.
7. Put the fire out with extra care. Wind will walk a coal into dry tundra.

### Cautions
- Do not burn in a tent vestibule to “make it work.” CO and flame do not care that you are cold.
- Above treeline, fuel is scarce and the weather is the real problem. Descent can beat a fire.
- **Rockies**: 14er saddles can blow 40 mph (64 km/h) on a blue morning. If the stove will not stand, move to the lee or skip the tea.
summary: Wind-screen, smaller fuel, lid on the pot, and extra time for the boil. Descent can beat a ridge fire.

title: Dead out. Cold to the touch.
body:
### Situation
You are leaving the site or going to sleep. The fire is still a fire until it is cold dirt.

### Do
1. Let it burn down. Stop feeding it 20–30 minutes before you need to walk.
2. Drown with water. Not a sprinkle — a soak. Steam should rise and then stop.
3. Stir. Turn the cobbles. Crush the charcoal. Drown again.
4. Feel with the back of the hand close over the soil. If it is warm, it is not done.
5. Scatter cold charcoal only if the site rules and the ground will not look like a dump. Otherwise leave a drowned pit you would accept.
6. Check downwind duff for crawl. Roots hide.
7. Snow: melt-drown still applies. A buried coal in dry duff under snow is a spring surprise.

### Cautions
- Dirt alone smothers and then stores heat. Water plus stir plus feel.
- Walking away from a “mostly out” ring in beetle-kill is how newsmaker fires start.
- **Rockies**: wind can revive a buried coal on a Front Range afternoon. Stay until it is cold, especially in July grass.
summary: Drown, stir, drown, then feel. Warm soil is still a fire.

title: Smoke by day, flame by night.
body:
### Situation
You need to be seen from a ridge or a helicopter and you have fire as a tool. Placement beats pile size.

### Do
1. Put the fire where sky can see it: clearing, rock slab, treeline edge. Not in a hole in the spruce.
2. Day: add green boughs or damp grass to a hot coal bed for a short white pulse, then let it breathe so you do not kill the fire.
3. Night: a bright, contained flame on a dark ridge is the signal. Keep it small enough to control.
4. Three is a pattern people look for: three fires, three blasts, three flashes. One good site beats three stupid ones.
5. Tend it. An unattended signal fire is a wildfire with a story.
6. Combine with a panel, mirror, and whistle. Fire is one channel.
7. If the aircraft makes a pass, do not run around. Stay by the signal and follow their signs.

### Cautions
- A smoke column in a fire ban and a dry wind is a second disaster.
- Do not burn the tarp you still need tonight.
- **Rockies**: valley inversions trap smoke low in the morning. A high clearing above the inversion is the one they will see.
summary: Site in the open, pulse smoke on coals by day, bright flame at night, and do not leave it.

title: Pick the ground before the roof.
body:
### Situation
You need to spend hours or a night out. The structure will not save a stupid site.

### Do
1. Walk a 50 yd (45 m) circle before you drop the pack. Look up, look down, look at the drain.
2. Rise: a slight bump, not a meadow frost hollow, not a dry creek, not a peak.
3. Wind: lee of timber or a boulder. Saddles and ridge noses are noisy and cold.
4. Water: close enough to fetch, far enough that a night rain does not join you in bed.
5. Deadfall: no widow-makers overhead. Beetle-kill snags are a no.
6. Lightning: not the tallest tree, not the isolated knoll, not the cave mouth that is a single rock tooth.
7. Ground: drain away from your hip, no ant nest, no obvious animal trail through the kitchen.

### Cautions
- The first flat spot after you decide you are tired is often a drainage.
- Game trails mean traffic at 02:00. Elk do not care about your tarp.
- **Rockies**: cold air slides down Front Range canyons after sunset. A bench 30 ft (9 m) above the creek can be 10 F (6 C) warmer than the waterline.
summary: Slight rise, lee of timber, no snags, no wash, not the tallest thing on a knoll.

title: A roof in the next twenty minutes.
body:
### Situation
Weather or injury just made tonight a field night and you do not have a tent. Speed beats architecture.

### Do
1. Site in one minute. Then stop scouting.
2. If you have a tarp or a strong contractor bag, that is the roof. Pitch it now. See the tarp card.
3. No tarp: dense evergreen with dead lower branches, or a rock overhang that is not a drainage.
4. Insulation from the ground before walls. Twig bed, pack, sit pad, dry duff on a scrape.
5. Wind wall: pack, log, piled debris on the weather side. Leave a low mouth, not a wind tunnel.
6. Get the wet person inside with calories before you pretty up the lashings.
7. Mark the site so you can find it if you step out: whistle, tape, a bright thing.

### Cautions
- A giant debris hut can eat two hours and all your dry layers. Small and soon.
- Do not strip the only living tree in a circle to the point it cannot be a windbreak.
- **Rockies**: krummholz at treeline is already a shelter. Crawl in the lee and add a tarp. Do not fight a full hut in a 30 mph (48 km/h) saddle.
summary: Site fast, roof with what you have, ground insulation first, then wind wall. Small and soon.

title: Tarp that stays in the wind.
body:
### Situation
You have a tarp, poncho, or sheet and you need it to still be there at 03:00.

### Do
1. Ridgeline first, taut, between two trees or trekking poles with guy-outs.
2. A-frame is the default in rain. Low sides. The lower the pitch, the less sail.
3. Peg every corner and every mid-side. Rocks on the pegs if the soil is rotten.
4. Nose into the wind or a steep wall to the weather. Do not present a flat billboard.
5. Dig a tiny trench only if water is already heading for your hip. Usually a better site beats a moat.
6. Keep cook and fire outside and downwind. Sparks own cheap tarps.
7. If it thunders, you are in a plastic roof, not a lightning shelter. See the lightning card.

### Cautions
- One skinny peg in Front Range decomposed granite will pull at the first gust.
- A high cathedral looks roomy and then becomes a kite.
- **Rockies**: afternoon wind shifts when the plains heat dies. Reset guys before dark, not after the first flop.
summary: Taut ridgeline, low A-frame, every corner guyed, weather wall into the wind.

title: Snow is insulation if you do not get wet.
body:
### Situation
You have snow deep enough to work and the air is colder than the pack. You need a hole or a trench, not a wet cave-in.

### Do
1. Probe the drift for rocks, creeks, and thin roofs. You want settled snow, not a cornice.
2. A trench with a tarp or ski roof is faster than a cave. Body-width, pack-length, plus a shelf for the kit.
3. Insulation under you is still the game. Pad, pack, boughs. Snow is a mattress only with a barrier.
4. Keep the roof thin enough to punch if it slumps. A ventilation hole is not optional.
5. Block the door with the pack, not your face. Leave an air gap.
6. Do not cook in a sealed hole. You will not like the air.
7. Mark the roof with wands or sticks so a searcher or a teammate does not walk through you.

### Cautions
- A pretty snow cave that took three hours can soak you. Wet plus cold is the fail.
- Cornices and avalanche slopes are not building material.
- **Rockies**: June drifts on north 14er faces are real. They also sit on steep ground. Build on a bench, not under a loaded slope. See avalanche watch.
summary: Trench on settled snow, pad underneath, vent the roof, never cook sealed in a hole.

title: Front Range wind will take the roof.
body:
### Situation
The wind is the weather. Ridges, saddles, and winter Front Range nights will peel a lazy pitch.

### Do
1. Get off the saddle. Even 20 yd (18 m) into timber changes the load.
2. Low pitch. Steep weather wall. More pegs than a calm-night habit.
3. Use trees, boulders, and the pack as part of the wall. Do not let the tarp be the only plane.
4. Double the guyline where you can. Truckers and taut-line, not a single slipknot on a twig.
5. Stake into packed snow or rock-deadman if the soil will not hold.
6. Sleep with a knife and a plan if a peg pulls. Fix it at the first slap, not after it shreds.
7. In true blow: ditch the cathedral. Bivy in the lee of a log with the tarp as a quilt.

### Cautions
- Trekking poles as a high A-frame on a 14er saddle is a sailboat.
- Do not tie to a dead snag that will join you in the bag.
- **Rockies**: west winds off the Divide and east-slope chinooks both happen. Plains-to-foothills nights can howl when Denver looks calm on the plains.
summary: Off the saddle, low pitch, extra guys, deadman the pegs. If it howls, bivy in the lee.

title: The ground is the thief.
body:
### Situation
You have a roof and you are still cold. Heat is leaving into dirt, snow, and the night sky.

### Do
1. Put something under the full body, especially the torso. Pad, pack, leaves, a twig bed.
2. Loft on top needs dry. Fluff the bag or quilt. Wet down is a blanket of noodles.
3. A hat and dry socks are cheap R-value. Change them before you lie down, not after you seize up.
4. A reflective tarp or space blanket as a roof liner bounces some heat. On the ground it is a sweat sheet unless you put duff over it.
5. Fill dead air in the shelter with packs and spare clothes so the cave is smaller.
6. Eat and drink before sleep. The furnace needs fuel.
7. If you wake cold, add a layer and fix the pad. Do not lie there being stoic.

### Cautions
- A huge airy lean-to in wind is a cooler. Smaller is warmer.
- Pine boughs: take dead lower branches, not a stripped living tree you still need as a windbreak.
- **Rockies**: radiating sky on a clear 11,000 ft (3350 m) night will frost a bag that was fine in Denver. A low roof helps.
summary: Insulate the full body from the ground, keep loft dry, shrink the shelter, eat before sleep.

title: Do not camp on the spark plug.
body:
### Situation
You need a night site or a wait-out hole and cells are building. Lightning cares about being the tall thing.

### Do
1. Off the summit, off the ridge, off the isolated tree, off the metal fence line.
2. A low spot in a clump of similar-height trees is better than one hero pine.
3. Not in a creek, not in a cave mouth that is a single boulder, not under the only tall snag.
4. Sit or crouch on a pad if you are caught. Feet together. Pack a bit away. This is a wait, not a camp.
5. After the cell, do not sprint back to the summit because the first blue hole looks pretty.
6. If you must sleep through a storm cycle, pick the boring bench in uniform timber.
7. Take metal poles off your shoulders when the hair tells you to. Poles on the ground, not in your hands.

### Cautions
- A rock overhang can be a side-flash path. Deep uniform cover beats a dramatic cave.
- Wet ropes and wet tents do not make you safe. Terrain does.
- **Rockies**: Front Range 14ers throw cells after noon. If you are still above treeline at 13:00, this card is already late.
summary: Uniform timber on a low bench. Not the ridge, not the lone tree, not the cave mouth.

title: Do not add a second patient.
body:
### Situation
Someone is down. Your urge is to run in. The slope, the water, the fire, or the next rock has a vote.

### Do
1. Stop the group. Point at the hazard. Assign a watcher if rock is still coming.
2. Approach from the safe side. Gloves on. Pack off if it will drag you.
3. Talk as you come: name, what hurts, can they move their feet and hands.
4. If the scene will kill them (fire, water, rockfall), drag on the long axis of the body the shortest distance that works. Otherwise treat in place.
5. Heavy bleed first, then breathing, then warmth.
6. One person talks. Everyone else fetches kit, shelter, and a written note of time.
7. Reassess the scene every time you look up. Weather and slopes change while you bandage.

### Cautions
- Hero jumps onto a ledge make two patients and no messenger.
- Do not twist a neck to “make them comfortable” if they fell from height.
- **Rockies**: afternoon rockfall on east faces after freeze-thaw. Park the group out of the fall line, not in a huddle under the same wall.
summary: Make the scene safe, approach from the safe side, bleed then breathe then warm.

title: Pressure. Pack. Do not peek.
body:
### Situation
Blood is leaving the person faster than you like. You can see it or the clothes are soaking.

### Do
1. Expose the site. Gloves. Find the hole, not just the soaked pant.
2. Direct pressure with cloth. Both hands. Hard. On the wound, not next to it.
3. If it soaks, do not take the first cloth off. Add more. Pack a deep hole with gauze or clean cloth and press.
4. If a limb is pumping and pressure fails, a tourniquet high and tight on that limb. Note the time.
5. Lie them down. Keep them warm. The next failure is cold and faint.
6. Do not keep peeking. Hold. Ten minutes is longer than you think.
7. Get to care. Write what you did and when.

### Cautions
- A trickle after a punchy fall can still be a lot of blood inside a boot.
- Improvised wraps that only circle the limb without pressure on the hole are decorations.
- Head and torso holes do not get a limb tourniquet. Pressure and pack, then move toward care.
summary: Expose, press hard, pack deep holes, tourniquet a pumping limb, keep them warm, get to care.

title: They twisted it. Decide if it walks.
body:
### Situation
A foot or knee went sideways. It swells. They want to try the trail. You need a walk-or-stay call.

### Do
1. Sit them. Pack off. Look at the joint. Compare to the other side.
2. If bone is poking, the joint is the wrong shape, or they felt a pop and cannot take any weight, treat as a fracture card.
3. Otherwise: rest, cold stream or snow in a cloth if it is close, compression wrap, elevate when stopped.
4. Tape or wrap in the boot they will walk in, not in a way that cuts the toes off.
5. Test: short level steps. If they can take weight with a pole and the trail is easy, go slow.
6. If they cannot take weight, or the trail is scree at dusk, this is a stay-and-signal or a carry you probably do not have.
7. Recheck swelling and color of toes. Loosen wrap if they go numb or blue.

### Cautions
- “Walk it off” on a 14er descent in the dark is how a sprain becomes a night out plus a fall.
- Numbness, cold white toes, or a wrap that is a tourniquet by accident: loosen.
- **Rockies**: talus hides holes. After a twist, shorten the day. The next hole is waiting.
summary: Compare joints, wrap and test on level ground. No weight plus hard trail means stay and signal.

title: Treat as if the bone is broken.
body:
### Situation
Wrong shape, bone out, they heard a crack, or they will not load the limb. You do not need an X-ray to stop using it.

### Do
1. Scene safe. Bleeding first if there is a hole.
2. Do not test it by twisting. Leave it in the position that they can stand if it is already there and circulation looks OK.
3. Pad. Splint the joints above and below with a pad, stay, or the other leg for a femur if that is all you have.
4. Check fingers or toes before and after: color, warmth, they can wiggle. If you lose that, loosen once.
5. Pain plus cold: warmth, food, water, and a pad under them while you wait.
6. This is not a walk-it-off. Signal and wait, or a planned carry toward care if you truly have the people and the trail.
7. Write time, what you saw, and what you splinted.

### Cautions
- Pulling a bone end back under the skin because it looks ugly can worsen bleeding. Get to care.
- A “maybe just a sprain” that cannot take weight on a remote slope is treated as a fracture for the night.
- Do not feed a person who may need a procedure soon if help is minutes away. If help is hours, small sips and warmth win.
summary: Do not test a wrong-shaped limb. Pad, splint above and below, check toes, stay and signal.

title: Cool the burn. Then cover it.
body:
### Situation
Stove flare, steam, hot pot, or a brush with the ring. Skin is angry or gone.

### Do
1. Stop the burning. Get them off the heat. Smother flame. Cool clothing if it is still hot and not melted into skin.
2. Cool with clean water 10–20 minutes. Not ice packed on the wound.
3. Remove tight things: rings, watches, hot belts, before swell.
4. Cover loosely with clean cloth. Do not pop every blister for fun.
5. Keep them warm. Burned people drop heat.
6. If the area is large, on the face, hands, genitals, or all the way around a limb, this is a get-to-care problem now.
7. Hydrate if they can drink and care is hours away.

### Cautions
- Butter, toothpaste, and mud are not dressings.
- Melted fabric stuck to skin stays. Cut around it.
- Do not use the last drinking water to flood a tiny finger burn if the group is already dry. A creek and then treat the remaining water.
summary: Stop the heat, cool with water, remove rings, loose clean cover, keep them warm, get to care if large.

title: Stop the hot spot while it is a hot spot.
body:
### Situation
A hot spot on a foot, heel, or pack strap. Tomorrow’s blister is still preventable.

### Do
1. Stop at the first complaint. Pack off. Sock off. Look.
2. Red hot skin: dry, then tape or a thin pad so the rub dies.
3. Closed blister that you can still walk on: pad around it, not a tight doughnut that becomes a pressure ring.
4. If it has torn and must be walked on: clean as you can, leave the roof if it is still a roof, dress, tape, dry sock.
5. Change to a dry sock. Grit in the sock is sandpaper.
6. Relace. Heel lock. Many blisters are a lacing problem, not a mystery.
7. Recheck at the next sit. Do not wait until blood is in the sock.

### Cautions
- Opening every blister in a dirty creek is a way to make a wound card.
- Duct tape on a wet hot spot can rip skin when you peel it. Use it over a film or paper if that is all you have.
- **Rockies**: long descents off 14ers grind heels. Tape before the downhill, not at the lake of regret.
summary: Stop at the hot spot, dry, tape, relace, dry sock. Dress a torn blister; do not excavate it in a creek.

title: They are cold in the middle, not just the hands.
body:
### Situation
Uncontrolled shivering, clumsy hands, mumbling, or “I’m fine” while they fumble a zipper. Wet plus wind is the usual recipe.

### Do
1. Stop heat loss: out of wind, off the ground, wet layer off the torso, dry or wrung layer on, wind shell on.
2. Insulate. Pad underneath. Hat. Dry socks. Shared quilt or bag if you have one.
3. Feed and water if they can swallow safely. Warm drink if you can make it without losing the shelter.
4. Buddy them. Do not send a clumsy person to “go get wood” alone.
5. If shivering stops and they are confused or slipping, this is a stay-and-signal emergency. Handle them gently.
6. Rewarm the trunk, not a fire roast of the hands that dumps cold blood.
7. After they improve, do not rush back into the same wet wind. Change the plan.

### Cautions
- Rubbing stone-cold arms, alcohol, and a forced march “to warm up” make this worse.
- A person who was shivering and then goes quiet is not “tough now.”
- **Rockies**: 50 F (10 C) rain on a June 13er is enough. Summer calendar does not block this card.
summary: Stop wind and wet, pad off the ground, fuel if they can swallow, trunk rewarm. Quiet after shivering is worse.

title: Pale, numb, frozen parts.
body:
### Situation
Fingers, toes, ears, or nose that are white or waxy, numb, or wooden. The rest of the person may still be talking.

### Do
1. Get out of the wind. Skin to warm skin for ears and nose if you can. Mitten the hands.
2. Do not rub snow on it. Do not beat it against a boot.
3. If you can reach a place the part will stay thawed, rewarm in warm water that is not scalding, 99–104 F (37–40 C) if you can measure. If you cannot measure, body-warm, not fire-hot.
4. If you must walk on a frozen foot to get to care, it may be better to walk frozen than to thaw and refreeze. That is a hard call. Favor getting to care without a second freeze.
5. Pad and splint a thawed part. It will hurt. Do not use it as a clamp.
6. Warm the whole person. Frostbite rides with hypothermia.
7. Get to care for white, wooden, or blistering parts.

### Cautions
- Fire and stove rewarm burns the numb skin you cannot feel.
- Refreeze after a field thaw is worse than a controlled walk on a still-frozen foot toward a real roof.
- **Rockies**: metal camera and axe heads, plus wind on a January Front Range ridge, will do this in minutes. Cover skin on the approach, not after it goes quiet.
summary: Wind off, no rubbing, rewarm only if it will not refreeze. Walk a frozen foot to care rather than thaw twice.

title: Too hot. Shade and sip.
body:
### Situation
Dizzy, nauseated, cramped, pounding head, or a person who is hot and not making sense on a climb.

### Do
1. Shade. Off black rock. Pack off. Fan them.
2. Loosen clothes. Cool neck, armpits, groin with water you can spare.
3. Sip water. Salt snack if they can keep it down.
4. If they are confused, collapsing, or the skin is hot and they are not sweating, cool hard and get to care. This is not a rest-and-go.
5. Legs up if they are faint and the scene is safe.
6. Descend when they can walk. Cooler air is treatment.
7. Hold the group. One more “short push” is how you carry someone.

### Cautions
- A person who stops sweating and stops making sense is not “getting used to it.”
- Piling on extra clothes because they have goosebumps while still in the sun is the wrong reflex if they are overheated.
- **Rockies**: foothill west faces in June plus Denver people who drove up at noon. There is almost no shade on the plains edge. Start earlier.
summary: Shade, cool, sip, descend. Hot, confused, and not sweating means cool hard and get to care.

title: The elevation is part of the picture.
body:
### Situation
Headache, nausea, odd fatigue, or clumsy thinking after a gain in elevation. You cannot name the diagnosis on the ridge. You can descend.

### Do
1. Stop the gain. Sit. Water. A snack. Sun off the head.
2. If the person is worse at rest, ataxic, confused, or gasping at rest, descend now. Do not wait for dawn on the summit.
3. Descent is the treatment you have. 1,000–2,000 ft (300–600 m) can change the picture.
4. Keep them warm and walking in control. No solo “I’ll catch up.”
5. Do not send them higher because the parking lot is on the other side of the peak unless that is truly shorter and downhill both ways — it almost never is.
6. Headache that improves with water and rest may just be that. Recheck before you climb again.
7. Get to care if descent does not improve them or they cannot walk a straight line.

### Cautions
- You do not get to call this “just dehydration” if they cannot tandem-walk and the lips are the wrong color.
- Sleeping higher after a bad day is a gamble. Down is the default.
- **Rockies**: Denver is already 5,280 ft (1609 m). Going to 14,000 ft (4267 m) in one morning is a common Front Range pattern. It is also a common fail.
summary: Stop climbing, water and rest, descend if they worsen at rest or cannot walk straight.

title: Clean what you can. Cover the rest.
body:
### Situation
A cut or scrape that is not pumping but is dirty. The trail is not a clinic. You can still make it worse.

### Do
1. Stop bleeding with pressure.
2. Irrigate with the cleanest water you have. Volume beats fancy. A stream from a bottle.
3. Pick out the obvious grit you can see. Do not excavate tunnels with a dirty knife.
4. Cover with a clean dressing. Change when soaked or filthy.
5. Watch for spreading red, fever, red streaks, or a wound that smells wrong the next day. That is a get-to-care flag.
6. Hands off. Do not keep poking it to show the group.
7. If it is deep, over a joint, from a bite, or you cannot stop the dirt, get to care.

### Cautions
- Super glue and duct tape on a dirty puncture trap the dirt.
- A puncture from a tool or a bite looks small and then goes deep. Take those to care.
- Do not use untreated ditch water as the irrigant if you have a treated bottle. Save a cup of treated for this.
summary: Pressure, irrigate with clean water, cover, watch for spreading red or fever, get to care if deep.

title: Pull the tick. Watch the skin.
body:
### Situation
A tick is in the skin, or you found one crawling. Spring foothills and brushy drainages are the usual story.

### Do
1. Tweezers close to the skin. Steady pull. Do not twist it into a trophy.
2. Do not burn it, grease it, or squeeze the body so it empties into the person.
3. Wash the site with soap or the cleanest water you have. Watch it.
4. Save the tick in a bag if you can. It helps later care. Do not play with it.
5. Note the date. A spreading bullseye or fever days later is a get-to-care problem. You do not name the disease on the trail.
6. Full skin check at night: belt line, behind knees, scalp, armpits, socks.
7. Pants into socks in brush. That is the field prevention that works.

### Cautions
- A rash or fever after a bite is not something to “wait and see” through a long trip. Get to care.
- Do not crush ticks with fingernails over the wound.
- **Rockies**: Front Range foothills in spring are tick country. High alpine is not a free pass on the hike out through oak brush.
summary: Tweezers at the skin, steady pull, wash, date it. Spreading rash or fever means get to care.

title: Bite. Keep still. Get to care.
body:
### Situation
A strike on a foot or hand, with or without a rattle you heard. You will not identify venom by folklore.

### Do
1. Move away from the snake. Do not hunt it.
2. Sit the person. Keep the bitten limb still and roughly at heart level if you can.
3. Remove rings and tight watches before swell.
4. Time it. Watch swelling and how they feel.
5. Walk them to care if that is faster than waiting in a place no one will find. Carry if you have the people. Running is not the plan.
6. Phone or messenger as soon as you have signal. This is a get-to-care problem.
7. Note color and pattern only if it costs you nothing. A photo from far away beats a second bite.

### Cautions
- No cutting, no sucking, no ice pack as treatment, no tourniquet as a default.
- A dry bite can still swell. Treat the person, not the story.
- **Rockies**: prairie rattlesnakes live on the Front Range foothills and hogback, not on the 14er talus. Watch hands on sunny rocks below about 8,000 ft (2440 m).
summary: Away from the snake, still limb, rings off, walk or carry to care. No cut, suck, or ice as treatment.

title: They cannot cough. You act.
body:
### Situation
A person is silent, clutching the throat, cannot cough or speak, and is still conscious — or they just went down over food.

### Do
1. Ask “can you cough?” If they can cough hard, let them cough. Stay close.
2. If they cannot cough or speak: stand behind, fist above the navel, inward and up. Repeat until it moves or they go down.
3. If you cannot reach around them, use the same idea against a solid back of a chair, or chest thrusts if that is what you can do.
4. If they go unresponsive: down to the ground, start chest compressions, look in the mouth when you can, hook out only what you see.
5. Do not finger-sweep blind.
6. When they breathe again, sit them up, keep them, get to care. The throat can swell later.
7. Watch the rest of the meal. One panicked group feed is how this repeats.

### Cautions
- Slapping a person who is still coughing hard can wedge it.
- Kids and pregnant people change the hand placement. Lower on a small child, chest for late pregnancy if you know that skill. Get to care either way.
- Food in the dark, walking, and laughing with a mouthful is the usual field setup. Slow down.
summary: If they can cough, let them. If silent, abdominal thrusts. If they drop, compressions and visible hook only.

title: They will not wake up.
body:
### Situation
They will not answer and will not open eyes to a shout and a rub. You are now keeping air in and getting help.

### Do
1. Scene safe. Shout their name. Tap. If nothing, call it: unresponsive.
2. Airway: head tilt, look in the mouth, no blind sweep.
3. Look, listen, feel for breathing. If they are breathing, recovery position if no trauma story, keep warm, watch the airway.
4. If they are not breathing: chest compressions on the sternum, hard and fast, let the chest come back. Switch rescuers before the first one dies too.
5. Send someone for signal and care. One person stays.
6. If this was a fall from height, protect the neck as you can while you still open the airway. Airway wins.
7. Write the time they went down and what you did.

### Cautions
- Do not declare a cause. Treat breathing and bleeding.
- A “let them sleep it off” on a cold slope is how hypothermia and airway joins the story.
- You are not a hospital. Compressions and an open airway plus a messenger is the field package.
summary: Open the airway. If they breathe, protect it and warm them. If they do not, compressions and a messenger.

title: Pale, faint, fading. Lie them down.
body:
### Situation
They are pale, sweaty, faint, thirsty, or fading after bleeding, heat, or a scare. You need blood to the brain and warmth.

### Do
1. Lie them down on a pad. Scene still safe.
2. If there is no breathing problem and no injury that forbids it, raise the legs 8–12 in (20–30 cm).
3. Keep them warm. Wind off. Ground insulation.
4. Stop the bleeding if that is the cause. Position is not a substitute for pressure.
5. Sips only if they are awake and can swallow. No gulps. No alcohol.
6. Talk to them. Watch breathing. Be ready to roll them if they vomit.
7. This is a get-to-care problem if it followed blood loss, a fall, or they do not come back after a short faint.

### Cautions
- Legs-up is wrong if it wrecks a broken pelvis, a breathing problem, or a head injury you are protecting. Then just keep them flat and warm.
- Slapping and shouting “walk it off” after a faint on a ridge is how they faint off the ridge.
- Do not pack five jackets on a heat casualty and call it shock care. See the heat card.
summary: Flat on a pad, legs up if the injuries allow, warm, stop bleeding, sips only if they can swallow.

title: Tell someone the plan before you need this.
body:
### Situation
You are still at the trailhead or you are now overdue. Rescue starts with a person who knows where to look.

### Do
1. Before you walk: name, route, trailhead, vehicle, turnaround time, and who will call if you miss it.
2. In the field: one page in the lid of the pack with those same facts plus last sure point and the time.
3. If you have a satellite messenger or phone Emergency SOS, know which button is real and which is a menu. Test it at home, not on the ridge.
4. When you are in trouble: message once with location, problem, and whether you can move. Then save battery.
5. Stay near the thing that can be seen unless the site will kill you.
6. Assign a signal person so not everyone is blowing the whistle.
7. If you self-rescue, cancel the overdue plan so a team does not walk into a night search for nothing.

### Cautions
- A vague “hiking the Front Range” is not a route.
- Do not send ten fragments from a dying phone. One complete note.
- **Rockies**: cell coverage dies in canyons a few miles from Denver suburbs. A messenger or an overdue person at home is the plan, not a bar of signal you remember from the parking lot.
summary: Leave a route and time. In trouble, one complete message, then stay by the visible site.

title: Make a mark a pilot can read.
body:
### Situation
You hear or hope for an aircraft. They cannot see a person in beetle-kill. They can see a pattern.

### Do
1. Pick the biggest open floor: rock slab, meadow, talus, frozen lake. Not a hole in the trees.
2. Contrast: bright tarp, space blanket, logs on snow, dark boughs on light granite.
3. Big. Think 8–10 ft (2.5–3 m) strokes at minimum. An X means you need help. A big V or arrow can show a direction if you must move.
4. Anchor it. Wind will steal the panel the moment you look away.
5. When they approach, stay by the mark. Follow any instructions they give. Do not run under a rotor.
6. If they rock their wings or circle, they likely saw you. Keep the mark out.
7. At night switch to light and fire signals. The panel still helps at dawn.

### Cautions
- A tiny handkerchief on a pack is a rumor, not a signal.
- Do not lie down on the only landing spot.
- **Rockies**: a helicopter may not be able to land at 12,000 ft (3660 m) in wind. A hover and a long line is still a see-you. Stay put.
summary: Open ground, huge contrast pattern, anchored. Stay by it when they come.

title: Flash the glass at the thing that can help.
body:
### Situation
The sun is out and there is an aircraft, a ridge with people, or a road far below. A flash carries farther than a shout.

### Do
1. Use a real signal mirror if you have one. A phone screen or a polished bottle can stand in.
2. Sight: flash on your hand, then walk the flash onto the target. Or use the sighting hole if the mirror has one.
3. Aim at the aircraft, the road cut, the lake with boats — not at the empty sky as a hobby.
4. Three short flashes, pause, repeat. Pattern beats random sparkle.
5. If the target is moving, lead it a little and keep bursting.
6. Practice once at camp so the first real try is not your first try.
7. Pair with a whistle and a panel. Clouds will cut the mirror without warning.

### Cautions
- Do not flash drivers on a highway at eye level as a game. You want help, not a wreck.
- A cracked mirror still works. A dirty one does not. Wipe it.
- **Rockies**: you can flash a Front Range ridge from a long way on a dry day. You can also miss because the aircraft is in the next canyon. Sweep, then hold.
summary: Put the flash on your hand, walk it onto the target, burst in threes. Pair with sound.

title: Three blasts. Then listen.
body:
### Situation
People or a search line might be in earshot. Your throat will die. A whistle will not.

### Do
1. Three short blasts, then a long listen. Repeat. Three is the pattern.
2. Face the likely approach: trail, drainage, ridge. Cup your hands around it if you have no pea whistle.
3. At night or in wind, blast from the open site, not from inside a spruce cave.
4. Answer any shout or blast with the same three. Do not invent a code nobody else knows.
5. Keep the whistle on a zip or around the neck. A whistle in the lid of a lost pack is a joke.
6. Kids and quiet people get a whistle too. The person who wandered is the one who needs it.
7. Combine with a bright panel. Sound finds the grid; color finishes it.

### Cautions
- Continuous panicked blasting eats the group’s nerves and the searchers’ bearings. Pattern, then listen.
- A metal pea whistle freezes to lips in hard cold. Plastic, or warm it.
- Shouting “help” into wind on a 14er is mostly for you. Use the whistle.
summary: Three blasts, listen, face the approach. Whistle on the body, not in the pack.

title: A short white column in the open.
body:
### Situation
Daylight, a chance of aircraft or a far ridgeline, and you already have a controlled fire. Smoke is the daytime flag.

### Do
1. Build or keep a hot coal bed in the open. See fire-signal.
2. Pulse: drop green boughs or damp grass for a thick burst, then let it breathe so the fire lives.
3. Time the pulse when you hear an engine or when the inversion might lift.
4. Do not make a smoke house in the timber. The column has to clear the trees.
5. Have water ready. A signal fire is still a fire.
6. If a plane rocks wings, stop feeding green and stay visible.
7. Night: switch to flame. Smoke is a day tool.

### Cautions
- A smoke column in July beetle-kill with wind is a wildfire request.
- Rubber and plastic smoke can poison the people sitting next to it. Use green vegetation, not trash.
- **Rockies**: morning inversions in Front Range canyons hold smoke at the creek. Move the fire to a bench if you can.
summary: Hot coals in the open, pulse green for a white column, water ready, flame at night instead.

title: Be the thing they can find.
body:
### Situation
You are overdue or you know you are lost. Walking in a new direction every hour draws a scribble, not a point.

### Do
1. Pick a survivable, visible site. Water if you can without losing the site. Color in the open.
2. Stay. Improve shelter, water, and signal. That is the work.
3. If the site will kill you (flood, rockfall, lightning magnet), move once to the nearest safe open ground and stay there.
4. Leave a note if you must move: direction, time, why. Arrow on the ground.
5. Run signals on a schedule so you can also gather wood and melt snow.
6. Keep one person at camp if others must fetch water.
7. At first light, refresh the panel. Do not take a “short look” over the next ridge.

### Cautions
- Moving to “get cell service” without a catching feature is how people walk out of the search box.
- Splitting up so someone can “go for help” creates two problems. Send a pair only on a known trail with a written plan.
- **Rockies**: a person who keeps descending random drainages can drop from alpine to a different county. Stay on the last known bench if it is safe.
summary: Visible survivable site, stay, signal on a clock. Move once only if the site will kill you, and leave a note.

title: The phone is a radio with a short life.
body:
### Situation
You might get a bar, or you have a satellite messenger. The battery is the limiting feature.

### Do
1. Airplane mode when you are not trying. Screen down. Cold kills batteries — sleep with it.
2. One try: pin drop or grid if you have it, short text, Emergency SOS if that is the tool you have.
3. Write the same message on paper. If the phone dies, the paper still briefs the next person.
4. Climb a small, safe rise for a try. Do not cliff-out for a bar.
5. A satellite messenger wants sky, not a spruce cave. Step to a clearing.
6. Spare power only for this and a headlamp. Not for a playlist.
7. If you get through, stay where you said you were unless you said you would move.

### Cautions
- Photo bursts and map apps in the cold will bury the SOS.
- A 911 call that drops is not a full briefing. Text if voice will not hold, then save the rest.
- **Rockies**: you can see downtown Denver and still have no usable signal in a foothill fold. Do not bet the night on one more rise.
summary: Airplane mode, one complete message, sky for a messenger, stay where you said you were.

title: Be a pattern in the dark.
body:
### Situation
Dark, and someone might be looking. Random sparkle is a cabin. A pattern is a person.

### Do
1. Three flashes, pause, three. Headlamp, strobe, or a controlled flame.
2. Hold the light high. Stand when you hear an engine. Sit between tries to save battery.
3. A small bright fire in the open beats a huge fire in a hole.
4. Reflective: space blanket, tape, watch face. Sweep a lamp across it toward the sound.
5. Save a reserve in the headlamp for when they are close. A dead lamp as the helicopter turns in is a fail.
6. Whistle with the flashes so a ground team can home.
7. At first gray light, put the panel back out. Night signals do not replace day shapes.

### Cautions
- Do not start a hillside fire to “be seen.” Control or skip.
- Laser pointers at aircraft are how you become the problem. Use a lamp or mirror, not a laser.
- **Rockies**: valley lights from the Front Range cities can drown a weak lamp. Get to a skyline or use fire plus whistle.
summary: Three flashes and a whistle, fire only if controlled, save lamp battery for the close pass.

title: Stop. Map. Then one move.
body:
### Situation
The picture in your head and the picture in front of you do not match. The next steps will either fix it or bury it.

### Do
1. Stop. Sit. Eat and drink. Adrenaline makes dumb azimuths.
2. Last sure point, time, direction since, distance by time or pacing.
3. Orient the map. Match two or three things you can see: a creek, a peak shape, a road cut.
4. If you cannot make the map match, you are lost. Switch to the lost card. Do not invent a match.
5. One test move: short, reversible, toward a catching feature. Not a new hour-long plan.
6. Write the decision. Dawn-you will not remember the clever theory.
7. Group: one navigator. Arguments happen on the sit, not while four people walk four headings.

### Cautions
- Bending the map to the gut feeling is the sport of the truly lost.
- Phone zoom without a north arrow and a scale is a picture, not a fix.
- **Rockies**: parallel drainages on the Front Range look like siblings. Confirm with a second feature, not just “a creek on the left.”
summary: Sit, last sure point, orient the map to two features, then one reversible test move.

title: The needle is not a suggestion.
body:
### Situation
You need a direction you can walk in timber or fog. The compass is the tool if you actually use it.

### Do
1. Know the declination you set for this map. Front Range is east of true. A wrong setting walks you off the page.
2. Take a bearing to a visible target, then walk to it, then take another. Do not stare at the needle for 400 yd (365 m).
3. In fog: bearing plus pacing plus a catching feature. See those cards.
4. Keep steel knives, speakers, and phone magnets off the housing when you sight.
5. Trust a bearing you took on a known peak more than a guess from the slope of the land.
6. If the needle sticks, tap it. If it still sits wrong, back up from metal and try again.
7. Write the bearing you intend. Groups argue less with a number.

### Cautions
- A cheap compass on a phone case full of magnets is art.
- Walking a bearing through a cliff band because the number said so is not navigation.
- **Rockies**: iron-rich rocks exist. If the needle and the sun disagree hard, believe the sun and the map until you sort it.
summary: Set declination, sight a target, walk to it. Keep steel off the housing. Pair with a catching feature.

title: Put the map on the land.
body:
### Situation
You have a topo and a piece of country. You need to know which square you are in.

### Do
1. Orient the map with the compass or with a known ridge so the shapes match the horizon.
2. Thumb your last sure point. Keep the thumb there.
3. Read contours: close lines are steep, rings are highs or bowls, a V in the lines often points up a drainage.
4. Match three things: “creek on left, road cut behind, peak with a cliff band ahead.”
5. Scale: a fingertip is not a mile. Use the bar. Front Range miles are slow in talus.
6. Fold the map to the area you are in so wind does not turn it into a kite.
7. If the map and the land fight, stop. See nav-stop-think.

### Cautions
- Old maps miss new roads and miss closed roads. Believe the contour more than a dashed line.
- Phone maps that recenter on a bad GPS pin will gaslight you. Lock the position or use paper.
- **Rockies**: 40 ft (12 m) contours hide a cliff that will end a descent. Read the tight bunch before you commit.
summary: Orient, thumb the last sure point, match three features, believe the contours.

title: The sun is a rough clock and a rough west.
body:
### Situation
You need a crude direction and the compass is gone or you do not trust it. The sun still moves.

### Do
1. In the middle of the day the sun is south of you in Colorado. Morning it is east-side, afternoon west-side. That is crude, not a bearing.
2. Stick and shadow: plant a stick, mark the tip, wait 15–20 minutes, mark again. The line from first to second mark runs west to east, first mark toward west.
3. Use that line only to pick a general walk, then confirm with terrain.
4. A watch method is a backup for analog faces. It is crude. Do not walk a cliff on it.
5. Clouds: a bright patch still has a side. If the sky is a bowl of milk, this card is closed. See whiteout.
6. Write down what you decided so you do not reverse it after lunch.
7. Pair with a handrail. Sun-only travel drifts.

### Cautions
- In summer the sun is high and south is a fat zone, not a line.
- A phone compass app plus a sun guess plus hope is three errors.
- **Rockies**: canyon shade can hide the sun until 10:00. Do not call east “north” because the first light hit a west wall.
summary: Sun is south at midday here. Stick-and-shadow gives west-to-east. Confirm with terrain.

title: Find north when the sky is honest.
body:
### Situation
Clear night, you need a direction, and you can see stars. Polaris sits over true north.

### Do
1. Find the Big Dipper. The two stars at the bowl’s outer edge point to Polaris, about five bowl-widths along that line.
2. If the Dipper is in the trees, Cassiopeia’s W sits on the other side of Polaris. Use both when you can.
3. Polaris is not the brightest star. It is the still one. The sky wheels around it.
4. Face it. That is north. Then pick a ground object on that line so you can walk without staring up.
5. Recheck every few minutes in timber. Trees eat the sky.
6. If clouds own the sky, stop using stars. Compass and terrain, or stay put.
7. Teach the second person in the group so a lone neck is not the whole system.

### Cautions
- Bright planets fool tired people. Polaris does not wander far. Planets do.
- Walking while staring up is how you find a hole.
- **Rockies**: Front Range light dome from Denver washes the east and south sky. Look north, give your eyes time, get a ridge if you can.
summary: Dipper pointer stars to Polaris, face it for north, transfer to a ground object, recheck in timber.

title: Read the ground like a map that cannot lie.
body:
### Situation
You need to know where you are from the shape of the land, not from a pin.

### Do
1. Name the big bones: which way does water run, where is the high spine, where is the plains edge.
2. Aspect: north holds snow and spruce, south holds open and dry. Use that as a check.
3. Saddles, cliff bands, and lake benches are fingerprints. Match them to the map.
4. If you are in a drainage, know whether it should be opening toward the plains or tightening toward a wall.
5. Count tributaries as you pass them if the map shows them. That is a position without a GPS.
6. When the vegetation suddenly changes, ask why: fire, beetle-kill, aspect, or a trail you missed.
7. Stop at every obvious feature and confirm. Navigation is a series of checks, not a vibe.

### Cautions
- “Downhill is out” is true until the drainage cliffs or dumps into a slot.
- Parallel ridges on the Front Range will agree with a sloppy story.
- **Rockies**: the plains-to-14er split is sharp. You can see the city and still be hours of bad terrain from a road. Terrain time is not skyline time.
summary: Name water flow, spine, and aspect. Match saddles and cliff bands. Check at every obvious feature.

title: Walk a feature you cannot lose.
body:
### Situation
Timber, dark, or fatigue. You need a line on the land that keeps you honest.

### Do
1. Pick a handrail the map actually has: creek, ridge crest, trail, power line, road, obvious cliff band.
2. Decide which side you will keep it on, and keep it there.
3. Know the catching feature at the end so you do not follow the creek past the turn.
4. If the handrail splits, stop. That is a junction. Map check.
5. In beetle-kill a creek is still a creek even when you cannot walk in it. Stay close, do not pretend you are on a trail.
6. Night: a ridge crest can be a handrail or a lightning wire. Choose with weather.
7. When you leave the handrail, take a bearing and a time. You just went off the rail.

### Cautions
- Game trails feel like handrails and then vanish.
- Following a fence the wrong way is still lost, just linear.
- **Rockies**: irrigation ditches on the foothills edge look like creeks and then go into pipes. Confirm on the map.
summary: Hold one mapped feature on a known side until a planned catching feature. Stop at splits.

title: Count the ground so distance is not a feeling.
body:
### Situation
You are walking a bearing in timber or night and you need to know when to stop.

### Do
