1. Know your pace: double-steps per 100 yd (91 m) on dirt, and a worse number for talus and snow. Count it on a known stretch.
2. Use a bead, pebble, or click on the pack every 100 yd (91 m). Brain-only counts die.
3. Start the count at a known point, not “sometime after the creek.”
4. When the count says you should see the feature, stop. Look. If it is missing, do not add another 300 yd (274 m) of hope.
5. Slope, snow, and deadfall inflate the count. Recalibrate when the ground changes.
6. Pair with a catching feature so a short count still hits a wall, a creek, or a road.
7. Teach a second counter. Two counts that agree are gold.

### Cautions
- GPS distance on a phone with a dying battery is not a reason to skip pacing when you already started a fog leg.
- Running the count while talking and scrambling is how you lose 40 percent.
- **Rockies**: a “mile” of Front Range talus is not a Denver mile. Count, do not clock.
summary: Know double-steps per 100 yards, bead every unit, stop when the count says stop, pair with a catcher.

title: Down a creek is a plan, not a reflex.
body:
### Situation
You want out and downhill has a creek. Sometimes that is the correct handrail. Sometimes it is a slot.

### Do
1. Check the map: does this drainage go to a road, a trail, or a cliff band with a waterfall.
2. If the map shows a gentle opening toward a known road, it can be a handrail. Stay off the wet rocks when you can.
3. If the contour lines pile up, you are walking into a gorge. Climb a side rib and reassess before the waterfall.
4. Unbuckle when you must cross. See the crossing card.
5. Count tributaries so you know which fork you took.
6. Night plus drainage is how people swim. Default to a bench and wait for light.
7. If you chose this as a catching feature, stop when you hit it. Do not “just a little more.”

### Cautions
- “Water flows to people” is false in the high country. Water flows to more water, then maybe a plains town hours later.
- **Rockies**: Front Range creeks cut slots in granite and then hit the hogback. Read the contours. A Denver-view does not mean a walkable creek.
summary: Only descend a drainage the map opens to a road. Contour piles mean gorge. Stop at the catcher.

title: When the world is one color, stop or crawl a bearing.
body:
### Situation
Cloud, snow, or fog has erased the horizon. Depth goes away. Cornices and holes hide.

### Do
1. Stop. If you are on a ridge or a glacier-like snowfield, staying put may be the whole plan.
2. If you must move: compass bearing, short rope or voice contact, pacing, and a catching feature you already chose.
3. Probe the snow in front if you could be near a cornice or a creek hole.
4. Mark the last sure point with a wand, a pack, or a trench so you can reverse.
5. No “short cut” off the bearing because a darker smudge looked like a tree.
6. Sit out a passing cell if you have the gear. Many Front Range whiteouts are a twenty-minute event.
7. When it lifts, reorient from terrain, not from the story you told in the milk.

### Cautions
- Speed in a whiteout is how people walk off the east face.
- Goggles and a hood are navigation gear here. Frozen eyelashes are not.
- **Rockies**: above-treeline 14ers can whiteout in July. If you cannot see the next cairn, you do not have a route.
summary: Default stop. If you move: bearing, spacing, probe, catching feature. No shortcuts toward smudges.

title: Night walking is a special case, not a habit.
body:
### Situation
You still want to move after dark. The trail is real, or you think it is.

### Do
1. Prefer staying. Move only on a trail or handrail you already trusted in daylight.
2. Slow. Short poles. Watch the edge. Night erases holes.
3. One light on the ground, not on faces. Save a spare lamp.
4. Count people at every stop. Night is when the last person vanishes.
5. No creek crossings, no cliff bands, no “this game trail is probably the trail.”
6. If the trail dies, stop and bivy. Do not invent a new one.
7. Dawn is a navigation tool. Use it.

### Cautions
- Headphones and night miles are how you miss the shout.
- Phone light plus a dying battery plus no spare is a trap.
- **Rockies**: timberline trails fade into tundra at night and the cairns become rocks. If you cannot feel the tread, you are off it.
summary: Move at night only on a known trail. Slow, count people, bivy if the tread dies.

title: Aim at a wall you cannot miss.
body:
### Situation
You are walking toward a line on the map — road, trail, creek, ridge — and you need to actually hit it.

### Do
1. Pick a long feature, not a point. A road is a catcher. A cairn is a hope.
2. Aim off: deliberately aim left of the junction so when you hit the road you know to turn right.
3. Know what it will look like: width, vegetation, noise of a highway, smell of a creek.
4. Pace so you know when you should have hit it. If you are over count, stop.
5. When you hit it, stop and confirm. Then turn the way you planned.
6. If you miss: do not wander. Reverse the bearing or pick the next bigger catcher.
7. Tell the group the plan in one sentence: “We aim left of the trail, hit it, turn south.”

### Cautions
- Aiming at a small lake in timber is not a catching feature.
- Crossing the feature without noticing is common at night and in beetle-kill. Look both ways.
- **Rockies**: the Peak-to-Peak highway and the plains roads are huge catchers. A social trail on a 14er is not.
summary: Aim off at a long mapped line, pace the leg, stop when you hit it, turn the planned way.

title: Be off the high point before the cell.
body:
### Situation
Summer in the Front Range. Blue morning, building towers after midday. You are still going up.

### Do
1. Start early. Turnaround time is a clock, not a feeling. Many teams are descending by noon.
2. Watch the west and the Divide. Towers with dark bases are the problem, not the pretty anvil after it already hit.
3. If you hear thunder, you are in range. Off the summit, off the ridge, toward treeline.
4. Do not wait for rain. Lightning leads.
5. A hole of blue is not a forecast. Cells train. The next one can be worse.
6. Plan the bail: the ridge you will leave, the valley you will accept.
7. After a soak, hypothermia is the second act. Dry layer, food, move.

### Cautions
- “We are already this close” is the line on a lot of 14er reports.
- Metal poles on a shoulder in a cell are extra tall.
- **Rockies**: July–August monsoon pattern plus Front Range heating. Plains can still be sunny while the 14er is a drum. Believe the mountain sky.
summary: Early start, noon turnaround, off the ridge at thunder. Blue holes are not a forecast.

title: Get off the spark plug. Wait it out.
body:
### Situation
Thunder, hair lifting, buzzing hardware, or a cell over the ridge. You need terrain, not a lucky hat.

### Do
1. Down. Off peaks, off saddles, off isolated trees, off fence lines and railings.
2. A stand of similar-height trees on a lower slope beats one tall pine and beats a cave mouth.
3. Crouch or sit on a pad, feet together, pack a little away, if you are caught in the open.
4. Spread the group 15–20 yd (14–18 m) so one strike is not everyone.
5. Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before you own the ridge again. More if the next cell is visible.
6. If someone is hit: scene safe, then unresponsive and burn cards. They may need breathing help.
7. Count seconds from flash to bang to know if it is closing. Closer means you stayed too high.

### Cautions
- A tent on a knoll is a wet flag, not a Faraday gift.
- Lying flat makes you a bigger ground path. Crouch or sit.
- **Rockies**: 14er summits in summer are magnets. If you are still on the boulder field at 13:00, you already lost the timing.
summary: Off the high point, uniform timber, sit on a pad, spread the group, wait after the last thunder.

title: Wind turns a cool day into a cold problem.
body:
### Situation
The number on the forecast was tolerable. The ridge is not. Wind is stripping heat and footing.

### Do
1. Layer: wind shell on, dry base, hat, mittens. Skin is the leak.
2. Off the ridgeline. Even a small drop into timber changes the number.
3. Short the exposure. Goggles or glasses, hood up, talk less with an open mouth.
4. Watch for clumsy zippers and quiet people. Wind plus wet is hypothermia weather at 40 F (4 C).
5. Stove and tarp need extra guys. See wind shelter.
6. If walking into a 40 mph (64 km/h) headwind is the plan, it is not a plan. Turn or wait.
7. After the blow, reassess fingers and faces for pale numb parts.

### Cautions
- A cotton hoodie is a sail and a sponge.
- Estimates of wind from the parking lot do not cover the saddle.
- **Rockies**: Front Range west winds and east-slope chinooks both hammer. A Denver calm can sit under a roaring foothill.
summary: Wind shell, off the ridge, watch for clumsy quiet people. 40 F plus wind is hypothermia weather.

title: Snow is weather, water, and terrain.
body:
### Situation
Snow is falling, falling later than you packed for, or still sitting on the route in June.

### Do
1. Layers and dry gloves before you are wet. Once mittens are soaked the day is shorter.
2. Track: follow a known line. New snow hides talus holes and the summer trail.
3. If it is a whiteout, that card owns the next move.
4. Snow on the route in June: north aspects and high gullies hold it. Early steps, kick solid, one at a time. Ice in the afternoon is worse than morning crust.
5. Melt for water with a starter puddle. Do not eat it as your ration.
6. Mark your return if you are breaking trail. The track will fill.
7. Bivy gear comes up in the pack when the forecast had a “slight chance.” Slight chances stick on 13ers.

### Cautions
- Postholing to the hip in a creek you cannot see is a breaking-leg activity.
- Wet snow plus a slope is avalanche country even in spring. See that card.
- **Rockies**: June snow above treeline is normal. So is a Denver 70 F (21 C) at the same hour. Pack for the route, not the city.
summary: Dry layers, known line, treat lingering June snow as terrain. Pack for the route, not Denver.

title: A distant cell can fill this creek.
body:
### Situation
You are in a narrow drainage, a wash, or a canyon, and a storm is on the basin above you — even if it is not raining on your hat.

### Do
1. Get out of the slot. Sidehill or the mouth, not a “better camp” on the gravel bar.
2. Do not wait to see the wall of water. Noise, sticks in the flow, and a sudden muddy pulse are late signs.
3. Crossings you liked this morning can be a different river now. See the crossing card. If in doubt, do not.
4. Park the night site above the obvious high-water rack of sticks.
5. After it drops, the bed will be greased and undercut. Probe.
6. If someone is swept: do not become the second swimmer. Point, follow on bank, throw a line if you have a real one.
7. Thunder on the plains edge with a blue sky over your foothill canyon still counts.

### Cautions
- A 2 ft (0.6 m) pulse in a slot is not a movie. It moves boulders.
- Cars at a low water crossing are not a shelter.
- **Rockies**: Front Range canyons have done this. The cell can be over the Palmer Divide while you are in a sunny hogback wash.
summary: Out of the slot when a cell hits the basin. Camp above the stick rack. Distant rain still counts.

title: Read the sky before it sits on you.
body:
### Situation
You need a next-hour guess and there is no new forecast. The sky is the instrument.

### Do
1. Towers with dark flat bases: convection. Count the time to your ridgeline.
2. Anvil spreading over you: the cell is mature. You are late.
3. A sheet of high thin cloud thickening from the west: a longer system, not a 20-minute shower. Plan a real shelter.
4. Fast low scud in the trees: the ceiling is coming down. Navigation just got worse.
5. Lenticular caps on peaks: wind aloft is strong. The saddle will be worse.
6. Watch the same sector for 15 minutes. One photo is not a trend.
7. Match the sky to a bail route, not to a wish.

### Cautions
- App radar from an hour ago in the parking lot is not the cell in front of you.
- A red sunset is pretty and not a permit for a night ridge.
- **Rockies**: you can watch a cell dump on the Divide while the plains stay gold. Your route is the Divide side.
summary: Towers mean convection, anvils mean late, thickening sheet means a system. Watch a sector for 15 minutes.

title: The temperature will fall when the sun does.
body:
### Situation
A warm afternoon and a clear sky. You will sleep colder than the hike felt.

### Do
1. Put the dry layer on before you feel heroic at dusk. The drop is fast at 10,000 ft (3050 m).
2. Expect 15–25 F (8–14 C) down from the afternoon high on a clear, still night. Wind can make it feel worse. Clouds hold some heat.
3. Meadows and creek bottoms collect the cold. Sleep on a slight rise.
4. Bottles in the bag. Filters emptied. Stove fuel works worse when it is a block.
5. Eat. The night furnace is food.
6. A 03:00 wake-up shivering is a fix-now: pad, hat, calories, not stoicism.
7. Dawn travel can be the coldest hour. Gloves on before the hands die.

### Cautions
- A T-shirt sunset photo is not a clothing plan.
- Wet feet that were fine at 16:00 are a problem at 02:00.
- **Rockies**: Denver 85 F (29 C) to a 38 F (3 C) night in the Indian Peaks is a normal summer split. Pack the puffy.
summary: Dress before dusk. Clear nights drop hard. Sleep off the frost hollow. Eat. Fix shivering at 03:00.

title: Snow on a slope is a system, not scenery.
body:
### Situation
You are on or under a steep snow slope, a gully, or a cornice, any month it holds snow. You do not need a forecast product to respect the shape.

### Do
1. Ask: is this slope steep enough to slide, is the snow a slab or a wet heap, and what sits below you.
2. Avoid: convex rolls, loaded gullies, terrain traps (gully, creek, trees that will bury you), walking under cornices.
3. One at a time in the suspect band. The rest wait out of the runout.
4. If you have no beacon, probe, or training, the field decision is to not be on that slope. Detour.
5. Wet afternoon slides on spring snow are a clock. Be off it before it turns to slush.
6. A whoomph, shooting cracks, or recent debris is a stop. Not a “quick look.”
7. If it runs: eyes on the person, then a planned search you actually know. Untrained heroics in debris make more bodies.

### Cautions
- A summer 14er couloir can slide. Calendar is not a control.
- Trees are not a shelter if they are in the runout.
- **Rockies**: north and east faces hold snow and wind slab. The sunny parking lot in May does not clear the gully.
summary: Steep snow plus a trap below is a no without training. One at a time, off it when it whoomphs.

title: Hunger is not the first problem.
body:
### Situation
The pack is light on food and the mind wants to forage. You have hours to days, not a famine.

### Do
1. Rank: bleeding, shelter, water, signal, then calories. A missed lunch does not change that order.
2. Eat what you packed, on a schedule, especially in cold. The furnace needs it.
3. Do not spend the dry, warm hours hunting mystery plants. That is how people get a gut problem and a lost afternoon.
4. If you have a real ration, stretch it with rest, not with experiments.
5. Foraging is not a plan unless you already know the plant from before this trip. Unknown stays unknown.
6. Signal and travel burn less than a day of bushcraft theater.
7. Write a food count so the group does not “share” into nothing on night one.

### Cautions
- A hungry brain makes plant mistakes. That is a medical problem you cannot unsay.
- Do not trade water volume for a long forage loop.
- **Rockies**: you will not starve on a two-night Front Range overdue. You can die of exposure in the same window. Eat the bar, build the roof.
summary: Calories rank after bleed, shelter, water, and signal. Eat what you packed. Unknown plants stay out of the mouth.

title: If you did not already know it, it is Unknown.
body:
### Situation
A plant looks familiar, or a person in the group “thinks it is fine.” You are not running an ID clinic.

### Do
1. Default: Unknown. Confidence does not rise because you are hungry or the leaf is pretty.
2. Do not put Unknown in your mouth. A “tiny taste test” is still a dose.
3. Record it if you want: photo, notes, place. Identification happens later with references you trust, not on a dare.
4. Lookalikes exist for the famous ones. Hemlock-family plants share neighborhoods with plants people brag about.
5. Kids and dogs get the same rule. Especially berries and umbels.
6. If someone already swallowed Unknown, see the wound/gut logic: do not induce drama, get to care, bring a sample if you can.
7. Spend the time on water and shelter instead.

### Cautions
- Phone ID apps in airplane mode are not magic, and live ID apps are still a guess. Unknown stays Unknown.
- “Wildlife eats it” is not a human rule.
- Cooking does not turn Unknown into Known.
summary: Unknown is the field ID. No taste tests. Record if you want, then go back to water and shelter.

title: If you log a plant, log it like a witness.
body:
### Situation
You want a note for later. That is fine. It is not a permit to eat.

### Do
1. Habitat: creek, dry slope, aspen, alpine, roadside, shade or sun.
2. Height, stem: round or ridged, hairy or smooth, hollow or pith, color, whether it branches.
3. Leaf: opposite or alternate, simple or divided, edge, smell when crushed (then wash your hands).
4. Flower or berry: color, cluster shape, number of parts if you can count them without destroying the only sample.
5. Lookalikes you already worry about. Write “umbel, white, purple blotch?” rather than a name.
6. One sample in a bag if someone is already sick. Do not pick a bouquet.
7. Label Unknown. Never label a field guess as a fact on the bag.

### Cautions
- Crushing a plant and then rubbing your eye is a separate incident.
- A single photo of a leaf with no stem or habitat is how people misname later.
- Do not trespass into a patch of ivy or hemlock-family plants to get a “better shot.”
summary: Log habitat, stem, leaf, flower. Label Unknown. A note is not an ID and not a meal.

title: Mushrooms stay Unknown.
body:
### Situation
Someone wants to pick a mushroom because it looks like a grocery store shape, or because a deer nipped it.

### Do
1. Treat every mushroom as Unknown. That is the whole field rule.
2. Do not cook, dry, or “just try a bite.” Traits do not become a verdict in this pack.
3. If you log one: cap, gills or pores, stem ring, base in the ground, color of the print if it drops, habitat. Still Unknown.
4. Keep kids from pocketing them as toys that later go in the mouth.
5. If someone already ate one: sample in a bag, time, get to care. Do not wait for a “mild” story to finish.
6. Spend the hour on known calories in the pack.
7. Kick nothing into the cook pot “for flavor.”

### Cautions
- Color, bugs in the cap, and silver-spoon myths are folklore.
- Boiling does not make Unknown into Known.
- **Rockies**: aspen and spruce duff throw a lot of fruiting bodies after monsoon rain. Pretty is not a category that helps you.
summary: Every mushroom is Unknown. Log if you must, never taste. If swallowed, sample and get to care.

title: Berries: traits only. Unknown unless you already knew.
body:
### Situation
A bush has fruit and someone is hungry. Color is not a sorting hat.

### Do
1. Stay on Unknown unless this exact plant was already known to you before the trip.
2. Note traits: cluster or single, crown or no crown, color, thorns, leaf shape, whether the plant is a vine, shrub, or ground cover.
3. White and umbel-like clusters on herb stems are a do-not-mouth zone. See hemlock-family.
4. Red is not a yes. Baneberry-type clusters exist in wet woods. You will not settle that debate here.
5. Birds eating a berry is not a human rule.
6. If someone already ate Unknown fruit: sample, time, get to care if they feel wrong or if the amount was more than a nibble.
7. Hands off the mouth until you wash. Berry juice in a cut is still a plant on a wound.

### Cautions
- “All blue berries are fine” is false and not a field rule in this pack.
- Do not use taste as ID. Taste is a dose.
- **Rockies**: chokecherry-looking shrubs and other fruiting bushes share drainages with plants you do not want in your mouth. Traits, then walk away unless you already knew it.
summary: Berry color is not a verdict. White umbels are a do-not-mouth zone. Unknown stays out.

title: White umbels. Treat as avoid.
body:
### Situation
A parsley-shaped plant with a white umbrella of flowers, often in wet ground or ditches. You need traits and distance, not a name you are sure of.

### Do
1. Traits to log: tall hollow stem, purple blotches on some stems, ferny divided leaves, white umbrella clusters, musty smell on some, wet ditch or meadow habitat.
2. Treat the whole lookalike group as avoid. Do not put any part in your mouth. Unknown.
3. Do not make a straw from the hollow stem. Do not use the leaves as a garnish.
4. Wash the knife if you cut one by mistake. Wash hands before food or eyes.
5. Kids pick umbels because they look like toys. Watch them in ditches.
6. If someone chewed it: sample in a bag, get to care. Do not wait it out on the ridge.
7. Other plants share the neighborhood. That does not make this one a meal.

### Cautions
- Root smell and “it looks like carrot” have killed people who were sure.
- Crushing and sniffing then touching your mouth is a dose.
- **Rockies**: wet Front Range ditches and montane creeks grow this look. It is not only a coastal story.
summary: White parsley umbels: log traits, avoid, Unknown. No stems as straws. Sample and get to care if chewed.

title: Pines: needles in bundles, pitch, cones.
body:
### Situation
You need to recognize a pine from spruce and fir for fire, pitch, and notes. This is not a food verdict.

### Do
1. Needles in bundles (fascicles) of two, three, or five. Spruce and fir sit needles one-by-one.
2. Ponderosa on the Front Range: long needles, often three, puzzle-bark on older trunks, vanilla-or-butterscotch bark smell on warm days.
3. Lodgepole: shorter two-needle bundles, skinny, often in beetle-kill stands.
4. Cones and pitch pockets. Resin is a fire note, not a candy note.
5. Dead lower twigs from pines are a tinder source. Live limbs are a poor trade for the tree and for your knife.
6. If you log it, say bundle count and habitat, not a grocery use.
7. Unknown remains if you cannot see the bundles. Do not guess from a distance of 100 yd (90 m).

### Cautions
- Yew-like shrubs and other evergreens are not “a kind of pine.” If it is not in bundles, do not file it as pine.
- Pitch on a wound is sticky, not a clinic dressing you chose from a manual.
- **Rockies**: beetle-kill lodgepole is tinder-dry and a widow-maker. See deadfall. This card is ID traits, not a permit to linger under snags.
summary: Pines have bundled needles. Count the bundle, note bark and habitat. No food verdict.

title: Cattail: sausage spike, wet feet, sword leaves.
body:
### Situation
A wet margin with a brown sausage-shaped spike and long strap leaves. You are logging traits, not making a meal.

### Do
1. Habitat: still or slow water, marsh, pond edge, ditch that holds water.
2. Leaves: tall, flat, strap-like, in a clump from the base.
3. Flower spike: dense brown cylinder on a stalk. Fluff later in the season.
4. Look around for lookalikes with triangular stems or different heads. If you are not sure, Unknown.
5. Standing water that grows cattail is often dirty water. Do not assume the pond is a clean bottle. Treat it.
6. Do not chew any part because a book you remember said something. This pack does not give that verdict.
7. Record and move. The wetland is also a mosquito and tick office.

### Cautions
- Iris-type leaves share wet ground and are a reason to stay on Unknown if you cannot see the spike.
- **Rockies**: cattail shows on plains-edge ponds and foothill ditches more than on 14er tarns. The pretty high lake is a different plant community.
summary: Marsh, strap leaves, brown sausage spike. Unknown for the mouth. Pond water still gets treated.

title: Oak: lobed leaves, acorns, foothill brush.
body:
### Situation
Foothill slopes with lobed leaves and hard fruit in a cap. Good for place-finding. Not a food call.

### Do
1. Leaves: lobes, sometimes spiny on Gambel-type scrub oak. Alternate on the stem.
2. Fruit: acorn in a cap. That trait family is the tell when leaves are confusing.
3. Habitat on the Front Range: foothill belts, often in thickets that hide ticks and ankles.
4. Thickets are travel terrain. Look for a game hole or a ridge walk rather than swimming the brush.
5. Dead oak is hard on knives and makes poor flexible cordage. Plan the tool.
6. Log it as oak-type if you see acorns. If you do not, it can still be Unknown.
7. Do not process acorns as a field project. This pack has no food verdict on them.

### Cautions
- Leaf galls and odd shapes still sit on oak. They are not a different permission.
- **Rockies**: Gambel oak on the Front Range foothills is a tick and lion-country thicket in spring. Pants in socks. See those cards.
summary: Lobed leaves plus acorns in a cap, foothill thickets. Travel around them. No food verdict.

title: Nettle-type: opposite leaves, sting, wet edge.
body:
### Situation
A plant along a creek or ditch that stings when you brush it. You want traits and a way not to repeat that.

### Do
1. Traits: opposite leaves, toothed, often heartish, tiny hairs on stem and leaf that sting. Wet or disturbed ground.
2. If it stung: do not rub dirt into it. Tape or a clean scrape of the hairs can help some people. Then leave it alone.
3. Long pants and a look before you drop a knee in the green at the water scoop.
4. Do not put it in the pot because you have a memory of a cooked dish. Unknown unless you already knew this patch from before, and this pack still offers no food line.
5. Lookalikes without the sting exist. Sting is a trait, not a prize.
6. Wash hands before you touch eyes or a wound.
7. Record and step around. The water source is still the job.

### Cautions
- A sting is not an excuse to dump untreated creek water on your face.
- Some people react more. If breathing changes, that is a get-to-care problem.
- **Rockies**: montane creek edges and valley bottoms. Less of a 14er-summit plant. You will meet it on the hike out.
summary: Opposite toothed leaves, stinging hairs, wet ground. Step around. No pot. Wash before eyes.

title: Three leaflets. Do not be a hero.
body:
### Situation
A vine or low plant with leaflets in threes, often shiny, sometimes with pale berries. You need not to wear the oil.

### Do
1. Leaflet count of three is the field flag. Alternate on the stem. Can be a ground cover or a climber.
2. Do not touch, burn, or use the stems as a toasting stick. Smoke carries the oil.
3. If you brushed it: wash skin with soap if you have it, or rinse, as soon as you can. Then wash the tools and the dog.
4. Clothes can re-dose you tomorrow. Bag them.
5. A rash later is a comfort and care problem. Do not scrape it open in a creek.
6. If the face or breathing is involved, get to care.
7. Teach the group the leaflet count before you enter the oak-ivy mix on the foothills.

### Cautions
- “Leaves of three” is a flag, not a full botanical key. If you are unsure, treat it as avoid.
- Scratching with dirt under the nails spreads it.
- **Rockies**: poison ivy shows on Front Range foothills and drainages. It is not a 14er-summit plant. You meet it on the way down, in shorts, in June.
summary: Three leaflets: do not touch or burn. Wash skin and tools. Face or breathing means get to care.

title: Eat the pack on a clock.
body:
### Situation
You have a known amount of food and an unknown number of hours. The pack is the plan.

### Do
1. Count meals and bars. Count people. Count nights you might actually sit.
2. Eat a little on a clock, especially in cold and at altitude. Skipping all day and then gorging at dark is a gut bomb.
3. Keep one emergency bar per person sealed until the real delay.
4. Water with the calories. Dry food without water is a brick.
5. Share from a plan, not from whoever is loud. Write it.
6. Do not cook a fancy one-pot if fuel is the boil-water fuel.
7. If food is gone, rest more, signal, and stop foraging theater. See food-not-first.

### Cautions
- Caffeine and nicotine on an empty stomach at 12,000 ft (3660 m) make drama.
- Open tuna in a bear-country night is a different problem. See food hang.
- **Rockies**: you burn more in wind and dry air than a Denver desk day. The “one extra bar” is the trip.
summary: Count it, eat on a clock with water, keep an emergency bar, do not spend boil fuel on a feast.

title: Black bear country. Make it boring.
body:
### Situation
You are in Front Range forests and foothills. Black bears live here. Surprise at a carcass or a cook site is the usual fail.

### Do
1. Make noise on blind corners and in loud creeks. Give them a door out.
2. If you see one: stop, talk low, do not run, do not kneel. Back away with your group tight.
3. If it comes in: hold ground, get big, use bear spray if you carry it and the bear is in range of the label. Aim low.
4. A bear on a food bag is a food problem. Let the bag go if that ends it.
5. Cook and sleep apart. Hang or canister. See food-hang.
6. A bear standing up is often trying to smell you, not starting a fight. Still give it the trail.
7. If it makes contact, fight. This is black bear range, not a play-dead lecture for a different species.

### Cautions
- Running downhill is prey language and you will lose.
- A cub is not cute. The other bear is the problem.
- **Rockies**: Front Range is black bear country. Grizzly range is not the Denver-adjacent default. Do not import a different region’s script without cause.
summary: Noise on corners, do not run, back away, fight if a black bear makes contact. Cook away from sleep.

title: Give a moose more room than you think.
body:
### Situation
A large dark animal in willows, a pond, or a winter park. Ears back, hackles, or a walk toward you. Moose are not cattle.

### Do
1. Distance. If you are close enough to need a photo zoom, you are close enough to be in range.
2. Do not block the gap between a cow and a calf, or between the moose and the water.
3. If it walks in, put a tree between you and it and keep moving off the line.
4. Dogs off. A dog that barks a moose and then runs to you has just handed you the problem.
5. In winter, they are on the energy budget. Give more space, not less.
6. If it charges: tree, pack up, get off the trail to the side. Do not turn your back and sprint in a straight line if you can break the line of sight.
7. After a close one, sit. The next mistake is rushing a creek crossing on adrenaline.

### Cautions
- A moose in the trail does not yield because you have a permit.
- Cars and moose at dusk on Front Range roads are a separate wreck. Slow.
- **Rockies**: Colorado moose are real in north-central parks and willow drainages, not a cartoon from somewhere else.
summary: Huge space, do not split cow and calf, dogs off. Tree and off-line if it walks in.

title: Cougar: see it, hold the line, do not run.
body:
### Situation
A long-tailed cat, a stalk, or a scream in the foothills at dusk. You want to look like a person, not a deer.

### Do
1. Face it. Stand. Pick up kids. Do not run. Do not turn your back.
2. Get big. Talk. Throw if it comes in. Fight if it hits.
3. Group up. A line of people is uglier than a lone jogger.
4. Give it a way out. Do not corner it in a boulder cave.
5. At dawn and dusk on the hogback, look up behind and to the sides, not just at your shoes.
6. Keep dogs close. A dog in the brush can start a story you then inherit.
7. If it follows at a distance, hold the face-on walk toward people, cars, or an open site. Do not jog.

### Cautions
- Crouching to pick a rock is prey-shaped. Step to the rock, stay tall.
- Playing dead is the wrong script for a cat.
- **Rockies**: lions live on the Front Range foothills and into the mountains. Deer are the pantry. You are crossing the pantry.
summary: Face it, stand tall, pick up kids, do not run. Fight if it hits. Give it an exit.

title: Hands and feet where you can see them.
body:
### Situation
Sunny rocks, hogback, and foothill grass. A rattle, a coil, or a surprise at a handhold.

### Do
1. Look before the hand goes onto a ledge or a log. Step on, not over, logs when you can.
2. If you hear it: stop, find it, step back. Give it the trail.
3. Do not kill it for sport. A second bite is a common trophy tax.
4. Night: lamp the trail. They sit on warm dirt.
5. Headphones off in rattlesnake season on the hogback. You want that sound.
6. If a bite happens, see the snake bite card. You are done with the hike as a hike.
7. Teach the group the sound once so the first time is not a panic sprint off a ledge.

### Cautions
- A strike range is longer than a tired brain thinks. More than a body length of space.
- Dead snakes still bite on reflex.
- **Rockies**: prairie rattlesnakes on the Front Range foothills and plains edge, not the 14er summit. Watch below roughly 8,000 ft (2440 m), especially May–September.
summary: Eyes before hands, stop at the rattle, give the trail. Night lamp. Bite means the snake-bite card.

title: Ticks: pants in socks, night check.
body:
### Situation
Brush, oak, grass, and a warm Front Range spring. Ticks work the edges of trails.

### Do
1. Pants into socks. Light-colored if you have them. Stay on the tread when the grass leans in.
2. Night skin check: belt, scalp, behind knees, armpits, socks, waistband. Partner check the back.
3. Pull what you find. See the tick first-aid card.
4. Pack the sleeping bag closed during the day so you do not wear them to bed.
5. Dogs get a check too. They are tick ferries.
6. After a sit in leaf litter, do a quick once-over before you walk.
7. A rash or fever days later is a care problem, not a trail diagnosis.

### Cautions
- Permethrin stories and folk oil do not replace the night check.
- Crushing ticks over the bite site is a bad finish.
- **Rockies**: foothill spring is the season. Alpine is not a free pass on the descent through oak.
summary: Socks over pants, night skin check, pull with tweezers. Rash or fever later means get to care.

title: Sleep away from the smell.
body:
### Situation
You have food, toothpaste, and a night site in animal country. The bag and the bed cannot share a vestibule.

### Do
1. Cook, eat, and brush 50–100 yd (45–90 m) from the sleep site if the terrain allows. Downwind of sleep if you can read it.
2. All smellables in the canister, the hang, or the locked box the site requires. That includes trash and the day’s tuna pouch.
3. Hang: a limb that holds the bag off the trunk and off the ground. If you cannot hang it right, canister or sleep farther and accept a worse night.
4. Do not cook in the tent. Ever. Sparks and smell.
5. If a bear gets the bag, let it. Then move camp. Do not fight a bear for granola.
6. Dawn: check the kitchen before you send a sleepy person into it.
7. Stock the night kit (lamp, layers, water) in the tent so you are not visiting the hang at 02:00.

### Cautions
- A “maybe hang” on a 6 ft (1.8 m) aspen is a piñata.
- Mint, soap, and empty food bags still count.
- **Rockies**: black bears work Front Range trailheads and popular lakes. A clean camp is not optional because you only came up from Denver for the night.
summary: Cook away from sleep, all smellables in hang or canister, never cook in the tent, let the bag go.

title: Elk: space in the rut, space with calves.
body:
### Situation
A herd in a meadow or timber, a September bugle, or a cow that does not yield the trail.

### Do
1. Glass from far. If they stand up and stare, you are already in their number.
2. Do not walk through the middle of a bedded herd to “hold the trail.”
3. Calves: if you see one alone, you are in the wrong place. Back out.
4. Rut: bulls are busy and stupid. Extra space. A tree is a tool.
5. Dogs off. Same story as moose.
6. Night travel through a dark meadow is how you end up in the middle. Skirt or wait.
7. If one charges, off the line, pack up, tree. Do not turn it into a photo.

### Cautions
- A quiet herd at 40 yd (37 m) is not tame.
- Winter range is their food. Pushing them costs them energy and can make them dangerous.
- **Rockies**: elk are the default big deer of the Front Range parks. You will meet them. They get the meadow.
summary: Do not bisect a herd. Extra space in the rut and with calves. Dogs off. Skirt night meadows.

title: The knife is a cutter, not a pry bar.
body:
### Situation
You need to process wood, cord, food, or a bandage. The blade will do that if it stays a blade.

### Do
1. Cut away from the body. The other hand is behind the spine or out of the lane.
2. Sit to carve. Lock the wrists on the knees. A chest-level cut on a log in the lap is a femoral story.
3. Baton through the back of the blade on wood you already chose. See baton skill. Do not twist the tip in a knot.
4. Dull is dangerous. A few strokes on a stone or the ceramic ring of a mug beats a press-hard hack.
5. Close a folder before you walk. Fixed blade in the sheath before you stand up from the fire.
6. Wipe pitch with a bit of wood scrap. Keep the pivot out of the dirt.
7. If you drop it, let it fall. Do not grab a falling blade.

### Cautions
- A knife is not an axe, a screwdriver, or a piton.
- Blood on the handle means you stop and wrap before you keep carving.
- **Rockies**: cold fingers plus a folding knife at dusk is how people close the blade on a tendon. Warm the hands, or wait.
summary: Cut away from you, sit to carve, baton don’t twist, keep it sharp, sheath before you stand.

title: String is shelter, hangs, and splints.
body:
### Situation
You need to hold a tarp, a hang, a splint, or a repair. The cord you packed is a finite tool.

### Do
1. Know what you have: diameter, length, whether the core is useful as finer line.
2. Cut less than you think. A bowline and a trucker’s hitch reuse the same piece.
3. Guylines live on the tarp. Do not raid them to play with a swing.
4. Natural cordage is a skill when the pack cord is gone. See bark cordage. It is slower and weaker.
5. Pad where cord meets skin or a tree you still want alive. A wide wrap beats a cheese-wire.
6. After a night of wind, retie. Knots creep.
7. Keep a few feet of spare in the lid for the splint you did not plan.

### Cautions
- Fishing line as a tarp guy will cut the hem and your hands.
- A knot you cannot untie in the cold is a one-use strap. Practice the two knots in this pack.
- **Rockies**: UV and dry wind make cheap cord brittle. If it fuzzes, retire that piece from life-support jobs.
summary: Know the length you packed. Reuse with bowline and trucker. Pad trees. Spare in the lid for a splint.

title: The rod is a shower of sparks. Give it fuel.
body:
### Situation
Matches are wet or gone. You have a ferrocerium rod and you need a flame.

### Do
1. Tinder first. A spark into air is a show. A spark into a nest is a fire.
2. Scrape a little pile of rod dust onto the nest if the tinder is marginal, then a long stroke.
3. Hold the rod still, pull the striker along it, so the nest does not scatter.
4. A knife spine works if it is square. A file striker is kinder to the blade.
5. Close the nest around the ember. Blow from the side, not spit from above.
6. Keep the rod dry-ish in a pocket. It still works wet better than matches, but tinder does not.
7. Practice at home so the first field stroke is not your first stroke.

### Cautions
- Sparks in the eye are a second incident. Look aside.
- Using the last of a tiny keychain rod on wet punk is a waste. Make the nest first.
- **Rockies**: wind on a saddle will steal the nest. Body as a wind wall, or kneel in a hole you scraped.
summary: Nest first, rod still, striker moves, dust then a long stroke, blow from the side.

title: Light is a tool. Battery is the limit.
body:
### Situation
You need to see hands, trail, or a signal. The lamp is also how people find you.

### Do
1. One task lamp, one spare or spare cells. Phone is the last reserve, not the plan.
2. Low mode for camp. High for a short look. Flood for trail, spot for a signal flash.
3. Cold: sleep with the cells. Lithium handles cold better than cheap alkalines.
4. Red or a dim white if you need night vision for navigation.
5. Strap on the head or the sternum, not in a pocket under a hip belt you will not feel in a fall.
6. Signal: three flashes. Then save the rest for the close work.
7. Check it at the trailhead. A dead lamp found at 21:00 is a night-out.

### Cautions
- High mode “just for a minute” is how the night ends in the dark.
- Pointing a lamp in a person’s eyes on a ridge is how they step off it.
- **Rockies**: long winter nights plus a 5:00 alpine start. If you only packed a phone, you packed a bet.
summary: Task lamp plus spare, low mode default, cells in the bag in the cold, three flashes then save it.

title: A tarp kit is more than a sheet.
body:
### Situation
You packed a tarp and then found out the night needs stakes, line, and a way to hold a ridge.

### Do
1. Minimum: tarp, 6–8 pegs, two long guys for a ridge, extra line, a small repair patch.
2. Pegs that survive decomposed granite and wind. Wire nails fail. Rocks as deadmen if they must.
3. Line already cut and on the corners so you are not tying with a headlamp in hail.
4. Two trees or two poles. A ridge without a ridge is a puddle.
5. Stuff sack that you can also fill with snow as a weight.
6. After a pitch, walk it. If a corner pops at a tug, it will pop at 02:00.
7. Dry and fold so the next pitch is not a frozen wad.

### Cautions
- A painter’s drop sheet without guys is a kite.
- **Rockies**: Front Range wind will inventory your kit for you. If you only packed four pegs, you packed a failure in a saddle.
summary: Tarp, 6–8 real pegs, ridge guys, corner lines pre-cut. Tug-test before you sleep.

title: Fix the thing that keeps you moving.
body:
### Situation
A strap, a pole, a pad, or a shoe just failed. You need a field fix, not a pretty one.

### Do
1. Stop before the failure becomes a fall. A floppy pole on scree is a tripwire.
2. Tape, cord, a needle, a spare buckle, a bit of foam, a small zip. That is a kit.
3. Pad a hot spot before it is a hole. Shoe delam: tape plus cord around the midfoot.
4. Pole: splint with a stick and tape, or shorten and use as a stake.
5. Pad puncture: tape on both faces, or a patch kit if you packed it. Sleep on the pack if the pad is dead.
6. Tarp tear: patch on the fly, then a guy that does not load the tear.
7. Test the fix on flat ground. Then walk.

### Cautions
- Super glue in the eye is a new patient. Cap it.
- Tape on wet dirty fabric is a rumor. Dry a patch first.
- **Rockies**: UV-rotted foam pads and cheap trekking poles fail on the first 14er descent. Carry the kit on the day you “will not need it.”
summary: Stop, tape-and-cord the failure, test on flat ground. Pad, pole, shoe, tarp are the usual four.

title: Craft is a tool. It is not the mission.
body:
### Situation
You know some skills and the day is failing. Building a pretty camp can eat the hours that should have been a descent or a signal.

### Do
1. Same rank as the situation hub: people, then shelter, water, signal, travel. Craft supports those.
2. Timebox. A debris hut gets 30–40 minutes, not a half day.
3. Use the kit you carried before you invent a primitive version. Tarp before hut. Stove before a bow drill fantasy.
4. If a skill is not working, switch methods. Wet fire dying? Shelter and a stove. Bark cordage failing? Tear a strap.
5. Keep a person on watch for weather and the group while you craft.
6. Stop when good enough. Perfect lashings on a hypothermic person is malpractice.
7. Reassess after each finished piece. Do you still need the next one?

### Cautions
- Skills content is not a dare to stay out longer.
- Knife work with cold hands is a bleeding card waiting.
- **Rockies**: afternoon cells do not care that you wanted to finish a lean-to. If the sky is towering, the skill is “get off the high point.”
summary: Craft supports people, shelter, water, signal. Timebox it. Kit before primitive. Good enough then stop.

title: Scree moves. So do the people below you.
body:
### Situation
A slope of fist-to-fridge rocks. The trail is a rumor. Ankles and rockfall are the tax.

### Do
1. One at a time in the fall line. The rest wait off to the side, not in the bowling alley.
2. Test the block before you weight it. Quiet hollow blocks lie.
3. Hands out. Short steps. Poles help on the down. Do not bound.
4. Helmet if you packed it. If you did not, do not linger under the cliff band that feeds the scree.
5. If a rock goes, shout “rock” and do not watch your own rock like a sport. Watch your feet and then the group.
6. After a twist, stop. See sprain. The next block is not a reset.
7. Descent: sidehill to a rib if the chute is a bowling alley.

### Cautions
- Running scree as a shortcut is how people go to the clinic.
- Headphones. You will not hear “rock.”
- **Rockies**: 14er gullies after freeze-thaw drop rock in the afternoon. Start earlier, get off the chute, do not picnic in the runout.
summary: One at a time in the fall line, test blocks, shout rock, do not run it. Afternoon chutes drop more.

title: Look up. Beetle-kill does not wait for wind season.
body:
### Situation
Gray standing trees, red-brown lodgepole, a night site that looks like a cathedral. The trees have a vote.

### Do
1. Look up before you sit. Dead tops, hanging widows, cracked stems.
2. Camp in a gap or among live smaller trees, not under the tallest gray mast.
3. In wind, get out of the stand. A meadow edge or a boulder field can be safer than a snag forest.
4. Cross deadfall by testing, three points, and not on a log over a hole you cannot see.
5. Do not fell a snag for fun. It can kick back or bring a friend.
6. Fire under beetle-kill is a spark into kindling that is still standing.
7. After a blow, the trail may be a pile. Detour around the hangers. Do not tunnel under a spring-loaded stem.

### Cautions
- A “solid-looking” gray tree with no needles can be rotten at the hinge.
- Hammocks on snags are a comedy with a bad ending.
- **Rockies**: pine beetle stands are a Front Range and high-country fact. Wind plus those stands is a hazard card, not scenery.
summary: Look up, camp out of snag-fall, leave the stand in wind, do not tunnel under hangers.

title: The creek is louder than this morning.
body:
### Situation
You need the other bank. The water is moving. This is a drowning site if you treat it like a puddle.

### Do
1. Scout up and down. Wide and knee-deep beats narrow and angry.
2. Unbuckle the hip belt and sternum. If you go in, the pack must come off.
3. Pole upstream, side to the current, short shuffling steps, downstream exit picked before you start.
4. One at a time. The next person starts when the first is on the bank.
5. If it hits mid-thigh and shoves, that is a no. Turn around.
6. After a storm, wait. See flash flood. Morning low water is a thing.
7. If someone is swept: bank chase, throw a real line, do not dive into a hydraulic.

### Cautions
- Crossing at the waterfall lip because it is short is a classic.
- Wet logs are skating rinks.
- **Rockies**: snowmelt afternoons run higher. A 07:00 ford can be a 15:00 swim. Front Range canyons rise on a cell you did not feel.
summary: Wide and shallow, belt unbuckled, pole upstream, one at a time. Mid-thigh shove is a no.

title: High is a load. Descend is a tool.
body:
### Situation
You drove up from the plains or Denver and you are going higher. The air is thinner. The decisions get dumber as you climb.

### Do
1. Slow the pace until you can talk. If you cannot talk, you are racing the mountain.
2. Water, food, sun on the head, and a real turnaround time.
3. Watch for the person who is unusually slow, nauseated, or off-balance. Sit them. If they worsen at rest, down.
4. Sleeping high after a bad day is a bet. Down is the default.
5. Weather hits harder up here. The afternoon-storm card is part of this card.
6. Do not stack alcohol with a first night at 10,000 ft (3050 m).
7. Know the bail ridge before you need it.

### Cautions
- Fitness on a bike path at 5,280 ft (1609 m) is not a 14er clearance.
- “We always summit” is not a medical plan.
- **Rockies**: Denver to a 14er parking lot in one morning is a common pattern and a common fail. Give the night, or give the summit.
summary: Talk-pace, water, watch the quiet nauseated one, descend if they worsen at rest. Denver-to-14er in a morning is a load.

title: Hands, holes, and group food.
body:
### Situation
A group, a creek, and a cook pot. Gut bugs travel on hands more than on legends.

### Do
1. Wash or sanitize after toilet and before food. This is the whole sermon.
2. Toilet: 200 ft (60 m) from water, camp, and trail. Hole, bury, pack out paper if that is the rule you live under.
3. One cook spoon that does not go in mouths and back in the pot.
4. Treat the water. Clean rims. See water cards.
5. Cuts get a cover. Dirt in a cut is tomorrow’s wound card.
6. Menstrual gear and waste go in the smellable bag, not under a rock by the creek.
7. If someone is already sick, they do not share the group jerky bag.

### Cautions
- A pretty creek is not a sink. Scoop, then wash away from the scoop site.
- Hand sanitizer on visibly dirty hands is a smear. Rinse first if you can.
- **Rockies**: high-use Front Range lakes have a people problem. The alpine is not sterile.
summary: Hands after toilet and before food. Toilet far from water. No mouth-to-pot. Sick people do not share the bag.

title: Sleep is a decision, not a leftover.
body:
### Situation
You are making navigation and weather calls on four hours and a sugar crash. Fatigue is a hazard.

### Do
1. Stop while you can still build a site. The hour after you should have slept is when ankles go.
2. Pad, dry layer, food, earshot of the group. See insulation.
3. Someone stays half-awake if a person is injured or a river is rising. Rotate.
4. Caffeine at 20:00 will not fix a 03:00 start. It will just steal the night.
5. If you cannot sleep for cold, fix the pad and the wind, not your character.
6. Dawn is allowed. A forced night march is a special case. See night travel.
7. After a bad night, shorten the next day’s objective out loud.

### Cautions
- “I’ll sleep on the summit” is not a sleep plan.
- Sleeping in a running car for warmth is a carbon monoxide story. This pack is field, not a garage.
- **Rockies**: early alpine starts plus a Denver workweek is how people miss the cairn. Budget the night.
summary: Stop in time to sleep, fix cold rather than endure it, shorten tomorrow after a bad night.

title: Feet are the vehicle. Service them.
body:
### Situation
A long descent, wet socks, or a hot spot. The trip ends when the feet do.

### Do
1. Dry socks in the bag. Change at the first wet or the first hot spot, not at camp pride.
2. Lacing: heel lock on the down. Toes should not hammer the front.
3. Nails short before the trip. Blood under a nail is a long walk.
4. Grit out of the sock when you feel it. Sand is a file.
5. Tape the known hot spots at the trailhead if you already know them.
6. At night: air them, check for hot spots, ticks, and mystery holes in the skin.
7. If a boot fails, tape and cord. See repair. Walking out barefoot on granite is a new patient.

### Cautions
- New boots on a 14er are a clinic appointment.
- River crossings then a long paved descent with wet socks is blister factory settings.
- **Rockies**: 3,000 ft (900 m) of Front Range down is where heels die. Tape before the downhill.
summary: Change socks early, heel-lock the down, tape known spots, air them at night. Feet end trips.

title: Throw a spark into a nest, not into the air.
body:
### Situation
You need a flame from a ferro rod. The nest is the skill. The spark is cheap.

### Do
1. Materials: ferro rod, striker or square spine, a tinder nest (dry grass, resin dust, inner bark, cotton if you packed it), pencil-thick kindling, a wind wall.
2. Build the nest in a palm-sized bundle with a dense center and a shaggy outside.
3. Stage kindling in a lean-to with a mouth toward you.
4. Hold the rod tip in the nest. Striker moves. Long firm scrape. Dust first if the tinder is shy, then a hotter stroke.
5. When the nest glows or flames, fold it, hold it in the kindling mouth, and blow from the side until kindling takes.
6. Feed pencil sticks one at a time. Do not dump the fuel pile.
7. If it dies, split new dry heart and try again. Do not spend the rod on wet duff.

### Cautions
- Sparks in the eye and a knife that slips toward the off hand.
- A plastic bag nest in a wildfire wind is a problem. Control the site first. See fire-site.
- **Rockies**: wind will scatter a loose nest. Kneel, back to wind, or scrape a hole.
summary: Palm nest, rod still, long scrape, fold onto kindling, blow from the side, feed pencil sticks.

title: Shave a dry heart into a bird.
body:
### Situation
Outside wood is wet or you need a tinder that lasts longer than grass. You will shave curls that stay on the stick.

### Do
1. Materials: a straight wrist-thick piece of dead wood, a sharp knife, a solid knee or log as a bench.
2. Split to the dry heart. The inside of standing dead is the bet.
3. Brace the stick. Cut away from the body. Thin, long curls, still attached. Rotate the stick. Make a skirt.
4. Make two or three sticks. One is a sample, three is a fire.
5. Put the skirt in the kindling mouth. Light the curls with ferro or flame. The stick is the next fuel.
6. If curls crumble, the wood is punk. Switch pieces.
7. If curls will not take, they are too thick. Thinner. Sharper knife.

### Cautions
- A knife toward the femoral artery is the wrong bench. Sit, lock wrists on knees, cut off-line.
- Green aspen makes limp curls. Dead pine heart is the usual Front Range win.
- **Rockies**: beetle-kill can be kiln-dry. Great curls. Still a wildfire neighbor. Site the fire.
summary: Split to dry heart, shave attached curls away from the body, light the skirt, use the stick as the next fuel.

title: Roof, split, shave, then spark.
body:
### Situation
Rain or snow is on everything and you still need a boil or heat. Sequence beats grit.

### Do
1. Materials: a roof (tarp, dense spruce), standing dead, a knife, ferro, a dry pocket bundle if you have one.
2. Roof first. Scrape a mineral patch under it.
3. Hunt standing dead. Split to heart. Make a pile of heart splits and three feather sticks.
4. Body-dry a fist of tinder in a pocket while you split.
5. Light under the roof. Small. Grow it. Dry the next sticks on the rim, not in the flame to quench.
6. Move to a safer open scrape if the tarp is at risk, once you have coals you can carry on a bark shovel.
7. Keep a dry bundle for the next cell. This fire is not immortal.

### Cautions
- Fuel on a tarp and a flare is a melt hole and a burn.
- Do not use stove fuel as a splash. Control is the skill.
- **Rockies**: monsoon cells pass. Start the splits when the first drops hit, not after you are shaking.
summary: Roof and scrape, split standing dead, feather the heart, light small, dry next sticks on the rim.

title: Rolling boil in a pot you can still hold.
body:
### Situation
You will treat water with heat. You need a rolling boil and a clean pour, not a scald.

### Do
1. Materials: pot with a lid if you have one, stove or coal bed, prefiltered water, a clean bottle, a wind screen.
2. Cloth-prefilter into the pot. Grit wastes fuel and scorches.
3. Lid on. Wind screen. Bring to a rolling boil — big bubbles across the surface.
4. Hold the roll one full minute at Front Range and higher. Time it.
5. Off the heat. Lid stays. Cool until you can pour without a steam burn.
6. Pour to the clean bottle. Dirty scoop never goes back in.
7. If you melted snow, there must be starter water in the pot or you scorch, then boil the melt.

### Cautions
- A grab of a wire bail that has been in the flame is a burn card.
- Boil is for living contaminants. Fuel sheen still means walk.
- **Rockies**: 12,000 ft (3660 m) needs the extra minute and the wind screen. Open flame in a saddle wastes the fuel.
summary: Prefilter, lid on, rolling boil plus one minute at altitude, cool, pour clean. Starter water for snow.

title: Take the grit out before the treat.
body:
### Situation
The water is cloudy, tea-colored, or full of bark. Filter, chemical, and pot all want that gone.

### Do
1. Materials: a bandana, shirt tail, or coffee filter, two containers, time to settle.
2. Scoop from mid-depth. Let the pot sit 5–10 minutes. Pour off the top.
3. Stretch cloth over the clean container. Pour slow. Do not press the mud through.
4. Rinse the cloth away from the source if you will use it again. Or flip to a fresh patch.
5. Then boil, filter, or chemical the clear-ish water.
6. Glacier flour may still pass a cloth. Settle longer. A second cloth helps. Your cartridge will thank you.
7. Keep the dirty scoop and the cloth on the dirty side of camp.

### Cautions
- A filthy sock is a bacteria rag. Use the cleanest cloth you can spare.
- Squeezing the cloth to “speed it up” injects the silt you just caught.
- **Rockies**: spring 14er streams are flour. Settle plus cloth or you will be back to boil by dinner.
summary: Settle, pour through cloth, do not squeeze the mud through, then treat. Dirty cloth stays dirty.

title: A small debris roof you can finish.
body:
### Situation
No tarp, a night coming, and you need a roof you can actually finish. Small beats cathedral.

### Do
1. Materials: a ridge pole that will not crush you, two forks or a boulder for the head, armloads of debris, a twig bed.
2. Ridge pole at hip height or lower. A-frame ribs, then lattice.
3. Pile debris from the ground up until you cannot see light through the walls. Thicker than you want. Especially the weather side.
4. Door at the lee. Small. Pack as the plug.
5. Twig bed inside before you pile the last roof. You will not want to build the bed after you are wet.
6. Stop at good enough. Get in with dry layers and calories.
7. Mark the hut. It disappears in timber at night.

### Cautions
- Two hours of building in rain is how the hut becomes the injury.
- Do not strip the live windbreak to death. Dead debris first.
- **Rockies**: krummholz may already be the hut. Add debris on the wind side and go. Do not fight a full build in a saddle.
summary: Low ridge, lattice, debris until opaque, lee door, twig bed before the last pile. Small and finished.

title: One wall to the weather, fire optional.
body:
### Situation
You have a wind direction and some time. A lean-to is faster than a hut and needs a weather wall that actually faces the weather.

### Do
1. Materials: a ridge between two trees or a pole on forks, rafters, debris or a tarp, a site with the weather on one side.
2. Ridge at chest or lower. Rafters on the weather side only, steep.
3. Lattice, then debris or tarp. Overlap like shingles, downhill edge low.
4. Side walls if the wind wraps. Leave a low front.
5. Bed off the ground. If you will have a fire, it sits in front, not under the lip to melt the roof.
6. If you have a tarp, the lean-to frame is optional. Tarp first, frame if the tarp needs help.
7. Reset after the first gust. The first flap is the warning.

### Cautions
- A high open lean-to in Front Range wind is a cooler and a kite.
- Fire plus hanging debris is a signal you did not want.
- **Rockies**: point the wall at the west or the actual weather, not at the view of Denver.
summary: Low ridge, steep weather wall, shingle the debris, bed off the ground. Tarp first if you have one.

title: Ridgeline taut, walls low, every corner guyed.
body:
### Situation
You will sleep under a tarp in rain or wind. The A-frame is the default pitch.

### Do
1. Materials: tarp, ridgeline or poles, 6–8 pegs, corner guys, two trees or two poles.
2. Ridgeline first, head-height or lower. Taut. Trucker's hitch on one end.
3. Drape. Tie or clip the ridge points so the tarp cannot skate.
4. Peg the four corners out and down. Then mid-sides. Rocks on pegs in rotten soil.
5. Drop the weather side lower. Leave a small lee door.
6. Tug every guy. If a peg walks, deadman it now.
7. Kit inside, up off the drip line. A trench only if water is already coming for the hip.

### Cautions
- A high church ceiling is a sail.
- Cooking under the A-frame is how you own a hole and a CO problem.
- **Rockies**: reset guys at dusk when the plains-to-mountain wind flips.
summary: Taut low ridgeline, corners then mids, weather side dropped, tug-test every peg.

title: A body-sized trench with a roof and a vent.
body:
### Situation
Snow is deep enough to dig and the air is the enemy. A trench is faster than a cave and easier to leave.

### Do
1. Materials: a scoop (pot, plate, snowshoe, hands), a roof (tarp, skis, poles and a sheet), a pad, a probe for hidden creeks.
2. Probe the drift. No cornice, no creek, no thin roof over a hole.
3. Dig a trench: pack-length, shoulder-width, plus a kit shelf. Pile the spoil on the wind side as a wall.
4. Roof it. Leave a vent. A closed white box is a bad air story.
5. Pad the floor. Snow is not a mattress.
6. Door: pack as plug with an air gap. Kit inside so you are not crawling out naked at 02:00.
7. Wand the roof so nobody walks through you.

### Cautions
- Three hours of cave-building soaks you. Trench and get in.
- Cook only with huge ventilation. Better: cook outside.
- **Rockies**: June drifts on north 14er benches work. Loaded slopes above you do not. See avalanche watch.
summary: Probe, dig body-sized, roof with a vent, pad the floor, wand the roof. Do not cook sealed in.

title: A dry platform thicker than your fist.
body:
### Situation
The ground will take your heat. You need a raised dry layer under the full body, especially the torso.

### Do
1. Materials: dead lower twigs, bark slabs, dry duff, a pad if you have one, a scrape that drains.
2. Scrape duff to a slight trench so the bed has a pocket, or build on a rise.
3. Lattice of thumb-thick sticks across the body line, then finer stuff, then duff. Thicker than a fist at the hip.
4. Cover the whole body map: shoulders to calves. A pillow of clothes for the neck.
5. Keep it dry. If snow or rain is falling, roof first, then the bed.
6. A pad on top of the twigs is better than twigs on top of a pad that will puncture.
7. In the morning, scatter if you must leave no obvious nest in a high-use site.

### Cautions
- Live bough stripping that kills the only windbreak is a bad trade.
- A bed of wet aspen leaves is a sponge.
- **Rockies**: dead beetle-kill twigs are plentiful and poky. Lattice first so they do not spear the pad.
summary: Fist-thick lattice under the full body, duff on top, roof before the bed if it is raining.

title: Bark and fiber when the pack cord is gone.
body:
### Situation
You need string and the paracord is doing another job. Natural cordage is slow and weaker. It can still hold a bundle or a light guy.

### Do
1. Materials: dead inner bark (juniper, some willows), long dead grass, or yucca-type leaves if you already know that plant. Do not strip a live ring around a trunk.
2. Peel long strips. Keep them damp enough to flex, not rotten.
3. Twist a single strand until it wants to kink. Fold in half and let it lay into a two-ply. Keep the twist even.
4. Splice by overlapping a new strip into a thinning tail before it dies.
5. Use for: bundle, light lash, marker. Not for a life-support rappel. Not for a bear hang of real weight unless you stacked many.
6. Test with a hard pull on a piece you can afford to break.
7. If it fails, tear a clothing strap. Cloth you know beats fiber you hope.

### Cautions
- Live bark girdling kills the tree and often gives you junk fiber.
- Ivy and unknown plants are not cordage class. See ivy and unknown rules.
- **Rockies**: juniper bark on the foothills is the usual story. High alpine has less of this. Do not waste the hour above treeline.
summary: Dead inner bark, two-ply twist, splice before the tail dies. Light lash only. Test-pull. Cloth strap if it fails.

title: A loop that does not cinch. Dress it.
body:
### Situation
You need a fixed loop: around a tree, a pad eye, a person’s harness you actually know, or a bear-bag toggle. The bowline holds and still unties.

### Do
1. Materials: cord you can hold, a standing part and a working end.
2. Make a small rabbit hole in the standing part, rabbit up through, around the tree (the standing part), back down the hole.
3. Dress it. Snug. A sloppy bowline is a slipknot in training clothes.
4. Finish with a backup around the loop if it is life-ish, or if the free end is short.
5. Dress again after the first load. Recheck at the next stop.
6. To untie: break the collar, dump the load. That is why you tied this and not a wet jam knot.
7. Practice in the dark at home. Field bowlines happen at 21:00.

### Cautions
- A bowline that is not dressed will walk. Look at it.
- Around a person: only if you know what you are doing. A bad loop is not a rescue.
- Do not use rotten cord and call the knot the problem.
summary: Fixed loop: up through the hole, around the standing part, back down. Dress, backup, recheck after load.

title: A line you can cinch and still pop loose.
body:
### Situation
A ridgeline or a guy that must be tight, then tighter, then released with cold fingers.

### Do
1. Materials: a line longer than the gap, an anchor on the far end (bowline or a tree wrap).
2. Near the second tree: a slip loop or a small directional loop on the standing part.
3. Working end through that loop, pull hard, then lock with two half hitches or a slipped half hitch so you can pop it.
4. Dress. The mechanical advantage is the point. Pull along the line, not out into space.
5. Recinch after the tarp stretches and after the first rain.
6. To release: undo the lock, dump the loop, the line goes slack. That is the feature.
7. If the line sings in the wind, it is too thin or too tight on a sharp bark. Pad it.

### Cautions
- A trucker on rotten webbing can cut the webbing. Wide tree wrap.
- Fingers in the loop while you cinch is a blood blister.
- **Rockies**: lines go slack overnight as the weather cools. Recinch at dusk and at first flap.
summary: Anchor far end, loop on the standing part, pull through, lock with a slipped hitch, recinch after stretch.

title: Split with a baton, not with a twist of the tip.
body:
### Situation
You need dry heart or kindling and you have a sturdy knife, not an axe.

### Do
1. Materials: a full-tang or stout knife, a wrist-to-forearm dead round, a wooden baton (another stick).
2. Stand the round on a stump or solid dirt. Not on your boot, not on your knee.
3. Set the edge on the end grain. Strike the spine with the baton. Walk the edge through. Do not pry.
4. If it binds, baton more, or start a new split from the other end. Twisting the tip is how blades die and how they bounce into you.
5. Split the splits until you have heart kindling and a feather-stick blank.
6. Sheath the knife before you gather the pile.
7. Stop if the knife is folding, cheap, or already bent. Find an axe-shaped rock or burn thinner twigs instead.

### Cautions
- Off-hand in the split is a surgery.
- Frozen wood bounces. Extra control, or wait.
- **Rockies**: beetle-kill splits easy and throws chips. Eye line. Site still matters for the fire that follows.
summary: Stout knife, round on a stump, baton the spine, no prying, sheath before you pick up the pile.

title: Build a mark bigger than your pride.
body:
### Situation
You need a ground-to-air shape. A pack lid is not a shape.

### Do
1. Materials: brightest sheet (tarp, blanket, clothing), logs or stones, a clearing, anchors.
2. Pick the open floor. Stamp snow or clear brush so the contrast is clean.
3. Lay an X or a V. Each stroke 8–10 ft (2.5–3 m) or bigger. Logs on snow, bright cloth on rock.
4. Anchor every corner. Wind is the thief.
5. Add a second color if you have it. Outline logs around a yellow tarp on granite.
6. Stay by it when you hear an engine. A panel with nobody home is a maybe.
7. Fold a night kit so you can reset at dawn in two minutes.

### Cautions
- A tiny pretty X in a spruce hole is invisible.
- Do not use the only sleeping tarp as a panel in a cell unless you have a backup roof.
- **Rockies**: light granite plus a gray tarp is low contrast. Dark boughs on snow, or the brightest thing you own on rock.
summary: Open floor, 8–10 ft strokes, high contrast, every corner anchored, stay by it.

title: Take a number, walk to a target, take another.
body:
### Situation
You will walk a line you cannot see the end of. The skill is a number plus a series of short targets.

### Do
1. Materials: baseplate compass, map with a known declination, a notebook, a catching feature.
2. Set declination for this map. Front Range is east of true. Confirm the box on the map.
3. Put the edge from here to there. Turn the housing until meridian lines match the map north. Read the number at the index.
4. Hold the compass flat at the belly. Turn your body until the needle sits in the shed. Walk that way.
5. Pick a tree or rock on the line, walk to it without staring at the needle, then repeat.
6. Pair with pacing and a catcher. Write the number.
7. If land and needle fight, stop. Metal, iron rock, or a wrong declination. See compass card.

### Cautions
- Phone in the same hand as the compass is a magnet story.
- A bearing through a cliff is still a cliff.
- Recheck the housing. Bumping it 20 degrees is a different valley.
summary: Set declination, edge on the map, housing to meridians, needle in the shed, walk to short targets.

title: Calibrate, then bead every hundred.
body:
### Situation
You need distance without a wheel. Your boots are the wheel if you calibrated them.

### Do
1. Materials: a known 100 yd (91 m) of dirt, a bead string or pebbles, a notebook.
2. Walk the known stretch. Count double-steps (every time the right foot hits). Write the number. Do it twice.
3. Repeat on talus or snow if that is the day’s ground. Write a worse number.
4. In the field: start at a feature, click a bead every 100 yd (91 m), stop when the plan says stop.
5. Two people count. If they disagree, stop early, not late.
6. Reset the beads at every feature you actually identify.
7. Recalibrate after a heavy pack day. Tired strides shrink.

### Cautions
- Counting every single step and then dividing in your head is how you lose the number. Double-steps.
- Talking, scrambling, and counting are two jobs too many. Quiet the count.
- **Rockies**: a Denver sidewalk count will lie on a 14er boulder field. Use the talus number.
summary: Calibrate double-steps per 100 yards on dirt and on talus. Bead every unit. Two counters. Stop on number.

title: Coals you still have in the morning.
body:
### Situation
You want heat or a fast boil at dawn without rebuilding from wet tinder. You will bury coals, not a flaming log.

### Do
1. Materials: a mature coal bed, dry hardwood or dense pine heart, ash, mineral soil, a morning tinder bundle.
2. Let flames die to coals. Feed a few dense pieces so you have guts, not a pile of ash.
3. Scrape a pocket in the ash and dirt. Nest the coals. Cover with ash, then a thin dirt cap. Leave a tiny breath if you know the site will not run.
4. Stage morning tinder in a dry bag.
5. Dawn: open, blow, feed shavings. If it is dead, you still have a dry site and a head start.
6. This is not a leave-it-and-hike. If you break camp, drown-stir-drown. See put-out.
7. Never bank in duff or peat. Mineral soil only.

### Cautions
- A banked fire in beetle-kill duff is a wildfire with a delay fuse.
- A flaming log under dirt is not banked. It is hidden.
- **Rockies**: wind can ravel a dirt cap. Check before you bag up, and drown if you are not sure.
summary: Mature coals in mineral soil, ash cap, dry morning tinder. Drown if you leave. Never in duff.

title: Pad, loft, smaller cave, then food.
body:
### Situation
You will lie down in the cold. The skill is a system: ground, loft, wind, fuel.

### Do
1. Materials: pad or twig bed, dry bag or quilt, extra clothes, a hat, a wind roof, a snack, a bottle.
2. Ground first. Full-length if you can. Torso is the minimum. Pack under the hips if the pad is short.
3. Dry layer on skin. Fluff the loft. Wet down stays in a stuff sack, not on you, until you can dry it.
4. Shrink the shelter. Packs as walls. Low tarp.
5. Hat, dry socks, maybe a bottle of warm water at the core if you can make it without a burn.
6. Eat. Then sleep. A 03:00 shiver: add a layer and fix the pad. Do not lie there proving a point.
7. Vent a little so the loft does not dew into a sponge.

### Cautions
- A space blanket as the only ground sheet sweats you, then freezes. Duff or a pad on top of it.
- Tight clothes crush loft. Loose layers trap air.
- **Rockies**: radiating sky at 11,000 ft (3350 m) on a clear night. Low roof matters as much as the puffy.
summary: Ground insulation, dry loft, shrink the cave, hat and calories, fix shivering at 03:00 instead of enduring it.

title: Put the flash on your hand, then on the target.
body:
### Situation
Sun is out and you have a mirror or a stand-in. You need the flash to hit an aircraft or a ridge, not random sky.

### Do
1. Materials: signal mirror with a sight hole if you have one, or a phone screen, a bright sun, a target.
2. Reflect sun onto your open hand. See the spot.
3. Move that spot onto the target. If the mirror has a hole, look through it, put the target in the hole, and still watch the flash land.
4. Burst: three flashes, pause, repeat. Sweep if the target is moving.
5. If you lose the spot, back to the hand, then walk it on again.
6. Pair with a whistle. Clouds end the flash without notice.
7. Practice once on a far rock so the first aircraft is not your first try.

### Cautions
- Do not fish the flash through a group’s eyes at ten paces.
- A laser is not this skill and is a problem at aircraft.
- Wipe mud off the glass. A dirty mirror is a dark plate.
summary: Flash on the hand, walk it onto the target, three-burst, reacquire from the hand if you lose it.

title: Unknown (Florida)
body:
### Situation
Vision did not lock a species. The photo stays Unknown. A blurry leaf, a coiled dark snake, or a wet log that might be a gator is still Unknown. Do not upgrade the guess because you are hungry, scared, or late.

ID confidence (typical visual): 8%. Runner-up/lookalike: 8% (saw palmetto).

### Traits
No lock. You may have a nearest card in this Florida deck — saw palmetto, cabbage palm, manchineel, poison ivy, water hyacinth, Brazilian pepper, coontie, Spanish moss, alligator, cottonmouth, eastern diamondback, coral snake, scarlet kingsnake, black bear, feral hog — but nearest is not identified.

### Documented parts
Unknown has no documented food parts on this card. Unknown also has no cleared toxin list. Do not mouth it. Do not put sap or latex near an eye. If the photo is a snake and you cannot name it from before this trip, give it space and treat a strike as a get-to-care problem.

Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Every card in this pack is a possible neighbor. Palms get mixed. Banded snakes get mixed. Dark heavy snakes get mixed. A floating mat can hide an alligator. If two stories fit the photo, keep Unknown.

### Do
1. Leave the specimen where it is. Photo from where you already stand if you need a record.
2. Open the nearest named cards in this deck and read Traits and Cautions. Reading is not a lock.
3. Do not mouth, cook, or burn Unknown to “see what it is.”
4. If skin oil or sap already got on you, rinse, then see plants-ivy-id and aid-wound. Do not rub an eye with that hand.
5. If a snake struck, see aid-snake. Do not hunt the animal for a better picture.
6. Spend the hour on water, shade, and a named route, not on a second forage loop.
7. Log place, time, and what you actually saw (leaflet count, bands, rattle, snout). Identification happens later.

### Cautions
- Phone ID is a pack-side guess. Unknown stays Unknown.
- **Florida**: heat, humidity, and afternoon cells punish extra wandering. A wrong plant or a second look at a cottonmouth is not worth the shortcut.
- Not a verdict. Confirm with more than the phone.
summary: Vision returned Unknown; read nearest Florida cards and do not mouth or handle the specimen.

title: Saw palmetto
body:
### Situation
Low fan palm in Florida scrub, pine flatwoods, and dune edges. Often waist to chest high, sometimes in thickets you cannot see through. Sharp teeth on the leaf stalk cut skin and clothing.

ID confidence (typical visual): 74%. Runner-up/lookalike: 18% (cabbage palm).

### Traits
Fan leaves, yellow-green to silver, folded from a short or creeping trunk that may lie along the sand. Petiole (leaf stalk) has a saw of hard teeth — run a stick along it, not a thumb. Flower stalk is a long cream brush among the leaves. Ripe fruit dark, about olive-sized (1 in / 2.5 cm). Clumps and colonies, not a single tall column.

### Documented parts
Ripe fruit documented as food and as a dried product in some traditions after harvest and drying. Terminal bud documented as food in some traditions; cutting it kills that stem. Saw teeth and fiber documented as a cut and splinter hazard. Do not mouth green fruit or unknown lookalikes.

Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Cabbage palm is the usual mix-up in a tight photo: same fan language, but cabbage palm grows a tall single trunk and the petiole lacks the saw. Young cabbage palms in a palmetto thicket fool people. Coontie is a cycad with pinnate leaflets, not a fan.

### Do
1. Give the thicket a lane. Palmetto hides hogs, diamondbacks, and ticks.
2. Look at the petiole. Saw teeth = this card’s flag, not a cabbage palm.
3. Do not grab a fan to pull yourself up a dune. The teeth open a hand fast.
4. Pants into socks before you push a palmetto edge. See animals-ticks.
5. If you log it, note trunk habit (creeping vs column) and petiole teeth.
6. Do not burn a mystery pile of palm boots in a closed shelter just to ID smoke.
7. Unknown fan without a clear petiole stays Unknown.

### Cautions
- Cuts go septic in Florida heat. Clean and cover; see aid-wound.
- **Florida**: saw palmetto is statewide in dry pine and coastal scrub. It is not a Keys-only plant and not a cabbage palm seedling.
- Not a verdict. Confirm with more than the phone.
summary: Low Florida fan palm with a toothed petiole; do not confuse with cabbage palm or push the thicket blind.

title: Cabbage palm
body:
### Situation
Florida’s tall native palm: single trunk, big costapalmate fans, often with a skirt or “boots” of old leaf bases. Hammocks, coastal strands, roadsides, and ranch edges.

ID confidence (typical visual): 72%. Runner-up/lookalike: 20% (saw palmetto).

### Traits
One trunk, often 20–50 ft (6–15 m) when mature, gray and cross-hatched or still wearing boot-like petiole bases. Leaf is a fan that also folds along a midrib (costapalmate) — a kink the low saw palmetto fan does not show the same way. Petiole is smooth-edged compared with saw palmetto’s teeth. Dead fans hang as a skirt and hold rats, snakes, and wasps. Fruit in dark hanging clusters.

### Documented parts
Terminal bud (the so-called heart) documented as food in some traditions; taking it kills the tree. Fruit documented as food in some traditions after processing. Boot skirts documented as a nest and bite hazard, not a harvest. Do not mouth an unknown palm heart.

Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Saw palmetto is the field mix-up: same fan vocabulary, low and colonial, saw on the petiole, no tall column. Other planted palms in towns have different trunks and leaflets; this card is the native sabal. A close photo of only fans without the trunk is how Vision drops to the runner-up.

### Do
1. ID from trunk plus petiole, not from one fan in the sky.
