body:
### Situation
A tan deer on a Hudson field edge, a Catskill woods road, or an Adirondack carry at dusk. The road and the startle are the hazards. You are not hunting from this card.

### Traits
Shoulder height often 3–3.5 ft (0.9–1.1 m). Coat tan to gray-brown by season. The tell: a white underside of the tail that flags when it bounds. Antlers on some adults in season, shed later. Tracks: paired heart-shaped splits, 2–3.5 in (5–9 cm). Beds in grass or snow. Fawns spotted. Eyes shine at night. They hold the edge of fields and the first timber.

### Documented parts
Some historical accounts list meat and hide as used parts. This pack does not treat a road-killed or standing deer as a field ration. Ticks ride the same beds. Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Moose (see the moose card) is the Adirondack size miss — taller, dark, with a palmate antler and a bell on the throat. Moose is not in this vision deck, so the runner-up is Unknown. Elk are not a NY wild problem. ID confidence (typical visual): 81%. Runner-up/lookalike: 11% (Unknown).

### Do
1. Give a wide berth to a doe that stamps; a fawn is often nearby.
2. Dusk pavement: they cross without a vote. Slow the group on woods roads.
3. Do not walk up to a “tame” park deer. Kicks and ticks both travel.
4. After a sit in a deer bed, do a tick check. See the tick cards.
5. A wounded or dying deer is a scene. Do not dress it as a plan.

### Cautions
- A flagging tail is a departure, not an invitation to follow into blowdown.
- Chronic-wasting stories do not change the field rule: this pack is not a butcher shop.
- **NY**: Statewide. Adirondack interiors also hold moose — if the animal looks too tall and too dark, give more room and see animals-moose.
- Not medical advice. Not a verdict. Confirm with more than the phone.
summary: White flag on the rump, dusk roads, ticks in the bed. Moose is the Adirondack size miss. Unknown.

title: Timber rattlesnake: chevrons, rattle.
body:
### Situation
A heavy-bodied snake on a sunny Catskill ledge, Hudson Highland talus, or a southern Adirondack rock slab. You heard a buzz or you almost put a hand on the same rock. Distance is the skill.

### Traits
Adults often 3–4.5 ft (0.9–1.4 m), thick. Pattern: dark chevron or V-bands across a yellow, brown, or almost black ground. Head triangular, pit between eye and nostril if you are foolishly close. Tail ends in a keratin rattle; a young snake may have only a button. They den on south-facing rock and may be on the same ledge in spring and fall. They do not chase. Most bites are on hands that reached into a hole.

### Documented parts
Venom is historically documented as a medical emergency. This pack does not treat snakes as food. Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Copperhead shares pit-viper shape and sunny rock in southern and Hudson NY; copperhead has hourglass bands and no rattle. Harmless racers and milk snakes sit outside this deck. ID confidence (typical visual): 67%. Runner-up/lookalike: 24% (copperhead).

### Do
1. Freeze the feet. Let it keep the rock. Walk around wide, not over.
2. Hands and eyes on the next hold in talus. Poles probe the blind grass.
3. If it rattles: you are already close. Back the group out of the fall line of the slope.
4. Bite: away from the snake, sit, still limb, rings off, get to care. No cut, no suck, no ice-as-treatment. See aid-snake.
5. Do not kill it for a photo. A second person then becomes the patient.

### Cautions
- A quiet snake is still a snake. The rattle is a courtesy, not a requirement.
- Dark “black” phase animals still carry the body shape.
- **NY**: Catskills, Hudson Highlands, and parts of the Southern Tier and eastern Adirondack fringe. Not a High-Peaks talus problem. Legal protections exist; leave them.
- Not medical advice. Not a verdict. Confirm with more than the phone.
summary: Heavy snake, dark chevrons, rattle on sunny NY rock. Space, still limb, get to care. Unknown.

title: Copperhead: hourglass, no rattle.
body:
### Situation
A camouflaged snake in Hudson Valley leaf litter, a Palisades talus pocket, or a southern NY woodpile. No buzz. You almost put the hand down. Stop the reach.

### Traits
Adults often 2–3 ft (0.6–0.9 m), stout. Head copper or pink-tan, wider than the neck. Pattern: chestnut hourglass or saddle bands that are narrow on the back and wide on the sides — the “bowtie” look from above. No rattle; the tail is a thin tip, sometimes yellow on the young. They sit still in oak leaves. Heat-sensing pits if you are already too close. They are not a High-Peaks animal.

### Documented parts
Venom is historically documented as a medical emergency, often less dramatic in story than a rattlesnake and still a get-to-care problem. This pack does not treat snakes as food. Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Timber rattlesnake is heavier, chevron-banded, and carries a rattle; ranges overlap on some Hudson and Catskill rock. Milk snakes and other banded colubrids sit outside this deck. ID confidence (typical visual): 68%. Runner-up/lookalike: 23% (timber rattlesnake).

### Do
1. Hands off rock lips, woodpiles, and the far side of a log. Look first.
2. Give it the tread. Walk around. Do not try to move it with a stick for a photo.
3. Kids and dogs nose the leaf pile. Short leash in southern oak woods in spring and fall.
4. Bite: away from the snake, sit, still limb, rings off, get to care. No cut, no suck, no ice-as-treatment. See aid-snake.
5. Note pattern only if it costs you nothing. A photo from far away beats a second bite.

### Cautions
- No rattle is not “harmless.”
- Young copperheads still bite. The yellow tail tip is not a toy.
- **NY**: Hudson Valley, southeastern counties, and some Catskill foothills. Not an Adirondack High-Peaks species. Statewide “I saw a copperhead” stories are often milk snakes.
- Not medical advice. Not a verdict. Confirm with more than the phone.
summary: Copper head, hourglass bands, no rattle. Leaf litter and Hudson rock. Space and care. Unknown.

title: Blacklegged tick: small, dark, check.
body:
### Situation
Brush, oak, grass, and a warm Hudson or Catskill spring — or an Adirondack low-elevation portage. A sesame-to-apple-seed speck is on skin or cloth. You need a pull and a date, not a trail diagnosis.

### Traits
Adults are small: about 1/8 in (3 mm) unfed, darker legs than some dog-tick types. Nymphs are poppy-seed small and do most of the quiet work in late spring and early summer. Scutum dark. They quest on grass and shrub edges at about knee-to-waist height, also in leaf litter. After a feed they swell gray. Color and size shift with life stage — that is why this card’s visual lock is modest.

### Documented parts
Mouthparts embed in skin. This species is a historically documented vector for several infections in New York. This pack does not name a disease from a rash on the trail and does not treat ticks as food. Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Dog ticks and other hard ticks share the same brush and are not in this deck, so the runner-up is Unknown. A freckle, a scab, and a spider bite also fool a camera. ID confidence (typical visual): 58%. Runner-up/lookalike: 30% (Unknown).

### Do
1. Pants into socks. Stay on the tread when grass leans in.
2. Night skin check: belt, scalp, behind knees, armpits, socks, waistband. Partner the back.
3. Tweezers close to the skin. Steady pull. Do not twist, burn, or grease it. See aid-tick.
4. Wash the site. Save the tick in a bag if you can. Write the date.
5. A spreading rash or fever days later is a get-to-care problem. You do not name the infection on the trail.

### Cautions
- Crushing the body over the hole is a bad finish.
- High Adirondack rock is not a free pass on the hike out through brush.
- **NY**: Hudson Valley and Long Island are heavy. Catskills and the Adirondack perimeter are in play. Statewide now, not a downstate-only story.
- Not medical advice. Not a verdict. Confirm with more than the phone.
summary: Tiny dark tick in NY brush. Pants in socks, night check, steady pull. Do not name a disease on the trail.

title: Raccoon: mask, night camp.
body:
### Situation
A masked night visitor at a Hudson lean-to, a Catskill lean-to, or an Adirondack dumpster trail. The pack zipper and the latrine are the problems. Do not make it a pet.

### Traits
Body like a small heavy dog, 15–25 lb (7–11 kg) common. Black mask across the eyes, ringed tail, grizzled gray coat. Hands look like hands; they open coolers. Tracks: five long toes, like a tiny human palm, often in mud at the water scoop. Latrine: repeated piles on a log or attic corner. Day dens in trees, culverts, and lean-to roofs. A waddle that can still climb.

### Documented parts
Some historical accounts list meat as a used part. This pack logs hazard and hygiene only. Bite and scratch are a care problem. Roundworm in latrines is a hand-and-water problem. Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
A distant dark climber at dusk can be a bear cub. Cats and foxes sit outside this deck. ID confidence (typical visual): 75%. Runner-up/lookalike: 16% (black bear).

### Do
1. Cook and sleep apart. Hang or canister. A “clever” camp is a training site.
2. Do not feed. A fed raccoon brings friends and teeth.
3. If it will not leave: make noise from a safe stance, keep the door, do not corner it in the shelter.
4. Bite or scratch: wash, then get to care. Do not run a home observation plan in the woods.
5. Do not sweep a latrine with a bare hand. Treat water below a den tree.

### Cautions
- Day-active and unafraid is a reason to give more space, not less.
- Dogs that fight a raccoon hand you the wound.
- **NY**: Statewide, including High-Peaks camps and Hudson towns. Winter does not empty the lean-tos.
- Not medical advice. Not a verdict. Confirm with more than the phone.
summary: Mask and ringed tail at a NY camp. Food discipline. Do not handle. Distant dark shape can be a bear.

title: Coyote: lanky, dusk call.
body:
### Situation
A lanky dog-shaped animal on a Hudson field edge, a Catskill woods road, or an Adirondack carry at first light. You heard yips after dark. Space and food discipline, not a chase.

### Traits
Shoulder height often 21–24 in (53–61 cm), slimmer than most pet dogs of the same height. Coat gray-tan with a darker back, tail usually down when it trots. Ears pointed, muzzle long. Tracks: oval, nail marks, a straight trot line more often than a dog’s wander. Calls: group yips and a high howl, often after dusk. They use edges — field, marsh, suburban woods — and the High Peaks too.

### Documented parts
Some historical accounts list meat and fur as used parts. This pack logs behavior only and does not treat wildlife as a field ration. Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Domestic dogs and foxes share the same roads and are not in this deck, so the runner-up is Unknown. A distant trot can also be a deer. ID confidence (typical visual): 72%. Runner-up/lookalike: 18% (Unknown).

### Do
1. Give the trail. Pick up small dogs. A dog that starts the chase hands you the problem.
2. If it follows: stand tall, make noise, do not run. Keep the group together.
3. Hang food. A sloppy camp trains a sloppy animal.
4. A sick or stumbling canid is a space-and-care problem. Do not corner it.
5. Night yips are information, not a reason to leave the shelter.

### Cautions
- Eastern coyotes can look large. Size alone is not a wolf lock in this pack.
- Feeding “just once” at a trailhead is how bold animals get made.
- **NY**: Statewide, including Adirondack interiors and Hudson suburbs. Catskill evenings are loud with them after a quiet day.
- Not medical advice. Not a verdict. Confirm with more than the phone.
summary: Lanky wild canid, dusk edges, group yips. Give space. Dogs on a short line. Specimen stays Unknown.

title: Unknown. Do not upgrade it.
body:
### Situation
A photo or a roadside plant does not match a card you already knew. New Mexico runs mountains into desert in one afternoon. Hunger and a pretty flower do not finish an ID.

### Traits
No stable traits. Leaf shape, spines, bark, and habitat disagree, or you only have a distant shot. Night, glare, and a 2 in (5 cm) crop are enough to break a match.
ID confidence (typical visual): 9%. Runner-up/lookalike: 24% (creosote).

### Documented parts
None you get to use. Historical food notes on other plants do not transfer to this specimen. Toxins are unlisted because the name is unlisted.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Everything. Creosote flats, locoweed meadows, and cactus joints all get dumped here when the picture is bad. Animals that are only a dark shape at dusk also belong on this hub until a body card fits.

### Do
1. Leave it in the ground. Hands off spines, sap, and unknown berries.
2. If you log it: whole plant, leaf, flower or fruit, bark, and the ground it sits on. Distance in yd and m.
3. Default the name to Unknown. Do not let a trail-name argument raise the percentage.
4. Spend the hour on water, shade, and signal. See food-not-first.
5. Kids and dogs get the same rule. Especially pea flowers and white umbels.
6. If someone already put Unknown in a mouth: sample in a bag, time, get to care. Do not invent a home remedy.

### Cautions
- Phone guess apps are still a guess in airplane mode.
- Cooking does not turn Unknown into Known.
- **New Mexico**: a 4,000 ft (1220 m) drop from ponderosa into creosote is normal. Do not import a mountain name onto a basin shrub.
summary: Unmatched NM photo stays Unknown. Log it if you want, then go back to water and shade.

title: Creosote. Rain-on-resin smell.
body:
### Situation
Low evergreen shrub on southern NM basins and alluvial flats. After rain the air smells like pharmacy resin. You are below the ponderosa belt, often under 5,000 ft (1520 m).

### Traits
Tiny olive opposite leaves, varnished, on brittle twiggy stems. Yellow five-petal flowers; fuzzy white seed balls later. Plants stand a few feet apart as if they agreed on spacing. Height often 3–6 ft (0.9–1.8 m). Crush a leaf: creosote-paint smell.
ID confidence (typical visual): 71%. Runner-up/lookalike: 18% (unknown desert shrub).

### Documented parts
Leaf and resin infusions appear in historical medicinal notes. Internal use has a liver-and-kidney toxicity record this pack will not turn into a recipe. Not a forage target.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Other dark basin shrubs in a bad photo. Tarbush shares Chihuahuan flats but is not on this NM card set — if the leaf is sticky-dark with nodding yellow heads, do not force creosote. Distant green lumps go to the unknown hub.

### Do
1. Name habitat first: open desert scrub, not a mountain meadow.
2. Check opposite tiny leaves and the rain smell before you lock the card.
3. Do not brew a “desert tea” because a story said so.
4. Use the plant as a place marker: creosote flats mean heat, little shade, and long water carries.
5. Log flower color and spacing if you photograph it.
6. Move on. Shelter and water beat a shrub clinic.

### Cautions
- Resin on cuts is sticky, not a clinic dressing.
- **New Mexico**: creosote is a south-and-basin plant. Do not file a Sangre de Cristo alpine shrub as creosote.
summary: Tiny varnished opposite leaves, yellow flowers, rain-resin smell on southern NM basins.

title: Soaptree yucca. Tall white plume.
body:
### Situation
A fountain of narrow leaves and, in season, a tall pale flower stalk on NM plains, dunes, and desert grassland. Soaptree (Yucca elata) is the common tall one on open ground, not a forest understory plant.

### Traits
Flexible, sharp-tipped leaves in a basal rosette; old leaves hang like a hula skirt on a trunk that may rise several feet. Fine white fibers peel from leaf edges. Flower stalk can top 6–15 ft (1.8–4.6 m) with creamy bells. Trunk spongy compared with a tree.
ID confidence (typical visual): 74%. Runner-up/lookalike: 16% (ocotillo).

### Documented parts
Flowers, stalks, and fruits show up in historical food notes for yuccas. Roots and trunk hold saponins — the “soap” in the name — which are a wash note, not a stew note. Leaf fiber is a cordage note. Toxins and saponins stay on the card.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Ocotillo is the tall desert mix-up: ocotillo is many unbranched spiny wands from one crown, with red tube flowers after rain, not a white plume on a leafy skirt. Other yuccas and sotol (Chihuahuan) share the rosette idea; soaptree’s peeling fibers and taller trunk help. Bad photos go unknown.

### Do
1. Count the habit: one skirted trunk plus a plume, or many coachwhip canes (ocotillo).
2. Do not grab leaf tips. The point is a puncture.
3. Fiber stripping is a craft note for people who already knew the plant, not a reason to cut a living crown.
4. Keep the soap story in the historical column. Do not put root foam in a wound or a pot.
5. Log stalk height and leaf-fiber peels if you photograph it.
6. Unknown if you cannot see the crown.

### Cautions
- Saponins foam. Foam is not a field-care product you chose from a manual.
- **New Mexico**: soaptree likes open basins and plains. A short stiff mountain yucca is a different card you do not have here.
summary: Skirted trunk, peeling leaf fibers, tall creamy flower plume on NM plains and desert grassland.

title: Prickly pear. Flat pads.
body:
### Situation
Flattened cactus pads on NM plains, foothills, and southern desert. Pads stack into a shrub or a low clump. Fruits (tunas) sit on pad edges in season. This is the cactus people sit on.

### Traits
Pads (cladodes) are flat, not round in cross-section. Large spines plus glochids — tiny barbed hairs in felt dots that slide into skin and stay. Flowers yellow, orange, or magenta. Fruits oval, often red or purple when ripe. Height from ankle-high to 4–5 ft (1.2–1.5 m) on some plains stands.
ID confidence (typical visual): 73%. Runner-up/lookalike: 20% (cholla).

### Documented parts
Pads and fruits appear in a long historical food record (nopales, tunas) across the Southwest. Glochids and spines are the immediate injury. Oxalate and mucilage notes exist; this pack still issues no field verdict on a wild pad.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Cholla: cylindrical joints that look like rope or a bristling stick, not paddles. If the stem is round in cross-section, it is not prickly pear. Hedgehog and barrel cacti are ribbed columns — different cards, not in this cut.

### Do
1. Look at the cross-section: paddle vs cylinder.
2. Do not brush it. Glochids ride socks into the sleeping bag.
3. If you are already full of glochids: tape or a smear of pitch to lift them, then tweezers. Do not rub.
4. Do not peel a wild pad into the cook pot because a restaurant used a farm pad.
5. Give javelina the patch; they use this country.
6. Log flower color and pad shape if you photograph it.

### Cautions
- Glochids are the injury that keeps giving. See aid-wound if a cluster embeds.
- **New Mexico**: plains and desert. A high wet meadow is the wrong habitat; do not force the name.
summary: Flat cactus pads with glochids and edge fruits. Cylinder joints are cholla, not this card.

title: Cholla. Round joints, dense spines.
body:
### Situation
A bristling cactus with cylindrical joints on NM desert and plains edges. Joints detach on contact and ride away on a boot or a dog. “Jumping” is detach, not a leap.

### Traits
Stems round in cross-section, segmented, often in a shrub or a short tree of joints. Spines dense, pale, covering the green. Flowers at joint tips, magenta or yellow depending on kind. Fallen joints root. Height from shin-high cane cholla to 4–8 ft (1.2–2.4 m). A detached joint looks like a spiny pickle.
ID confidence (typical visual): 70%. Runner-up/lookalike: 22% (prickly pear).

### Documented parts
Flower buds appear in historical food notes for some chollas after serious spine work. Spines and glochids are the injury. This pack does not convert a bud story into a field meal.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Prickly pear: flat pads. If you can set a notebook on the stem, it is not cholla. Young cholla and a fat prickly-pear fruit can fool a cropped photo — zoom out to the whole plant.

### Do
1. Step around, not over. A joint on the far side of a boot is how it travels.
2. Dogs up or around the patch. A muzzle full of cholla is a care problem.
3. Comb a joint out with a stick or pliers. Do not slap it with a bare hand.
4. Night: lamp the trail. Detached joints sit in the tread within a step — 2 ft (0.6 m) is enough.
5. Do not harvest buds off a wild plant because a cookbook mentioned them.
6. If spines are deep, see aid-wound. You are not “toughing out” a dozen barbed points.

### Cautions
- A joint in skin is a puncture set, not one poke.
- **New Mexico**: common on southern desert and lower plains. Alpine tundra does not grow cholla.
summary: Cylindrical spiny joints that detach into boots and dogs. Flat pads are prickly pear.

title: Juniper. Scale-leaf woodland.
body:
### Situation
Open woodland on NM foothills and mesas: short evergreens, shredded bark, pale “berries.” Pinyon-juniper (PJ) sits between grassland and the ponderosa belt, often 5,000–7,500 ft (1520–2290 m).

### Traits
Leaves are scales pressed to the twig, or short awls on young shoots — not long needles in bundles. Bark shreds in strips. Seed cones look like small blue or copper berries with a waxy bloom. Crown irregular, often several stems. Height commonly 8–25 ft (2.4–7.6 m). Crushed spray: gin-closet smell on many trees.
ID confidence (typical visual): 69%. Runner-up/lookalike: 21% (ponderosa).

### Documented parts
Fleshy cones (“berries”) appear in historical flavoring and medicinal notes. Some people get a gut revolt from them. Inner bark and twigs have craft and fire notes. This is not a snack card.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Ponderosa: long needles in bundles of two or three, puzzle-plate bark on older trunks, a real forest tree. If you see needle bundles, it is not juniper. Pinyon pine (not in this cut) also shares the woodland — bundles of short needles, nuts that other books treat as food; still Unknown here if you cannot see bundles vs scales.

### Do
1. Check leaf type: scales/awls vs needle bundles.
2. Use dead lower twigs as a fire note if you already needed tinder. Live limbs are a poor trade.
3. Do not graze the berries because a cocktail used a farm juniper.
4. PJ woodland is dry, lightning-friendly, and short on surface water. Plan the carry.
5. Log berry color and bark shred if you photograph it.
6. Widow-makers: dead juniper tops snap. See deadfall logic in hazards.

### Cautions
- Scale-leaf evergreens that are not juniper exist. If the berry-cones and shred bark are missing, Unknown.
- **New Mexico**: PJ is the mesa default. Do not call a yellow-bark giant on a mountain slope a juniper.
summary: Scale leaves, shredded bark, waxy berry-cones in NM pinyon-juniper woodland. Bundles mean pine.

title: Ponderosa. Long needles, puzzle bark.
body:
### Situation
Yellow-bark pine forest on NM mountains: Sandias, Jemez, Sacramentos, Gila high country. You have left the desert scrub. Often 6,000–9,000 ft (1830–2740 m). Vanilla or butterscotch bark smell on warm afternoons.

### Traits
Needles long, typically 4–8 in (10–20 cm), in bundles of two or three. Older bark in jigsaw plates, yellow-orange in the cracks. Cones armed with a prickle on the scale tip. Trunk tall and straight in a park-like stand, or a single giant over oak brush. Needles in bundles — that is the pine flag.
ID confidence (typical visual): 78%. Runner-up/lookalike: 14% (juniper).

### Documented parts
Inner bark and needle infusions appear in historical emergency and tea notes. Ponderosa needles have an abortifacient toxicity record in cattle; do not invent a needle tea for anyone. Pitch is a fire note, not candy.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Juniper: scale leaves, berry-cones, shredded bark, shorter woodland tree. If there are no needle bundles, it is not ponderosa. Other pines (pinyon, limber, bristlecone in high ranges) share bundles — pinyon needles are short; if you cannot count bundles and length, Unknown.

### Do
1. Confirm bundles of long needles and, on older trees, puzzle bark.
2. Dead lower twigs and pitch are tinder notes. Do not ring a live trunk.
3. Do not brew needle tea because a blog did.
4. Lightning and snags: ponderosa stands run fire. Look up before you camp.
5. See plants-pine-traits if you are arguing pine vs spruce.
6. Log bundle count and needle length if you photograph it.

### Cautions
- Spruce and fir sit needles one-by-one. Wrong family if you skip the bundle check.
- **New Mexico**: ponderosa is a mountain belt plant. Creosote flats do not grow it. A basin “pine” in a photo is probably not this card.
summary: Long bundled needles and yellow puzzle bark in the NM mountain pine belt. Scales mean juniper.

title: Locoweed. Livestock toxin.
body:
### Situation
A low pea-family plant in NM meadows, plains, and open slopes. Purple, blue, or white pea flowers; livestock men already swore at it. You are not here to graze horses. Locoweed is a toxin card first.

### Traits
Compound leaves, lots of small leaflets, often silvery-hairy. Pea flowers in a spike or head; later inflated or tight pods. Sits in the open, not a desert wand. Many Astragalus and Oxytropis species wear the loco name — that is why visual confidence stays modest. Height often 4–16 in (10–40 cm).
ID confidence (typical visual): 46%. Runner-up/lookalike: 32% (unknown).

### Documented parts
No historical food part you should care about. Swainsonine and related alkaloids: livestock (horses, cattle, sheep) get locoism — neurologic damage, wasting, abortion. Selenium-accumulating milkvetches add a second toxin story. Humans are not a loophole.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Other pea-family wildflowers, vetch, and lupine-type spikes. A cropped flower is not a species. Creosote is a woody desert shrub, not this. If you cannot see pea flowers plus compound leaves in a rangeland setting, send it to the unknown hub.

### Do
1. Treat pea flowers in NM range as a do-not-mouth problem until you already knew the plant from before this trip.
2. Keep horses and pack stock off the patch if you are traveling with them.
3. Do not “try a leaflet.” Loco is a dose over days in stock; you still do not run the experiment.
4. Log flower color, leaflet count, and habitat. Still Unknown at species.
5. Kids: pea pods look like a garden. They are not.
6. If stock or a person already ingested a pea-family unknown: get to care. This is not trail-treatable.

### Cautions
- Not medical advice. Locoism is a veterinary and clinic problem.
- **New Mexico**: locoweed is a mountains-to-plains plant, including high meadows. It is not a cactus-belt look.
summary: Pea-family rangeland plant. Livestock toxin (swainsonine). Mouth stays empty. Species often Unknown.

title: Ocotillo. Coachwhip wands, red tips.
body:
### Situation
A spray of long unbranched canes from one crown on southern NM desert — Organ–Franklin country, bootheel, Las Cruces basin. Dead-looking sticks until rain, then leaves, then fire-red tube flowers at the tips.

### Traits
10–60 canes, 6–20 ft (1.8–6.1 m), gray with stout spines, little side branching. After rain: oval leaves along the cane. Flowers in a cluster at the tip, red to orange, tubular. Canes rise from a tight base, not a leafy yucca skirt. Dry-season plants look like a bundle of fishing rods.
ID confidence (typical visual): 81%. Runner-up/lookalike: 12% (soaptree yucca).

### Documented parts
Flowers appear in historical nectar-sucking notes. Canes used as living fence posts in border country. Not a staple food plant. Spines are a puncture. Sap is not a water source.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Soaptree yucca: one skirted trunk and a white flower plume, not a bouquet of spiny wands. Sotol sends one tall stalk from a saw-leaf rosette (Chihuahuan card). If you see many gray coachwhips from one crown, it is ocotillo.

### Do
1. Confirm many unbranched spiny canes from one base.
2. Do not grab a cane. The spines are real.
3. After-rain leaves are a weather note: the basin got water. Your bottles may not have.
4. Do not strip flowers into a bottle because a story mentioned nectar.
5. Use the silhouette as a south-desert flag. You are not in the Sangres anymore.
6. Log cane count and flower color if you photograph it.

### Cautions
- A leafless ocotillo is still ocotillo. Do not call it dead sticks and snap canes for fun.
- **New Mexico**: southern desert. A mountain “wand shrub” at 8,000 ft (2440 m) is the wrong habitat.
summary: Many unbranched spiny canes from one crown; red tube flowers after rain on southern NM desert.

title: Western diamondback. Diamonds and a banded tail.
body:
### Situation
A heavy rattlesnake on southern NM desert, scrub, and lower rocky slopes. Rattle, coil, or a still snake on warm dirt at dusk. Hands and feet where you can see them.

### Traits
Thick body, keeled scales, brown-to-gray diamonds down the back with light edges. Tail has bold black-and-white rings before the rattle — the “coon tail.” Head triangular, heat pits. Adults often 3–4 ft (0.9–1.2 m), sometimes more. Does not have to rattle before it strikes.
ID confidence (typical visual): 72%. Runner-up/lookalike: 17% (gila monster).

### Documented parts
Venom glands in the head. A bite is a medical evacuation, not a field clinic. Historical trophy and meat notes exist in ranch country; this pack is not a hunting tag and not a kitchen.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Other rattlesnakes (prairie, black-tailed) share NM; tail rings and diamond pattern help, but a cropped tail is not a species. Gila monster is a beaded lizard, not a snake — fat tail, orange-pink and black, no rattle. People dump both into “desert venom” in a blurry photo.

### Do
1. Stop. Find it. Step back more than a body length of the snake.
2. Give it the trail. Do not kill it for sport; a second bite is a common trophy tax.
3. Night: lamp the tread. They sit on warm roads and rock.
4. Headphones off in snake season on desert trails.
5. Bite: see aid-snake. You are done hiking as a hike. Keep the bitten part still-ish, walk out if that is the only clock, get to care.
6. Teach the group the rattle once so the first time is not a sprint off a ledge.

### Cautions
- Not medical advice. Do not cut, suck, or ice a bite into a worse problem.
- Dead snakes still bite on reflex.
- **New Mexico**: southern and lower country. This is not an alpine-tundra snake. Watch below roughly 6,000–7,000 ft (1830–2130 m) in the heat months.
summary: Heavy desert rattler with back diamonds and black-white tail rings. Space, then the snake-bite card.

title: Black bear. Mountains, not the creosote flat.
body:
### Situation
A dark bear in NM mountain forest and foothill oak — Gila, Jemez, Sangres, Sacramentos. Surprise at a carcass, berry patch, or a sloppy cook site is the usual fail. Desert basins are not the default.

### Traits
Shoulder hump modest compared with a grizzly lecture you imported. Profile doglike-to-round, ears round, tail short. Color black, brown, or cinnamon — “black” is the species, not the paint. No rump higher than shoulder like a javelina herd on a trail. Adult much larger than a peccary — often 4–6 ft (1.2–1.8 m) long; cubs still do not look like a pig with a white collar.
ID confidence (typical visual): 73%. Runner-up/lookalike: 16% (javelina).

### Documented parts
Historically taken as game in some seasons and units. Fat and meat show up in old notes. This pack is not a tag and not a field-butcher class. A bear on a food bag is a food problem.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Javelina: smaller, herd, coarse salt-and-pepper coat, pale collar, snout, rump-high, desert and southern scrub. A dusk blob in prickly pear is more often peccary than bear. Elk is a hoofed ungulate with a pale rump patch. Mountain lion is a long-tailed cat.

### Do
1. Make noise on blind corners and in loud creeks. Give it a door out.
2. If you see one: stop, talk low, do not run, do not kneel. Back away, group tight.
3. If it comes in: hold ground, get big, bear spray if you carry it and the range matches the label.
4. Cook and sleep apart. Hang or canister. See animals-food-hang.
5. A bear standing up is often trying to smell you. Still give it the trail.
6. Contact: fight. This is black bear range.

### Cautions
- A cub means another bear.
- **New Mexico**: mountains and timbered foothills. Do not write a bear story onto a javelina trail in the bootheel without cause.
summary: Mountain forest bear, any color. Dusk desert pigs with collars are javelina. Cook away from sleep.

title: Mountain lion. Long tail, do not run.
body:
### Situation
A long-tailed cat on NM mountains, canyons, and foothill deer country — statewide where deer live. A stalk, a track the size of your palm, or a glimpse at dusk. You want to look like a person, not a deer.

### Traits
Tan to tawny, no spots as an adult. Tail long, thick, black-tipped, often a third of the animal. Head small for the body, hind legs built to leap. Tracks: four toes, no claw marks most of the time, bigger than a big dog. A 7–8 ft (2.1–2.4 m) animal including tail is not a rumor.
ID confidence (typical visual): 58%. Runner-up/lookalike: 24% (black bear).

### Documented parts
Historically taken under game laws in some units. This pack is not a tag. Claws and teeth are the injury. Not a food plan.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Bobcat (not in this cut): spots, short tail, smaller. A blurry tan mammal in timber gets dumped on bear — bear is bulkier, no long tail. House-cat scale is wrong. If you only have a rump in brush, Unknown.

### Do
1. Face it. Stand. Pick up kids. Do not run. Do not turn your back.
2. Get big. Talk. Throw if it comes in. Fight if it hits.
3. Group up. Give it a way out. Do not corner it in a boulder cave.
4. Dawn and dusk: look up-slope and behind, not just at your shoes.
5. Dogs close. A dog in the brush can hand you the cat.
6. If it follows at distance, hold the face-on walk toward people, a vehicle, or an open site.

### Cautions
- Playing dead is the wrong script for a cat.
- Crouching to pick a rock is prey-shaped. Step to the rock, stay tall.
- **New Mexico**: lions use mountains and desert canyons. Deer are the pantry. You are crossing the pantry.
summary: Tawny cat with a long black-tipped tail. Face it, stand tall, do not run. Fight if it hits.

title: Javelina. Collared peccary, not a bear cub.
body:
### Situation
A grizzled, pig-shaped herd animal in southern NM desert and scrub — prickly pear country, bootheel, Las Cruces basin. Musk, a cough-grunt, or a dozen low bodies crossing an arroyo. Not a feral hog lecture from another state, and not a bear.

### Traits
Shoulder height often 18–24 in (45–60 cm). Coarse salt-and-pepper coat, pale collar from shoulder to shoulder, big head, snout, tiny tail. Rump looks high. Herds of several to a dozen-plus. Musk gland on the rump. Canids they are not; collared peccary they are.
ID confidence (typical visual): 71%. Runner-up/lookalike: 18% (black bear).

### Documented parts
Historically taken as game in southern units. Musk gland taints careless butchery in old notes. This pack is not a tag and not a field-kitchen.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Black bear cub or small bear at dusk: no pale collar, no herd of pig-bodies, wrong habitat if you are in high spruce. Feral hogs (not in this cut) are taller, longer-snouted, often with floppy ears — do not force a hog name onto a collar. Elk is huge and hoof-wrong.

### Do
1. Give the herd the trail. Dogs off or tight — dogs start the charge.
2. Do not corner a band in a wash. They want an exit through you if you block it.
3. Night camps in prickly pear: hang food anyway; peccary will wreck a loose kitchen.
4. If one clicks teeth or bluff-charges: get off the line, put a shrub between you, do not kick.
5. Photograph the collar and the herd, not a cropped snout.
6. You are in southern desert if this card fits. Water and heat still rank above a wildlife moment.

### Cautions
- They are not cute pigs. Tusks cut.
- **New Mexico**: south. A Sangre de Cristo meadow does not hold javelina. Do not paste this card on a mountain bear.
summary: Small herding peccary with a pale collar in southern NM cactus country. Not a bear cub.

title: Elk. Pale rump, mountain parks.
body:
### Situation
A large tan-and-dark ungulate in NM mountain parks, meadows, and timber — north-central ranges, Gila, high Sacramentos. Rut in fall: bugle, herds, stupid tourists walking in. Calves in early summer. Space.

### Traits
Horse-sized. Dark neck and head on a paler body, cream rump patch. Antlers on bulls, swept back. Cows look like big deer with a shaggy neck. Tracks split-hoof, much larger than deer. A standing elk at 50 yd (45 m) is still too close if it is a cow with a calf or a September bull.
ID confidence (typical visual): 77%. Runner-up/lookalike: 12% (black bear).

### Documented parts
Historically taken as game under license. Meat shows up in every mountain freezer story. This pack is not a tag.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Deer are smaller, no cream billboard rump like elk. Moose (rare to absent on most NM units) is darker with a palmate antler and a bell — do not import a Colorado moose script without cause. A dark timber blob can get called bear; elk has legs, a rump patch, and a deer face.

### Do
1. Distance. If you need a phone zoom, you are in range of a charge.
2. Do not plant yourself between a cow and a calf, or on a rutting bull’s line to the herd.
3. Dogs off. A dog that barks elk and runs to you has handed you the problem.
4. In timber, give the trail. They were using it.
5. After a close one, sit. The next mistake is rushing a talus slope on adrenaline.
6. See animals-elk for the behavior card this vision card is not replacing.

### Cautions
- A bull in the rut does not yield because you have a trail name.
- **New Mexico**: mountains and high parks. Desert creosote is the wrong habitat. A basin “elk” is probably livestock or a wish.
summary: Large mountain ungulate with a cream rump patch. Space in the rut and around calves.

title: Gila monster. Venomous lizard. Do not handle.
body:
### Situation
A thick, beaded lizard on southwestern NM rock and desert — bootheel, Hidalgo and Grant country, adjacent low canyons. Slow, often in a burrow or at a trail edge after rain. This is the venomous lizard, not a cartoon. Do not pick it up.

### Traits
Heavy body, short legs, bead-like scales (osteoderms). Pattern black with orange, pink, or salmon blotches — not stripes like a racer. Tail fat, stores reserves, not a rattle. Tongue flicks. Adults often 14–20 in (35–50 cm) total. Moves slow until it does not want to be held.
ID confidence (typical visual): 76%. Runner-up/lookalike: 14% (western diamondback).

### Documented parts
Venom delivered by a chewing bite from glands in the lower jaw — not a rattlesnake strike. Painful, medically significant. Historical curiosity and trophy notes exist. Never a handle-and-show animal. Not a food animal.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Western diamondback: a snake with diamonds and a rattle, not beads. Other lizards (chuckwalla, collared) lack the orange-black bead armor. A cropped fat tail in gravel gets dumped on “baby rattler” — look for legs.

### Do
1. Do not handle. Do not move it off the trail with a boot or a stick unless you must pass, and even then give it the trail.
2. Teach kids: pretty beads are the warning, not a pet.
3. Dogs off. A chew-fight is how people get involved.
4. If a bite happens: the lizard may hold on. Get free without tearing a bigger wound if you can, then aid-wound and get to care. This is not a suck-the-venom story.
5. Photograph from well back. A 3 ft (0.9 m) selfie is how bites start.
6. You are in SW NM if this card is in play. Water and heat still rank.

### Cautions
- Not medical advice. No field antivenom ritual. Clinic.
- Illegal to harass or collect in many jurisdictions. Leave it.
- **New Mexico**: southwestern low desert and rocky canyons. Not a Sangre de Cristo animal. Not an alpine sighting.
summary: Beaded black-and-orange venomous lizard of SW NM. Do not handle. Chewing bite, then clinic.

title: Unknown. Basin photo stays Unknown.
body:
### Situation
A Chihuahuan basin photo does not match a card you already knew. Creosote flats, limestone bajadas, and arroyo mesquite all throw lookalikes. Heat and a cropped spine are enough to break a name.

### Traits
No stable traits. You have a gray shrub, a rosette, or a road-killed blur. Night, dust, and a 2 in (5 cm) frame are the usual fail.
ID confidence (typical visual): 9%. Runner-up/lookalike: 26% (creosote).

### Documented parts
None you get to use. Fiber, sap, and pod stories on named plants do not transfer here. Toxins unlisted because the name is unlisted.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Creosote is the shrub people force onto every basin photo. Tarbush, lechuguilla, and a young mesquite all sit in the same rectangle. Animals that are only a dust cloud belong here until a body card fits.

### Do
1. Hands off sap, spines, and unknown berries.
2. If you log it: whole plant, leaf, flower, the limestone or sand it sits on, and a scale (boot, tool).
3. Keep the name Unknown. A basin nickname is not a species.
4. Rank shade, water, and the next mile. See food-not-first.
5. Kids and dogs: same rule. Pea flowers and milky sap especially.
6. If someone already put Unknown in a mouth: bag a sample, time, get to care.

### Cautions
- Airplane-mode ID apps are still a guess.
- **Chihuahuan**: basin-and-range, often 3,500–5,500 ft (1070–1680 m). Do not paste a Sonoran saguaro name or a Rockies pine name onto this ground.
summary: Unmatched Chihuahuan photo stays Unknown. Log habitat, then go back to shade and water.

title: Creosote. Chihuahuan co-dominant.
body:
### Situation
The gray-green shrub that owns Chihuahuan basins from southern NM through west Texas into northern Mexico. After rain the flats smell like resin and wet dust. Plants spaced as if each had a survey crew.

### Traits
Tiny opposite varnished leaves, yellow flowers, fuzzy white seed balls. Height often 3–6 ft (0.9–1.8 m). Stems dark, brittle. Crush a leaf: creosote-paint. Stands mix with tarbush on many flats — two shrubs, one landscape.
ID confidence (typical visual): 68%. Runner-up/lookalike: 24% (tarbush).

### Documented parts
Leaf and resin infusions appear in historical medicinal notes. Internal use has a liver-and-kidney toxicity record. Not a forage target. This pack will not write a tea.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Tarbush: darker, stickier, broader leaves, nodding yellow flower heads, tar smell rather than pharmacy resin. A distant gray shrub on a basin photo is a coin flip — get a leaf. Ocotillo is wands, not a rounded bush.

### Do
1. Get a leaf: tiny opposite varnish vs broader sticky tarbush.
2. Use the stand as a place marker: open basin, heat, long water carry, little shade.
3. Do not brew desert resin because a story said so.
4. After-rain smell confirms habitat, not a recipe.
5. Log spacing and flower if you photograph it.
6. Move. Shade and water beat a shrub argument.

### Cautions
- Resin on skin is a mess, not a dressing.
- **Chihuahuan**: creosote–tarbush flats are the basin default. A mountain meadow plant is the wrong card.
summary: Tiny varnished opposite leaves on Chihuahuan basins. Tarbush is the sticky dark runner-up.

title: Lechuguilla. Shin dagger on limestone.
body:
### Situation
A small vicious agave on Chihuahuan limestone bajadas and slopes — the desert’s shin dagger. You meet it with a calf, not a field guide. Indicator plant for this desert, not a pot succulent.

### Traits
Tight rosette of stiff yellowish-green leaves, each ending in a needle spine that holds a hole in nylon. Leaf margins have small teeth. Height of the rosette often 1–2 ft (0.3–0.6 m); a skinny flower stalk much taller once in the plant’s life. Grows in colonies on caliche and limestone, not in a lawn.
ID confidence (typical visual): 66%. Runner-up/lookalike: 24% (sotol).

### Documented parts
Leaf fiber (ixtle) is the historical industrial note — cordage and bagging, not a meal. Sap and juice are irritant to skin and eyes. Livestock, especially sheep and goats, have a toxin record on this plant (steroidal sapogenins and related chemistry). Do not treat sap as water or as a dressing.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Sotol: long ribbon leaves with hooked teeth along the edge, more grass-like, “desert spoon” base; less of a stiff dagger rosette. Other small agaves exist; if you cannot see the terminal spine and limestone habit, Unknown. Ocotillo is wands, not a ground rosette.

### Do
1. Watch your shins on limestone slopes. Step around colonies.
2. Do not grab a leaf to “see if it is sharp.” It is.
3. Fiber stories do not authorize stripping a living rosette on a day hike.
4. Keep sap off cuts and eyes. Rinse if you get it.
5. Stock: do not bed goats on a lechuguilla slope.
6. Log the spine, teeth, and rock type if you photograph it.

### Cautions
- Not medical advice. Sap in an eye is a care problem.
- **Chihuahuan**: limestone and caliche flag. A sandy dune yucca is not this card.
summary: Small stiff agave on limestone. Fiber and toxin notes. Sap is irritant. Specimen stays Unknown.

title: Ocotillo. Basin coachwhips.
body:
### Situation
A bouquet of spiny unbranched canes on Chihuahuan bajadas and rocky basin edges. Looks dead until rain, then leaves, then red-orange tubes at the tips. South-facing rock is a typical stand.

### Traits
Many gray canes from one crown, 6–20 ft (1.8–6.1 m), stout spines, almost no side branches. Leaves oval, appear after rain, drop in drought. Tip flower clusters red to orange, tubular. Silhouette is a spray of fishing rods, not a yucca skirt and not a sotol fountain.
ID confidence (typical visual): 80%. Runner-up/lookalike: 12% (sotol).

### Documented parts
Flowers appear in historical nectar notes. Canes as living fence posts in ranch country. Spines puncture. Not a water plant. Not a staple.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Sotol: saw-toothed ribbon leaves in a big rosette and one tall woody stalk. Lechuguilla: tiny dagger rosette on the ground. Soaptree yucca (NM card, not this file) has a white plume and a leafy skirt. If the plant is many spiny wands from one base, it is ocotillo.

### Do
1. Confirm the wand bouquet before you lock the name.
2. Do not use a cane as a walking stick you grab mid-spine.
3. After-rain leaves mean the basin got a pulse of water. Your bottles still empty themselves.
4. Do not strip tip flowers into a jug.
5. Photograph the crown, not just one cane.
6. Habitat check: open Chihuahuan desert, not a pine forest.

### Cautions
- Leafless is the dry-season default. Do not snap “dead” canes.
- **Chihuahuan**: common on rocky slopes above the creosote flat. A high mountain “ocotillo” is a misfile.
summary: Many unbranched spiny canes from one crown; red tubes after rain on Chihuahuan rock slopes.

title: Sotol. Saw-leaf desert spoon.
body:
### Situation
A big grassy rosette with hooked teeth on Chihuahuan slopes and rocky benches. One tall woody flower stalk in season. People mix it with yucca, agave, and lechuguilla from 40 yd (37 m).

### Traits
Leaves long, ribbon-like, with backward-hooked teeth along both edges — a saw, not a smooth yucca. Base of a leaf is a spoon-shaped expansion (the “desert spoon”). Rosette can be 3–5 ft (0.9–1.5 m) across. Stalk rises like a mast, often 8–15 ft (2.4–4.6 m), with small pale flowers packed on it. No trunk skirt like soaptree.
ID confidence (typical visual): 69%. Runner-up/lookalike: 22% (lechuguilla).

### Documented parts
Trunk interiors appear in historical roasting and fermentation notes (regional spirits). Leaves are a fiber, thatch, and mat note. Saponins live in the plant. The saw-edge is the cut. This pack issues no food verdict and no still recipe.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Lechuguilla: smaller, stiffer, yellowish dagger leaves with a wicked terminal spine, limestone colonies. Yucca (soaptree on the NM deck): smoother leaf edges, peeling fibers, white bell plume. Ocotillo: wands, no rosette. If the leaf edge is a row of hooks, start with sotol.

### Do
1. Run a look, not a finger, along the leaf edge. Hooks point back.
2. Do not harvest a heart or a trunk because a bottle in a store had a Spanish name.
3. Fiber notes do not authorize stripping a living crown on a waterless afternoon.
4. Watch legs on a traverse; the saw is at shin height.
5. Log leaf-edge teeth and the spoon base if you photograph it.
6. Unknown if you only have a distant stalk against sky.

### Cautions
- Saponins and a saw-cut are two different ways to ruin a day.
- **Chihuahuan**: rocky slopes and benches. Not a wet mountain meadow plant.
summary: Ribbon leaves with hooked teeth and a spoon base. Fiber and saponin notes. No food verdict.

title: Tarbush. Sticky dark partner of creosote.
body:
### Situation
The darker, stickier shrub that shares Chihuahuan creosote flats — a co-indicator of this desert, not a weed from somewhere else. You smell tar more than pharmacy.

### Traits
Leaves broader than creosote, deep green to dark, sticky-resinous. Flower heads yellow, often nodding. Plant rounded, often 2–5 ft (0.6–1.5 m). Stems woody. Stands mixed with creosote: two textures in one photo if you get close. Crushed leaf: tar, not creosote varnish.
ID confidence (typical visual): 64%. Runner-up/lookalike: 26% (creosote).

### Documented parts
Not a food-plant record you should chase. Resin and livestock-browse notes exist; some stock avoid it, some get into trouble on poor range. No tea, no chew.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Creosote: tiny opposite varnished leaves, five-petal yellow flowers, white fuzzy balls, pharmacy smell. A phone shot from the truck is why these two swap names. Honey mesquite is a tree-shrub with ferny leaflets and thorns in drainages, not a tarry rounded bush on the open flat.

### Do
1. Leaf check: sticky-broad vs tiny-opposite.
2. Smell is a field note, not a recipe.
3. Do not put resin in a wound or a cup.
4. Use the mix (creosote + tarbush) as a Chihuahuan basin flag.
5. Log nodding yellow heads if you photograph it.
6. Unknown if you only have a gray lump in heat shimmer.

### Cautions
- Sticky leaves on clothes will remind you all day. That is not a toxin panic by itself, and not a reason to taste.
- **Chihuahuan**: open flats with creosote. A riparian mesquite bosque is a different card.
summary: Sticky dark Chihuahuan shrub with nodding yellow heads. Tiny varnished leaves are creosote.

title: Honey mesquite. Arroyo thorns and pods.
body:
### Situation
A thorny shrub or small tree along Chihuahuan arroyos, playa edges, and disturbed flats. Ferny leaves, long pods, yellow-white catkins in season. This is the drainage plant, not the open creosote boss.

### Traits
Bipinnate leaves — tiny leaflets on a ferny spray. Paired white or pale thorns at nodes, often 1–2 in (2.5–5 cm). Yellowish pods, long and slightly flattened, in clusters. Height from a multi-stem shrub to a 15–20 ft (4.6–6.1 m) tree in a wash. Bark rough, dark on older trunks.
ID confidence (typical visual): 72%. Runner-up/lookalike: 16% (unknown).

### Documented parts
Pods appear in a long historical food record for Southwest peoples (flour, meal). Thorns puncture. Seeds are hard; processing stories are not a trail recipe. This pack still files a wild tree as Unknown for a mouth.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Other mesquites and acacias (not all in this cut): thorn length, pod shape, and leaflet count separate them — a cropped ferny leaf is not enough. Tarbush and creosote are not ferny and not in the wash the same way. If you cannot see paired thorns plus long pods, Unknown.

### Do
1. Confirm ferny leaflets, paired thorns, and (in season) long pods.
2. Watch eyes and shins in a thicket. Thorns go through thin shirts.
3. Do not mill wild pods into a dinner because a museum panel mentioned flour.
4. Arroyo mesquite means a drainage. That can be a handrail — and a flash-flood trench.
5. Javelina and livestock use these thickets. Make a little noise.
6. Log thorn pairing and pod length if you photograph it.

### Cautions
- A wash camp under mesquite is still a wash camp. See weather and crossing logic.
- **Chihuahuan**: drainages and flats with extra water. The open tar-and-creosote plain is a different shrub.
summary: Ferny leaflets, paired thorns, long pods in Chihuahuan drainages. Historical pod notes, still Unknown.

title: Javelina. Collared peccary of the basin.
body:
### Situation
A low, grizzled herd in Chihuahuan scrub — prickly pear, mesquite edges, arroyos. Musk and a grunt. This desert’s pig-shaped resident, not a feral hog from a different ecoregion, and not a bear.

### Traits
Shoulder 18–24 in (45–60 cm). Salt-and-pepper bristly coat, pale collar, snout, high rump, almost no tail. Herds. Musk gland. Moves as a unit through cactus with less drama than you would.
ID confidence (typical visual): 73%. Runner-up/lookalike: 14% (unknown).

### Documented parts
Historically taken as game in desert units. Musk gland taints a sloppy job in old notes. Not a tag in this pack. Not a camp kitchen.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Feral hogs (not in this deck) run larger. A dusk blob with no collar and no herd may be Unknown — or a dog. Bears are a mountain story; on a creosote flat the dark low mammal is usually this card if the collar shows.

### Do
1. Give the band the trail. Dogs tight.
2. Do not block a wash they are using as a hallway.
3. Camp kitchens: peccary will open a loose bag. Hang or canister anyway.
4. Tooth-click or bluff: off the line, shrub between you.
5. Photograph collar plus herd, not a cropped snout.
6. Heat and water still outrank the wildlife moment.

### Cautions
- Tusks cut. This is not a petting zoo.
- **Chihuahuan**: basin and desert scrub. A high pine park is the wrong habitat for this card.
summary: Herding collared peccary in Chihuahuan cactus and mesquite. Not a hog lecture. Give them the wash.

title: Western diamondback. Basin rattler.
body:
### Situation
The heavy rattlesnake of Chihuahuan scrub, arroyo banks, and rocky basin edges. Warm roads at night. A rattle, a coil, or a still S-shape in the tread.

### Traits
Diamonds down the back with pale edges. Tail: bold black-and-white rings, then the rattle. Thick body, triangular head, heat pits. Often 3–4 ft (0.9–1.2 m). May not warn. Sits tight in mottled gravel.
ID confidence (typical visual): 74%. Runner-up/lookalike: 15% (unknown).

### Documented parts
Venom glands. A bite is an evacuation. Historical trophy notes exist; this pack is not a kill-it lesson and not a kitchen.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Other rattlers share edges of this desert. A cropped coil without the coon-tail rings goes Unknown — do not force atrox. Non-rattling whips and racers are thin and fast. A beaded orange-black lizard is a gila (NM card), not this snake.

### Do
1. Stop. Find it. Back up more than a body length.
2. Give it the tread. Do not pin it with a tool for a photo.
3. Night: lamp. They use the warm road and the warm rock.
4. Headphones off.
5. Bite: aid-snake. Hike becomes a medical carry. No cutting, no sucking.
6. Group: one person watches the snake while others step wide.

### Cautions
- Not medical advice. Dead snakes still bite on reflex.
- **Chihuahuan**: basin, scrub, and rocky slopes. Not a 10,000 ft (3050 m) meadow animal.
summary: Heavy Chihuahuan rattler with diamonds and black-white tail rings. Space, lamp at night, snake-bite card.

title: Roadrunner. Long tail, desert cuckoo.
body:
### Situation
A long-tailed ground bird sprinting a Chihuahuan road, ranch two-track, or arroyo bench. Crest up, streaked, not interested in your sandwich. Classic basin bird. Not a threat to people.

### Traits
Streaked brown and white, shaggy crest, long tail with white tips that flash when it runs. Strong legs, short rounded wings — it runs first, flies as a burst. Length often 20–24 in (50–60 cm) including tail. Zygodactyl feet (two toes forward, two back) if you get a track. May carry a lizard or a small snake.
ID confidence (typical visual): 83%. Runner-up/lookalike: 9% (unknown).

### Documented parts
Historical cultural notes exist; this is not a food bird in this pack and not a permitted take by default. Beak is a stab for prey, not for you. Leave it.
Specimen verdict: Unknown.

### Lookalikes
Other cuckoos are shy and in trees. A blurry streak on a road can be a thrasher or a lizard in a bad crop — if you do not have the long tail plus crest plus run, Unknown. Not a raptor. Not a road-killed “chicken.”

### Do
1. Give it the road. Do not chase it for a photo from a vehicle.
2. Dogs in. A dog that “herds” a roadrunner into cactus is your problem.
3. If it has a snake, back off. You do not need to finish that story.
4. Use the sighting as a habitat check: you are in desert scrub, plan water.
5. Log crest, tail, and gait if you photograph it.
6. Enjoy the one that pauses on a fence post, then walk your own mile.

### Cautions
- Protected in many places. Do not handle a stunned bird in the road without a reason and a plan.
- **Chihuahuan**: open desert and mesquite edges. A high spruce forest “roadrunner” is a misfile.
summary: Streaked crested ground cuckoo with a long tail on Chihuahuan roads. Runs first. Not a people threat.

title: I have nothing.
body:
### Situation
You have the clothes on your body and nothing in a pack. No knife, no ferro rod, no bottle, no tarp. That is the kit state. Say it once so you stop waiting for a tool to appear.

### Do
1. Stop. Sit. Name people, injuries, daylight, wind, and rain. Rank the next hour: people, then shelter, then water, then signal. Fire is a tool for heat, boil, or smoke. Calories last.
2. Heavy bleeding or a person who does not answer: that job wins. Use the aid cards you already have. Then come back to this tree.
3. If night, wind, rain, or a cold person is the killer, shelter first. Windbreak, then a small debris roof, then a twig bed. Finish something you can lie in. See skill-shelter-nothing.
4. Fire next only if you still need heat, a boil, or smoke, and you have dry deadwood and a site you will not ignite. Nest first, then a coal. Bow if you can make a string. Hand drill if you cannot. Green pine will not pay you. See skill-bow-drill.
5. Water: a source you can name, a vessel you can hold, then heat. Bark trough, hot rocks. Never take boil-rocks from the creek. Rolling boil is the disinfection. See skill-rock-boil.
6. Signal as soon as you have a site. Contrast, noise, a smoke column you can still control. Stay findable. See skill-signal-from-nothing.
7. Cordage only when it serves shelter, fire, or signal. Grass two-ply is slow. Timebox it. See skill-cordage-grass.
8. Food last. Unknown plants stay unknown. A missed dinner does not outrank a roof. See food-not-first.

### Cautions
- Walking while you “look for a better spot” is still walking the error larger.
- Do not put untreated still water in your mouth because you are scared. Heat it.
- **Rockies**: if it is already late morning above treeline, descent and a lee beat a pretty camp. Dry standing deadwood, not green pine, for any friction coal.
summary: Empty hands: stop, rank people then shelter, water, signal. Fire is a tool. Food last.

title: Knife only.
body:
### Situation
You have a knife and the clothes you are wearing. Maybe a belt. That is the kit state. The blade multiplies shelter, fire prep, and a vessel. It does not change the rank.

### Do
1. Stop. Sit. Sheath the knife while you think. Name people, daylight, weather. Same rank: people, shelter, water, signal. Calories last.
2. If the blade is a cheap folder, treat it as a cutter, not an axe. A stout fixed blade can baton. See tools-knife. Dull is dangerous — touch up before you need curls. See skill-knife-sharpen.
3. Shelter first if night or weather is the killer. Baton stakes and a ridge if the knife will take it. A debris hut still wins over a carved palace. See skill-debris-hut. Timebox 30–40 minutes.
4. Fire: split to dry heart, then a feather stick. A knife spine is not a ferro rod. Rounded stainless will not throw a useful spark. If you have no spark kit, you still need a coal method after the wood is prepped. See skill-feather-stick, skill-baton-wood.
5. Water: carve or fold a bark trough, then heat. The knife speeds the vessel. Disinfection is still a rolling boil. See skill-container-bark.
6. Signal as soon as you have a site. Cut bright cloth strips if that is the contrast you own. Stay put unless the site will kill you.
7. Cuts you actually use: slice, push, baton, a stop-cut notch for a lash. Never pry, never twist the tip, never cut toward the femoral. See skill-knife-cuts.
8. Food last. The knife is not a hunting license and unknown plants stay unknown. See food-not-first.

### Cautions
- A folding knife closed on a cold tendon is a bleeding card. Warm the hands or wait.
- Do not spend the dry hour carving art while the roof is still sky.
- **Rockies**: beetle-kill splits easy and throws chips. Eye line. Afternoon cells still own the ridge. Get the roof up, then play with curls.
summary: One blade: same rank as empty hands. Shelter, prep wood, vessel, signal. Food last. Sheath to think.

title: Lost, daylight.
body:
### Situation
You cannot name your location and you still have light. Light is the resource. Walking it away on a guess is the usual fail.

### Do
1. Stop. Sit. Pack stays with you. Mark this spot with a hat, stick, or cairn you can see from 50 yd (45 m).
2. Last sure point: name it, time you left it, direction of travel, time walking since. Look back. The route you came from is still a route.
3. Cheap reverse once: 10–15 minutes back toward the last sure feature. Do not reverse for an hour. If it fails, you are lost. Switch to stay-put as the default. See situation-lost, nav-stop-think.
4. Spend remaining light on a survivable, visible site — not on “one more ridge.” Shelter site, then a panel. See shelter-site, skill-signal-panel.
5. Signal now, not after dark: contrast on open floor, noise on a clock, a person by the mark. Stay findable. See signal-stay-put.
6. Walk-out only if you can defend it on paper while it is still day: catching feature you can name, heading, turnaround time, who stays with the signal. If you cannot write that, you do not walk. See skill-walk-out-plan.
7. Weather and injury raise the stay-put threshold. A storm cell or a person who cannot take weight ends the debate.
8. Food last. Use the last hour of light for roof and water fetch that does not lose the site, not for a forage loop.

### Cautions
- “Just a little farther while we can still see” is how people walk into the next drainage at dusk.
- Splitting the group to “find the trail” creates two lost parties.
- **Rockies**: Front Range drainages braid in beetle-kill. A creek is a handrail only if you already chose it. Afternoon cells steal the last of the light — start the roof before the first rumble.
summary: Lost with light: stop, last sure point, reverse once if cheap, then stay and signal. Walk only if you can defend it.

title: Civilization is not coming soon.
body:
### Situation
You will be here for days, not a missed dinner. Search may come late, or not on your clock. That is the kit of time. It does not change the rank. It changes how finished each job must be.

### Do
1. Stop. Rank the same: people, then shelter, then water, then signal. Fire supports heat, boil, and smoke. Calories last. A long stay is not a forage holiday. See food-not-first.
2. If you truly have no kit, run path-nothing for the first night. Survive tonight. Improve tomorrow. Do not start a village in the first hour.
3. Shelter becomes a system you can sleep in twice: wind, roof, ground insulation, a door you can find in the dark. Improve, then stop at good enough. See skill-long-term-shelter.
4. Water becomes a routine: a named source, a vessel, disinfection every time, a clean pour. Haul on a schedule so you are not thirsty at dusk. See skill-long-term-water.
5. Signal becomes a place, not a wave: open floor, a panel you refresh at first light, smoke or noise on a clock, a person who can be seen. See skill-long-term-signal.
6. Camp layout next: sleep, sit, wood store, and latrine on separate pads. Water and wood have paths that do not wreck the bed. See skill-camp-layout.
7. Tools and cordage as force multipliers — flake, cobble, grass two-ply — only when they serve the jobs above. Timebox craft.
8. Reassess each morning: weather, injury, fuel, water, will the site still be found. Walk-out stays a written plan, not a mood.

### Cautions
- Days of boredom make plant mistakes. Unknown stays unknown.
- A pretty camp that cannot be seen from the air is a hide, not a rescue plan.
- **Rockies**: Front Range nights drop hard even in August. A long stay at 10,000 ft (3050 m) is an insulation problem first. Afternoon cells still own the high points — wood store and roof before noon projects.
summary: Days not hours: finish tonight first, then systems for shelter, water, signal, camp. Food last. Reassess each morning.

title: The first hour with empty hands.
body:
### Situation
You have no pack tools and about sixty minutes of useful head. The hour is for a site you can survive and a mark they can find. It is not for a tour.

### Do
1. Materials: the clothes you have, a watch or the sun, a voice, dead debris, a stick to mark the spot. That is the inventory. Say it.
2. Minutes 0–5: stop. Sit. Pack stays if there is one. Name people, bleeding, daylight, wind, rain. Write last sure point on dirt or a scrap.
3. Minutes 5–10: pick the site you can see from open ground and not die in — lee of timber or a boulder, not a wash, not a saddle. Mark it. Stop scouting.
4. Minutes 10–35: windbreak on the weather side, then a small debris roof, then a fist-thick twig bed under the torso. Good enough. See skill-shelter-nothing, skill-windbreak-nothing.
5. Minutes 35–50: make yourself big. Log or stone X on open floor, bright cloth if you own it, noise on a clock. Stay by the mark. See skill-signal-from-nothing.
6. Minutes 50–60: water plan with remaining light — named drainage or snow you can melt later — and a fire decision. Fire only if heat, boil, or smoke still matters and dry fuel is already in reach. Skip a friction fantasy if the roof is still sky.
7. Calories last. Do not spend this hour on unknown plants. Reassess at the end of the hour: roof, mark, people.

### Cautions
- A perfect site two drainages over is how the hour dies on the walk.
- Splitting up in the first hour creates two overdue people.
- **Rockies**: if cells are already towering, the first hour is descent into timber and a lee, not a bow-drill seminar on the tundra.
summary: Sixty minutes, empty hands: stop, pick a site, roof, mark, then water and fire decisions. Food last.

title: A debris roof when you have no blade.
body:
### Situation
Night or weather is coming and you have no tarp and no knife. You will break deadwood by leverage and pile debris until the sky is gone. Small beats cathedral.

### Do
1. Materials: a ridge pole you can snap or wedge, two forks, a boulder, or a leaning deadfall for the head; armloads of dead debris; a twig bed; a lee site that is not a wash.
2. Site in one minute. Weather side named. Then stop walking.
3. Ridge at hip height or lower. Use a crotch, a boulder, or two forked sticks shoved in. Break poles by bending over a rock, not by hero kicks that spike your shin.
4. Ribs from ridge to ground on both sides, then a lattice of twigs so debris does not fall through. No fancy lash if you have no string — friction and weight work at this scale. If you have grass two-ply, one tie at the peak is enough.
5. Pile debris from the ground up until you cannot see light through the walls. Thicker on the weather side. Door at the lee, small, pack or a debris plug.
6. Twig bed inside before the last roof pile. You will not want to build the bed after you are wet. See skill-twig-bed.
7. Mark the hut. It disappears in timber at night. Get in with dry layers. Stop at good enough.

### Cautions
- Two hours of building in rain is how the hut becomes the injury.
- Do not strip the live windbreak to death. Dead debris first. A live ring around a trunk is not a roof.
- **Rockies**: krummholz may already be the hut. Add debris on the wind side and go. Do not fight a full build in a saddle. Beetle-kill deadfall is plentiful and poky — lattice first.
summary: No blade: low ridge from deadfall, lattice, debris until opaque, lee door, twig bed, then stop.

title: Stop the wind before you stop the sky.
body:
### Situation
The wind is stripping heat and you do not have time or debris for a full roof. A wall on the weather side is the first shelter. Roof can wait one job.

### Do
1. Materials: a boulder, a dense thicket, deadfall, or armloads of debris; a site with a clear weather direction; something to weight the top so the wall does not fall on you.
2. Name the weather. Front Range default is often west or the actual gust you feel, not the view.
3. Sit in the lee of what is already there — boulder, spruce skirt, cutbank that is not a flood channel — before you build. Steal the free wall.
4. If you must build: pile dead wood and debris on the weather side of your sit, hip high or a bit more, packed so it does not stream air through. Leave a low mouth, not a wind tunnel.
5. Weight the top with heavier pieces. A wall that falls inward is a new injury.
6. Ground insulation under you while the wall goes up. A roof of any kind — leaning poles and a debris skin — attaches to this wall, not the other way around. See skill-shelter-nothing.
7. Reset after the first hard gust. The first flap is the warning. Then stop and get the person out of the wind.

### Cautions
- A high open wall in a saddle is a cooler and a kite.
- Do not wall yourself into a wash because it is calm right now.
- **Rockies**: west wind on the Front Range is the usual story. Point the wall at the weather, not at Denver. Krummholz is already a windbreak — crawl in and add debris.
summary: Name the weather, steal a lee, pile a low weighted wall, insulate the ground, then add roof if you still need it.

title: A coal from bow, spindle, and hearth.
body:
### Situation
You need a coal and you have no ferro and no lighter. You will make heat with a bow, a spindle, and a hearth, then dump that coal into a nest.

### Do
1. Materials: a slightly bent bow about arm length; a string that will not slip (shoelace, belt strip, grass two-ply); a straight dry spindle about thumb-thick and forearm-long; a flat dry hearth thicker than a finger; a bearing block with a socket (a greasy knot, a stone dimple, or hard wood); a tinder nest; pencil kindling; a bark ember pan.
2. Wood test: standing dead, dry, not punky, not green. Spindle and hearth from the same dry piece when you can. Split to the dry heart if the outside is damp. Green pine will not give you a coal.
3. Shape: round the spindle, blunt the working end, slightly point the top. Carve a shallow socket in the hearth. String the bow with a little slack.
4. Set: hearth on hard ground, pan under where the notch will be. Wrap the string once around the spindle so it does not stack. Top of spindle in the bearing. Off-hand on the bearing, wrist locked against the shin. Bow in the other hand.
5. Burn-in: long even strokes until the socket is brown-black and the fit is round. Stop. Cut a V-notch from the board edge into the center of the socket, wide enough for dust to fall onto the pan.
6. Drill for a coal: same set, notch over the pan. Smooth strokes, then faster as dust fills the notch and smoke thickens. When the pile smokes on its own, stop. Lift the spindle. A coal is a glowing bead in the dust, not a flame.
7. Rest the coal a breath so it grows. Tip it into the nest. Fold the nest. Blow from the side until flame. Feed pencil sticks. If you get only cold dust, dry the wood, recut the notch, and stop bouncing.

### Cautions
- The bearing hand will blister. A leaf or a scrap of cloth in the socket saves the job.
- A bouncing drill smears dust and kills the coal. Lock the wrist.
- **Rockies**: dry dead aspen, sage-country deadwood, and dead juniper beat any green lodgepole. Beetle-kill can be kiln-dry — good spindle, bad wildfire neighbor. Site the fire.
summary: Dry set, burn-in, V-notch, coal on the pan, nest, then kindling. Green pine will not pay you.

title: A coal from two sticks and stubborn work.
body:
### Situation
You need a coal and you have no bow string that will hold. Hands on a long dry spindle, same hearth, notch, coal, and nest. This is slower and meaner on the skin. It still needs dry wood.

### Do
1. Materials: a long straight dry spindle, thinner than a bow spindle — roughly finger-thick and as long as your arm if you can find it; a flat dry hearth; a tinder nest; pencil kindling; a bark pan; a callus or a scrap of cloth for the palms.
2. Wood: light, dry, dead. Same rule as the bow: standing dead, not green pine, not punky. If you cannot already name a stalk as a tool you knew before this trip, pick obvious deadwood instead. Nothing from this pile goes in your mouth.
3. Socket in the hearth. Burn-in with straight down-pressure and a long rub until the socket is dark and round. Then cut a V-notch to the center, pan underneath.
4. Set: kneel or sit so your chest is over the work. Spindle vertical. Palms start high, rub down the shaft, reset without lifting the working end out of the socket if you can.
5. Dust first, then speed. When the notch fills and the smoke stays after you pause, you are close. A coal is glow in the dust. Do not blow it off the board.
6. Transfer to the nest the same as any coal: rest, tip, fold, blow from the side, feed pencil sticks.
7. If palms shred before a coal, wrap them, shorten the stroke, or switch to a bow if you can make a string. A bloody drill is not a moral victory.

### Cautions
- This is a low, dry-day skill. Do not bet a hypothermic night on it above treeline.
- Wet spindle, green wood, and a bouncing shaft make dust that will not live.
- **Rockies**: save hand drill for foothill deadwood on a dry afternoon. At 11,000 ft (3350 m) with wind, build the roof and try a bow if you have cordage. Green pine is still a lie.
summary: Long dry spindle, same hearth and notch, palms down the shaft, coal into a nest. Dry wood or it fails.

title: A nest from dead fiber, not from hope.
body:
### Situation
You need a nest that will take a coal or a shy flame and you packed no cotton. The forest will give you dead fiber if you pick it dry and keep it dry.

### Do
1. Materials: a palm-sized bundle of the finest dry fiber you can find; a pocket or a bark wrap to keep it; a denser center and a shaggy outside; pencil kindling already staged.
2. Hunt dead, not green. Dry grass and seed heads from a sun pocket. Dead inner bark from standing dead wood — peel long, then rub it into fluff between dry palms. Resin dust from wounded pines if it is already on the tree. Fine, dry, and dead is the test.
3. Build the nest in the hand: tight bird’s-nest center where the coal will sit, loose whiskers on the outside for air. Too tight smothers. Too loose dumps the coal.
4. Make two nests. One is a sample. The second is the fire.
5. Keep it off the ground and out of the wind until the coal exists. A pocket inside the shirt beats a pretty pile in the dew.
6. When the coal lands, fold the nest around it. Blow from the side, not straight down. When flame shows, hold it in the kindling mouth.
7. If it will not take, the fiber is damp, too coarse, or too packed. Rub finer, dry it against skin, or split a new dry heart and scrape dust.

### Cautions
- Live green bark and wet duff will not be a nest no matter how long you wish.
- A plastic scrap as a wind cup is fine. A plastic scrap as the only tinder in beetle-kill wind is a wildfire problem. Site first.
- **Rockies**: ponderosa whiskers and dead lodgepole inner bark light when dry. Green aspen is a liar. Pocket the nest before the afternoon wind.
summary: Dead dry fiber, dense center, shaggy outside, keep it dry, fold onto the coal, blow from the side.

title: Hot rocks in a vessel. Never from the creek.
body:
### Situation
You need to heat water and you have no metal pot. You will heat dry rocks in a fire and move them into a vessel until the water holds a rolling boil. That roll is the disinfection.

### Do
1. Materials: a vessel that can take heat without collapsing (bark trough, a scooped hollow lined with bark); dry rocks; a fire with a coal bed; two stick tongs; prefiltered water; a clean pour-off.
2. Rock rule: never take boil-rocks from the creek, a seep, or a wet fire ring. Water in the stone flashes to steam and the rock can explode. Pick dense, dry stones from high and dry ground. Skip layered shale, hollow stones, and anything that rings like a bottle.
3. Prefilter the water into the vessel. Grit wastes heat and hides the roll. See skill-cloth-prefilter if you have cloth; a settle-and-pour if you do not.
4. Build a fire. Seat the rocks in the coals, not in the wet margin. Heat until they are too hot to spit-test — you will see heat-shimmer and they may dust.
5. Move rocks with two sticks, not hands. Lower in. Replace fading rocks with fresh hot ones. Keep people and the shelter wall out of the splash line.
6. Watch for a rolling boil: big bubbles across the surface, not a shy simmer. At Front Range and higher, hold that roll a full minute. Time it. Then fish the rocks out so you can pour.
7. Pour to the clean container. Dirty scoop never goes back in. Cool with the cover on if you have one.

### Cautions
- Creek rock in a fire is a shrapnel card. Do not.
- Boil is for living contaminants. Fuel sheen still means walk.
- **Rockies**: granite cobbles from a dry bench beat anything you pry out of a creek. Wet stones from a spring snowmelt bed are still creek rocks. Eyes and shins away from the fire.
summary: Dry rocks only, never from the creek. Heat, then into the vessel, until a rolling boil you can time.

title: A bark trough that holds a boil.
body:
### Situation
You need a vessel for water and you have no bottle that will take a rock boil. A sheet of bark, folded and tied, can hold enough to heat. It is a trough, not a canteen for a march.

### Do
1. Materials: a large sheet of bark from deadfall or a standing dead tree; cordage or a twig clamp; a scrape or two logs as a cradle; optional: a knife or a flake to score fold lines.
2. Take bark without girdling a live trunk. Dead sheets peel cleaner and you do not kill the tree. If a live peel is the only option, a small patch, never a ring.
3. Score two fold lines so the long sides stand up. Pinch or fold the ends and lash them with grass two-ply, a root, or a twig that springs shut. A double fold at each end leaks less.
4. Cradle the trough in a scrape or between two logs so the sides do not splay when you fill it. Test with a little water. Patch a seep by pinching, a second inner sheet, or a dab of pitch on the outside if you already have pitch on the wood.
5. Fill with prefiltered water. Do not rest the trough in the flames. Heat is rocks in, or a coal bed beside, not a bark boat on the fire.
6. After the boil, pour off. A trough is overnight-fragile. Make a second if this one is the day’s only vessel.
7. If bark will not peel, a scooped hollow lined with a bark or clay-ish smear is a backup. Same rock-boil rules apply.

### Cautions
- Live girdling wastes a tree and often gives you junk sheets.
