- Unknown plants stay unknown. This is a vessel, not a tasting cup.
- **Rockies**: foothill juniper and some aspen country peel better than high spruce. Above treeline you may be on a rock scrape and a snowmelt plan instead. Do not burn an hour on a trunk that will not give.
summary: Dead bark sheet, fold and lash the ends, cradle it, fill, heat with rocks beside — never on the flames.

title: Two-ply string from long dead grass.
body:
### Situation
You need string and the pack cord is gone. Long dead grass will make a light two-ply. It is slow and weaker than paracord. It can still hold a bundle, a trough end, or a bow string if you stacked enough.

### Do
1. Materials: the longest dead dry grass you can pull, seed heads stripped; a little water to keep fiber flexible if it is brittle; a place to sit so the twist stays even.
2. Pick dead. Green grass is weak and shrinks. Avoid unknown plants you would have to crush into juice — this is fiber, and it stays out of the mouth.
3. Lay a small bundle as one strand. Twist until it wants to kink. That strand is now live.
4. Make a two-ply: fold the twisted strand in half and let it lay into itself, or run a reverse wrap — one strand twisted tight, then rolled over the other, switching hands in a rhythm. See skill-reverse-wrap. Keep the diameter even.
5. Splice by laying a new bundle into a thinning tail before it dies. Do not wait for a bald end.
6. Test-pull on a piece you can afford to break. Use for: bundle, light lash, marker, a bow string you have thickened. Not for a rappel. Not for a hang of real weight unless you stacked many and still do not trust it with a life.
7. If it fails, tear a clothing strap. Cloth you know beats fiber you hope.

### Cautions
- Brittle sun-killed grass will dust instead of twist. Dampen slightly, or switch to root.
- A pretty cord that fails on the first guy is wasted hour.
- **Rockies**: valley grass and foothill parks beat alpine turf. Do not spend this hour above treeline. Juniper bark may be the better fiber on the dry Front Range. See skill-cordage-bark.
summary: Long dead grass, twist, two-ply or reverse wrap, splice before the tail dies, test-pull. Light jobs only.

title: Root fiber when grass will not hold.
body:
### Situation
Grass two-ply is too weak or too short for the lash you need. Fine roots under the duff of a fallen conifer can make a tougher line. Still not a rappel rope.

### Do
1. Materials: long, thin, flexible roots from under the duff of a fallen tree or from the surface of a blowdown mound; a scrape of water to keep them from drying into wire; a place to split and twist.
2. Take from down wood and duff, not a live ring around a standing trunk. A handful of long fines beats a thick cable you cannot bend.
3. Split thick roots down with a thumbnail, a flake, or a knife until they flex. Keep them damp. Peel the rough bark if it is what makes them stiff, and keep the inner strap.
4. Twist a two-ply the same as grass: twist until it kinks, fold or reverse wrap, splice a new tail in before the old one dies. See skill-reverse-wrap.
5. Use for: square lash, trough ends, a bow string you trust more than grass. Test-pull. Double it for anything that holds a roof pole.
6. Dry it under tension if you can, then keep a coil in the shade so it does not go brittle before you need the next lash.
7. If the roots crumb or go ropey-rotten, they are junk. Switch to bark strips or a clothing strap.

### Cautions
- Live roots you strip in a ring can kill a tree and often give you junk fiber. Down wood first.
- Unknown plants stay unknown. This is string. Do not brew it.
- **Rockies**: spruce-fir duff on the north slopes hides long fines. High alpine and dry south scree will not. Do not mine a krummholz island for one lash.
summary: Fine roots from down wood, split, keep damp, two-ply, test-pull. Roof lash maybe. Rappel never.

title: A two-ply that keeps its own twist.
body:
### Situation
A single twisted strand will unwind the moment you let go. A two-ply reverse wrap locks the twist so the cord stays a cord while you lash.

### Do
1. Materials: two working ends of the same fiber — grass, bark strip, or root — already started as even bundles; clean dry hands; a knee as a third hold if you need it.
2. Start a small loop or a fold at the top so you have a bite to hang on a thumb or a twig.
3. Twist one strand hard away from you until it is tight and wants to kink. That is the live strand.
4. Lay that live strand over the other strand, toward you, so the twist tries to bite into the pair. The second strand is now in front. Switch. Twist the new front strand away, then wrap it over. Rhythm: twist, wrap, switch.
5. Keep diameters even. If one strand goes skinny, splice a new bundle into that tail before it dies — overlap a few inches (5–8 cm), keep wrapping.
6. When the cord is long enough, tie off with a simple overhand in the pair or a hitch around the work. Do not drop the live twist or the whole piece will bloom.
7. Test-pull. Use it. If it piped open, you under-twisted the singles or you wrapped with the twist instead of against it. Start a short sample until the hands remember.

### Cautions
- Fast and sloppy makes a braid that looks busy and holds nothing.
- Wet then freeze will stiffen natural fiber into a stick. Make what you will use today.
- **Rockies**: dry air sucks moisture out of grass while you work. A breath of damp on the fiber, not a soak, keeps it from dusting.
summary: Twist one strand tight, wrap it over the other, switch, splice before a tail dies, then test-pull.

title: Square-lash two poles that must stay crossed.
body:
### Situation
Two poles must stay at a right angle — a ridge on a fork, a frame cross, a drying bar. A square lash wraps the cross, then binds the wraps so they do not slide.

### Do
1. Materials: two poles that actually cross near a right angle; a piece of cordage long enough to wrap many times (grass two-ply, root, pack cord); a start-hitch that will not slip.
2. Seat the poles. The load should rest in a crotch or on the ground so the lash is not doing sculpture in mid-air.
3. Clove or a simple wrap-hitch on the first pole, close to the cross. Leave a tail you can finish with.
4. Wrap: several tight turns around the pair, following a square path — over the top pole, around the far, under, around the near — so each wrap sits next to the last, not on top of it. Three to six wraps is a start.
5. Frap: now bind the wraps. Take the working end between the two poles, around the wrapping turns, and pull. Two or three frapping turns squeeze the wraps tight against the wood. This is the part that makes it a lash instead of a pile of string.
6. Finish with a hitch on a pole, or tie the working end to the starting tail. Clip the extra only if you are sure. Test by twisting the cross. It should fight you.
7. Recheck after the first wind. Natural fiber dries and creeps. Add a wrap rather than trusting yesterday.

### Cautions
- A lash on a smooth green pole without frapping turns is decoration.
- Do not square-lash a ridge that could drop on a skull if the fiber fails. Back it with a crotch or a boulder.
- **Rockies**: dry wind loosens natural cord overnight. Morning retie is part of the shelter, not extra credit.
summary: Hitch, square wraps around the cross, frapping turns between the poles, hitch off, test, retie after wind.

title: A sharp flake when there is no knife.
body:
### Situation
You have no knife and you need a cutting edge for cord, bark, or a notch. A flake is a sharp chip, not a pocketknife. Safety is the first step, not a footnote.

### Do
1. Materials: a fine-grained cobble that will break with a sharp edge (quartzite, some chert if you find it — granite just crumbs); a hammer stone; a pad of leather, bark, or cloth for the holding hand; eye line clear of people.
2. Sit. Off-hand behind the work or in a bark pad, never in front of the strike. Legs out of the bounce line. Face slightly turned so a chip does not own an eye.
3. Choose a platform: a flat face near an edge. Strike down and off that platform with the hammer stone so a chip flies away from you into dirt, not into a lap.
4. Pick the flake that has a thin edge and a thick back you can hold. Dull the holding back with a rub on a rock if it is a second knife.
5. Cut by drawing the flake on the work, away from the body, on a log or the ground. Bark, cord, a stop-cut in a stick. Not butchery, not a pry, not a twist.
6. Make two or three flakes before you need them. Edges die fast. Retire a flake that chips into your grip.
7. If the stone only crumbs, stop. A cobble chopper is the other tool. See skill-cobble-chopper. A broken glass-hard edge in a femoral cut is an aid card.

### Cautions
- Eyes, flying chips, and a flake held in a bare fist are the usual injuries.
- Do not flake over your thigh. Do not test the edge on skin.
- **Rockies**: creek quartzite on a dry bench can work. Do not sit in a scree chute to knap. Chips plus a slope is a fall. See hazards-scree.
summary: Pad the hand, strike a flake away from the body, cut on a bench, retire a dying edge. Eyes first.

title: A cobble edge for chopping, not for surgery.
body:
### Situation
You need to break deadwood, dig a scrape, or smash a dry limb and you have no axe and no stout knife. A cobble with a crude edge is a chopper. It is not a scalpel and it is not a thrown weapon.

### Do
1. Materials: a fist-to-two-fist cobble you can hold without a death-grip; a second rock as a hammer if you must make an edge; a log or dirt anvil; eyes and shins out of the bounce.
2. Safety first: sit or kneel with the work on the ground or a stump. Off-hand behind the cobble or on the far side of the wood. Never hold a stick where the chopper will finish.
3. If the cobble already has a useful edge, use it. If not, set it on the anvil and strike to take a few big chips off one face so a rough bevel appears. Stop when you have a chopping edge, not a pile of gravel.
4. Chop by dropping the edge into the wood, then rolling. Short blows. Let the mass work. A wild overhead swing is how you hit a knee.
5. Jobs it is for: cutting a dead wrist-thick by chewing a notch around, digging a scrape, breaking joints in deadfall you already levered. Jobs it is not for: fine cutting, food experiments, prying frozen rock.
6. Dull or broken: rotate to a new edge or pick a new cobble. Do not keep a shattered face that sprays grit at your eyes.
7. Set the tool down the same way you sheath a knife — out of the bed, out of the walkway — before you gather the pile.

### Cautions
- A cobble is still a rock. Missed blows break fingers and bounce into faces.
- Do not heat this cobble for a rock-boil later. Tool stone and boil stone are different piles. Creek rock still explodes if you fire it.
- **Rockies**: river cobbles from a dry terrace, not from the wet channel. Scree is already trying to roll. See hazards-scree.
summary: Mass and a crude edge on a cobble, short blows, work on the ground. Chop wood. Not surgery.

title: The cuts a field knife actually makes.
body:
### Situation
You have a knife and a job. The blade will do four useful things in the field: slice, push, baton, and a stop-cut notch. Everything else is how knives die or how people bleed.

### Do
1. Materials: a sharp knife, a sheath, a log or knee as a bench, the work held so the off-hand is behind the spine or out of the lane. Sit to carve.
2. Slice: draw the edge along the work, away from the body. Long light strokes beat a press-hard hack. Cord, tape, a feather-stick curl.
3. Push cut: lock both wrists, blade pointing off-line, push the edge through a small piece braced on the bench. Stop when the cut is done. Do not follow through into a thigh.
4. Baton: edge on end grain, wooden baton on the spine, walk it through. Do not twist the tip in the split. Folders and cheap tangs skip this. See skill-baton-wood.
5. Stop-cut: a shallow notch that ends a split or seats a lash. Cut down to a line, then stop. This is control, not a chop.
6. Sheath before you stand, before you pick up the pile, before you walk to the fire. A folder closes before you move.
7. If blood is on the handle, you stop and wrap. See aid-bleeding. Then recut the plan, not the same stroke.

### Cautions
- A chest-level cut on a log in the lap is a femoral story.
- Prying, twisting, throwing, and using the tip as a screwdriver are how you own a broken blade and a puncture.
- **Rockies**: cold fingers plus a folding knife at dusk is how people close the blade on a tendon. Warm the hands, or wait. Beetle-kill throws chips — eye line.
summary: Sit, cut away from you: slice, push, baton, stop-cut. Sheath to move. No pry, no twist, no throw.

title: Put the edge back before it fails you.
body:
### Situation
The knife has started to skate instead of bite. Dull is dangerous. You will put a working edge back with a stone you find or a ceramic you packed, then stop before you round it off.

### Do
1. Materials: a flat fine stone (river cobble with a true face, a ceramic mug bottom, a packed stone), a little water, a strop (belt, cardboard, a piece of wood), the knife, a rag.
2. Clean pitch and grit off the blade so you are not grinding dirt into the edge.
3. Wet the stone. Set a low, repeatable angle — the same tilt every stroke, not a search. Count.
4. Stroke into the edge or with it, but pick one and keep it. Same count each side. Light. You are raising a small burr, not carving a new knife.
5. When you feel a burr along one side, switch and take it off. Then a few light even strokes to finish.
6. Strop away from the edge on leather or wood. Wipe. Test on a twig shaving or a curl, not on your thumb.
7. Field is not a mirror polish. Stop at a working bite. Touch up often so you never need a rescue grind with cold hands at dusk.

### Cautions
- A wheel or a rock that is coarser than the job will eat the knife in a minute.
- Folders: keep grit out of the pivot. Wipe before you close.
- **Rockies**: fine sandstone and some creek cobbles with a flat face work. Do not sharpen on granite grit that rolls. A mug ring in the cook kit is the cheat you should have packed.
summary: Clean, low even angle, burr then flip, strop, test on a twig. Touch up often. Not a thumb test.

title: A shadow stick that names west, then south.
body:
### Situation
You need a crude west–east and the compass is gone or you do not trust it. The sun is still moving. A stick and two marks will name that line if you wait.

### Do
1. Materials: a straight stick about knee-high, level open ground, two pebbles or twigs as markers, a way to wait 15–20 minutes without wandering off the plot.
2. Plant the stick vertical. Mark the tip of the shadow with a pebble. That is mark one.
3. Wait 15–20 minutes. Mark the new tip. That is mark two. Do not kick the stick.
4. The line from mark one to mark two runs west to east. First mark is the west end. A line off that, to your right if you face east, is a crude south in this country.
5. For a tighter line when you have hours: mark a morning tip, wait until the afternoon shadow is the same length, mark that tip. The line between equal-length tips is a better east–west. Midpoint toward the stick is south here.
6. Use the line only to pick a general walk or to orient a stick map. Then confirm with terrain — a ridge, a drainage, a known peak shape. See nav-sun, nav-terrain.
7. Write what you decided. Clouds or a canyon wall will steal the sun. If the sky is a bowl of milk, this skill is closed.

### Cautions
- In summer the sun is high and south is a fat zone, not a survey line. Do not walk a cliff on it.
- Canyon shade can hide the sun until late morning. First light on a west wall is not “east.”
- **Rockies**: this is a daylight skill on open benches. Timber and a north slope will lie. Pair with a handrail, not with hope.
summary: Plant a stick, mark the shadow tip, wait, mark again. First to second is west to east. Confirm with terrain.

title: Lay the country you already know on the ground.
body:
### Situation
The picture in your head is not shared and the paper map is gone or does not match. You will lay sticks on the dirt so the group can see one country: last sure point, drainages, ridges, you.

### Do
1. Materials: sticks of two lengths, a few stones, a scrape of dirt, the last sure point named out loud, a sitting circle so nobody is still walking.
2. North edge of the plot: mark it with a long stick if you have a crude north (shadow stick, known ridge, north star last night). If you do not have north, label the plot “not oriented” and still lay what you remember.
3. Last sure point is a stone. The trail or bearing you left on is a stick. Time and distance since, in words, next to it.
4. Drainages as bent sticks, ridges as parallel sticks, the peak shape you can still see as a wedge. You are a twig. The mark you just built is another twig. Keep scale ugly and honest.
5. Draw the catching features you could actually hit: a road cut, a named creek, a trail you would know by feel. If you cannot name one, you do not have a walk-out. See skill-walk-out-plan.
6. Group: one person talks, one person lays. Arguments happen on the sit. When the plot matches two things you can still see, you have a picture. When it does not, you are lost — stay and signal.
7. Photograph it with your eyes. Kick it apart only after the decision is written.

### Cautions
- A pretty map of a guess is how four people walk four headings.
- Do not add a drainage you hope is there.
- **Rockies**: parallel Front Range forks look like siblings. A stick map that has only “a creek on the left” is not confirmed. Need a second feature.
summary: Sit, lay last sure point, drainages, ridges, and you on the dirt. If it does not match the view, stay put.

title: A walk-out you can defend on paper.
body:
### Situation
Stay-put is the default when you are lost. You will walk only if you can defend the walk on paper while you still have light: a catching feature, a heading, a turnaround, and someone on the signal if the group splits.

### Do
1. Materials: a scrap of paper or a dirt plot, a timepiece or the sun, the stick map, a named catching feature, enough daylight to fail and still return.
2. Test: will this site kill you (flood, rockfall, lightning magnet)? If yes, move once to the nearest safe open ground, leave a note, and stay there. That is not a walk-out. See signal-stay-put.
3. If the site is survivable, stay is still the default. Walk-out needs a feature you would know when you hit it — trail, road, a creek you already chose — not “downhill until town.”
4. Write: from where, heading or handrail, catching feature, what you will do when you hit it, turnaround time. Daylight budget: about a third out, a third back, a third for error.
5. One navigator. Pair if you must send. Someone stays with the panel if the group is large enough. Splitting into two lost parties is not a plan.
6. Reversible: if the feature does not appear by the turnaround, you reverse to the mark. You do not invent a second feature on the walk.
7. Night and weather cancel the walk. Shelter and signal beat a night march into a new drainage. See nav-descend-drainage only if that drainage is the catching feature you already wrote.

### Cautions
- “Get cell service over that ridge” without a catching feature is how people leave the search box.
- A person who cannot take weight does not “try the trail.”
- **Rockies**: descending a random Front Range fork can drop you into a different county. Write the fork, or stay on the last known bench.
summary: Stay is default. Walk only with a named catching feature, heading, turnaround, and daylight to fail and return.

title: Make yourself big with empty hands.
body:
### Situation
You need to be found and you packed no mirror, no whistle, no tarp. Contrast, shape, noise, and a person in the open are still a signal. Small and hidden is how you stay lost.

### Do
1. Materials: logs, stones, the brightest cloth you are wearing, a clearing or a snow patch, a voice, a fire site you can still control if smoke is the play.
2. Pick the open floor. Stamp snow or clear brush so the contrast is clean. A pretty X in a spruce hole is invisible.
3. Lay an X or a V. Each stroke 8–10 ft (2.5–3 m) or bigger. Dark boughs on snow, light wood or cloth on dark timber shadow. Anchor every corner with stones. Wind is the thief.
4. Noise on a clock: three shouts, three rock-on-rock, then rest the voice. Listen. Repeat. Save the throat for engines and dawn.
5. Smoke only if the site is safe and you already needed a fire. Dry fuel for a column, a little green for color if you can spare it without a crown fire. Beetle-kill wind can turn a signal into the incident. See fire-signal, fire-site.
6. Be the moving mark when you hear an engine. A panel with nobody home is a maybe. Night: keep a fire you can feed without burning the camp, and reset the panel at first light.
7. Stay. Improve the mark. Do not take a “short look” over the next ridge.

### Cautions
- Three of anything is a pattern. One shout while you walk is not.
- Do not burn the only windbreak to make a column.
- **Rockies**: light granite plus a gray shirt is low contrast. Move to snow, a meadow, or a talus that reads from above. Stay on a bench they can search.
summary: Open floor, big X, contrast, noise on a clock, smoke only if the site will not ignite. Stay by the mark.

title: A wall that throws heat back at you.
body:
### Situation
You have a small fire and a shelter mouth, and most of the heat is leaving into the trees. A low wall behind the fire, opposite you, throws some of it back. It is not a fireplace from a story.

### Do
1. Materials: dry-ish stones or short logs; a fire already sited on dirt, not on duff; a shelter mouth facing the fire; space so sparks cannot eat the debris roof.
2. Site first. Fire in front of the lean-to or hut door, not under the lip. See fire-site. Distance: close enough to feel, far enough that a pop does not light the bed.
3. Build the wall on the far side of the fire, opposite the shelter. Knee to hip high. Wider than the fire. A slight curve toward you helps. Leave air under and beside the fire — do not close a ring that starves it.
4. Stones beat green logs if you have dry stones that are not creek rocks. Do not use boil-rocks and wall-rocks from the same wet pile. Creek stone in a fire can explode. See skill-rock-boil.
5. Weight the wall. Front Range wind will drop a loose stack into the coals.
6. Sit or lie off the ground on the shelter side. Adjust distance once. If your face cooks and your back freezes, the wall is too short or the bed is still on dirt.
7. Kill the fire before you sleep if the roof is debris and the wind is up. A reflector that falls inward is a new incident. Morning: the wall is still a windbreak. Rebuild the fire in the same pad.

### Cautions
- Sparks plus hanging debris is a signal you did not want.
- A tight stone ring with no mouth is a dead fire.
- **Rockies**: west wind will try to lay the flame into the hut. Wall on the weather side of the fire, you on the lee, roof still not over the coals.
summary: Low wall opposite the shelter mouth, air for the fire, dry stones not creek rocks, sparks off the debris roof.

title: Sleep, cook, and wood are three sites.
body:
### Situation
You will spend a night or more in one place. One pile for everything is how smell, sparks, and a night trip to the hole all land on the bed.

### Do
1. Materials: a sleep site you already chose for ground and overhead, a cook pad of mineral soil, a wood stack, cord or a hat to mark paths, a lamp.
2. Walk a 50–80 yd (45–75 m) triangle before you unpack. Sleep at the best ground. Cook downwind of sleep if you can read the breeze. Wood lives off the cook pad, not in the vestibule.
3. Sleep: slight rise, no snag overhead, no wash, no animal trail through the hip. See site card.
4. Cook: mineral soil, water fetch downhill of sleep, smellables never staged at the bed. Hang or canister stays at the cook node.
5. Wood and tools: a dry stack and a chopping stump on the cook side, not next to the bag.
6. Paths: one beaten line between the three so night walking is not a new bushwhack. Mark the latrine spur so nobody hunts for it in the dark.
7. If the wind flips, move cook, not sleep. Re-walk the triangle after the first storm cell.

### Cautions
- Cooking at the tent door puts smell in the only dry loft you have.
- A “tight camp” in beetle-kill is a spark and a snag in the same circle.
- **Rockies**: Front Range evening wind often drops downhill. Put sleep uphill and off the drainage, cook slightly down-canyon, not in the frost hollow.
summary: Triangle of sleep, cook, and wood. Sleep on the best ground. Cook downwind. Mark night paths.

title: The hole is downhill, downwind, and far.
body:
### Situation
People will need a toilet. If it sits by the creek or by the kitchen, the camp fails on hands and water.

### Do
1. Materials: a small trowel or a stout stick, a marked path, a wipe kit you will pack out if that is the rule you live under, a hand-wash bottle.
2. Site: 200 ft (60 m) from water, camp, and trail. Downhill of the scoop point. Downwind of sleep if you can tell.
3. One-night: a cathole 6–8 in (15–20 cm) deep, 4–6 in (10–15 cm) across. Sit or squat, then fill, then stomp, then a rock or stick marker so the next person does not reopen it.
4. Multi-day: one trench in the same rules, used in a line, each deposit covered as you go. Do not make a ring of surprise holes around camp.
5. Urine: same distance from the water scoop. Do not pee on the cook pad or the wood pile.
6. Hands: wash or sanitize after, before any cook or water job. See hygiene.
7. When you leave: fill the trench, scatter duff, take paper with you if required. Do not advertise a latrine on a social trail.

### Cautions
- A pretty creek is not a toilet. The next scoop is someone else’s bottle.
- Do not site the hole uphill of camp “for privacy.” Gravity is not private.
- **Rockies**: thin soil over granite means you may hit rock at 4 in (10 cm). Move, do not leave a smear. Snowpack is not a bury.
summary: 200 ft from water and camp, downhill of the scoop, cover as you go, wash hands. Pack out paper if that is the rule.

title: Dry wood lives under a roof, sorted.
body:
### Situation
You have a fire job tonight and maybe at dawn. A wet heap by the ring is not a store. Rain and dew will take the next start.

### Do
1. Materials: a lean or tarp scrap, a few poles, cord, a sorting space on mineral soil, tinder in a bag, a cover that is not the only sleeping sheet.
2. Sort before you stack: tinder (pencil-lead and smaller), kindling (pencil to thumb), wrist-thick fuel, a few denser splits for coals. Keep the sorts apart so a night grab is not a log on a baby flame.
3. Off the ground 4–6 in (10–15 cm). Two rails or a bark sheet. Duff and snow wick.
4. Roof: a steep lean, open on the lee, low on the weather side. Overlap like shingles. Weight the corners.
5. Stage a dawn bundle in a dry bag or under the inner edge: tinder plus a handful of splits you already shaved.
6. Restock before dark, not at 05:00 in a cell. The store is a job, not leftover wood.
7. If you break camp, the store goes back to scatter or into the last fire, then drown-stir-drown. See put-out. Do not leave a hidden dry pile against a snag.

### Cautions
- Fuel stacked in the ring “to dry” is a fire that can walk.
- Live limbs are green and a waste of the hour. Dead, up off soil, snapped, then split.
- **Rockies**: afternoon cells wet the upwind face of a stack. Face the open side away from the usual west-southwest push. Beetle-kill is plentiful and pops; keep the store off the sleep roof.
summary: Sort tinder, kindling, and fuel. Off the ground, roofed, dawn bundle staged. Drown the pile if you leave.

title: Stake it taut. Dry it. Use the sheet.
body:
### Situation
A hide is already in hand. You need a sheet, a wrap, lashing strips, or a rough bag. This card is stake-and-dry, not a harvest sequence.

### Do
1. Materials: the hide you already have, smooth stakes or awl-holes, cord or bark strip, a shaded rack or four corner stakes, a dull scraper (a rounded stone or the back of a blade).
2. Lay it hair-side down on clean ground or a pole rack. Scrape remaining soft tissue off the inner face so the sheet can dry instead of rot. You are preparing a material, not starting a kitchen.
3. Stake the four corners taut, then add mid-edge stakes so it does not bag. Punch holes 1–2 in (2.5–5 cm) from the edge, not in the middle of the working face.
4. Dry in moving air, out of noon bake if you can. Flip once. Shade plus wind beats a hard cook that cracks it.
5. When the inner face is dry to the touch and holds a fold without weeping, take it down. Store off the dirt, folded with the dry face in.
6. Use: ground sheet under a bed, wind wall, pack cover, a folded pouch, or cut edge-strips for lashing. Test-pull a strip before you trust it as cord.
7. If it starts to stink or stay wet in the middle, restake thinner, more air, more scrape. A wet wad in a pack is a lost sheet.

### Cautions
- This is not a butcher-to-mouth card. Do not turn the drying rack into a cook site.
- A hide left in a creek “to soak” in warm weather can fail before you use it.
- **Rockies**: dry air helps; freeze-thaw at night can stiffen a sheet into a board. Take it down before the hard freeze if you still need it to fold.
summary: Hide already in hand: scrape the inner face, stake taut, air-dry, then use as sheet, pouch, or lashing. Not a harvest sequence.

title: Coil a bowl. Bind as you go.
body:
### Situation
You need a bowl, a scoop, or a small carry that is not your only shirt. A coil basket is slow and useful. It is not a metal pot.

### Do
1. Materials: long dead grass, pine needles, or thin flexible twigs you can bundle; a binder (bark cord, grass cord, or pack thread); a blunt awl (bone, thorn, or a sharpened stick).
2. Make a thumb-thick core bundle, about 1 in (2.5 cm). Wrap the start tight and spiral it into a flat disk. That disk is the floor. Keep the coil snug or the bowl leaks later.
3. Stitch or wrap the new coil to the last with the binder every finger-width. Awl a gap, binder through, cinch. Same direction the whole way.
4. When the floor is fist-wide, about 4–5 in (10–13 cm) or bigger, stack the coil on itself to raise a wall. Steeper wall, smaller mouth if you want a carry. Open bowl if you want a scoop.
5. Finish the rim with extra wraps so it does not fray. Tuck the binder tail back into the last three stitches.
6. Optional: smear a thin clay or pitch on the inside if you already have it, then let it dry. That only slows a drip. It is not a boil vessel.
7. Test with a handful of water over dirt, not over the bed. A slow weep is a scoop. A collapse is kindling. Make another.

### Cautions
- Live green stems shrink and pop the stitches as they dry. Dead and flexible, or you rewrap tomorrow.
- Do not set a coil basket on coals. It is a container, not a pot. Heat belongs in metal, rock-boil, or a known vessel.
- **Rockies**: long dead grass is in parks and ditch edges, not on talus. Do this job in camp hours, not above treeline in a cell.
summary: Coil a core bundle into a disk, stitch each wrap, raise a wall, bind the rim. Test for weep. Not a fire pot.

title: A roof you can keep, not a one-night pile.
body:
### Situation
You are not walking out tonight. The emergency pile will sag, wet out, and fail if you do not upgrade it and then maintain it.

### Do
1. Materials: the existing frame or tarp, extra debris or poles, a drainage ditch stick, a door plug (pack or woven mat), cord, a reflector wall if you will have fire.
2. Keep the site. Moving camp every day spends the calories you do not have. Fix the ground: a shallow ditch 3–4 in (8–10 cm) on the uphill side, drain away from the bed, bed thicker than a fist (4 in / 10 cm packed).
3. Lower the roof. Wind and heat loss love a cathedral. Hip or lower — about 3 ft (90 cm). Weather wall steep. Lee door small.
4. Thicken until daylight does not show through the weather side. Add a second lattice if the first sagged.
5. Door plug and a drip line so melt and rain do not sheet onto the bag. Hang wet layers to dry in moving air, not in the loft.
6. If you use fire: reflector opposite the opening, mineral pad, spark gap from the roof. Bank or put out. See fire cards.
7. Dawn job: shake snow, recinch, restock debris, check snags. A long stay is a maintenance schedule, not a monument.

### Cautions
- A bigger hut is a longer build and a colder cave. Small, thick, finished.
- Do not trench into a root ball or a duff slope that can smolder.
- **Rockies**: snow load on a low ridge pole is real. Knock it. Beetle-kill overhead still counts on night three. Re-look up.
summary: Stay on the site, drain it, lower and thicken the roof, plug the door, maintain at dawn. Small and kept beats a new cathedral.

title: A known scoop, a clean cache, every batch treated.
body:
### Situation
You will need water for days, not one bottle. The fail is a dirty scoop, an empty cache at dark, or a source you never named.

### Do
1. Materials: two containers (dirty scoop and clean cache), a cloth prefilter, a pot or known treat method, a marked path to the source, a lid or cover for the cache.
2. Name the source and walk it in daylight. Same scoop rock every time. Do not trample the bank into mud.
3. Dirty container scoops. Cloth-prefilter into the treat vessel. Treat every batch — boil or the method you already trust. See boil cards.
4. Pour to the clean cache. The dirty scoop never enters the cache. Cover it. Shade it. Off the ground so it does not walk or freeze to dirt.
5. Keep at least 2 qt (2 L) in the clean cache before you go to the source late. Night ice and a lost path are how a camp goes dry.
6. Snow is a slow well: starter water in the pot, then melt, then treat. Do not fill the cache with untreated melt because it looks clean.
7. If the source fails (dry, iced, animal wreck, a cell in the slot), pick the next named drainage on the map and move the scoop job. Do not invent a seep.

### Cautions
- This card does not say untreated water is fine. Treat.
- Do not wash bodies or pots in the scoop hole. Wash downhill, then fetch above that.
- **Rockies**: August west-aspect creeks can quit in the afternoon. Fill in the morning. High camps: the pot needs a lid or you spend the wood store on steam.
summary: Named scoop, dirty vs clean containers, treat every batch, cache covered in camp. Fill early. Never untreated into the cache.

title: A mark that still reads on day seven.
body:
### Situation
Search may not be this afternoon. A one-hour X that blows into the spruce is not a plan. The camp must stay findable while you live in it.

### Do
1. Materials: the brightest sheet you can spare, logs or stones, a clearing you will keep open, a night reset kit, a whistle, a smoke bundle staged dry.
2. Pick the open floor that a passing aircraft or ridge walker can see. Not the hut clearing if the hut hides the mark. A second opening is worth the walk.
3. Build a large X or V. Strokes 8–10 ft (2.5–3 m) or bigger. High contrast. Anchor every corner. Outline with logs on pale rock.
4. Duty: someone is on listen and watch during the day. The panel has a person near it when an engine is possible. Night: pattern light or fire only if it does not burn the camp.
5. Reset at dawn. Wind, frost, and snow will steal the shape. Two-minute job if you staged the kit.
6. Keep a smoke bundle (dry stuff that makes a thick column) off the wood store, ready, not the only tinder for the cook fire.
7. Write the stay-put decision. If you must move, leave a pointer of stones toward the next camp and take a panel with you.

### Cautions
- A perfect hut in timber with no overhead mark is a hide, not a rescue.
- Do not burn the only roof for a pretty column.
- **Rockies**: granite and a gray sheet are low contrast. Dark boughs on snow, or the loudest color you own on rock. Cloud decks sit on the peaks; a lower opening can be the one that is seen.
summary: Open floor, large anchored X, a person on duty, dawn reset, smoke staged. A long stay is still a stay-put signal.

title: Close the hole before the weather uses it.
body:
### Situation
A seam split, a cuff blew out, or a sock hole is growing. Heat and skin leave through that gap. Fix it at the next sit, not after the next peak.

### Do
1. Materials: needle, thread or dental floss or bark cord, a patch of spare cloth or tape, scissors or a knife, a dry work surface, something round to hold the fabric taut (knee, log).
2. Dry the fabric. Dirt and wet make tape a rumor and stitches slip.
3. Small hole: a few over-and-over stitches, knot both ends, trim. Do not pull so hard you gather the cloth into a new tear.
4. Larger hole: patch on the inside if you can, outside if that is the only reach. Stitch around the patch, not just a blob of tape. Tape can go over the stitches as a wind layer.
5. Seam blowout: restitch along the old holes if they are sound, or add a second line a needle-width off. Backstitch the last three.
6. Cuffs, sock heels, glove tips: these fail first. Wrap a cloth strip and stitch it as a sacrificial layer. See feet card if it is a sock.
7. Test the flex. Then wear it. Recheck at the next stop. Carry the needle in a cork or tape wrap so it is not a puncture in the kit.

### Cautions
- A knife used as a needle in a hurry is a wound card. Awl slowly, or heat a pin if you have one.
- Super glue on a moving joint cracks and then holds dirt in the hole.
- **Rockies**: UV-rotten nylon on a south-facing pack strap fails at the sun line. Patch early. Wind at 11,000 ft (3350 m) finds every gap you left for later.
summary: Dry the cloth, stitch small holes, patch large ones, restitch blown seams. Tape is a layer, not the whole fix.

title: A weighted line, a hook, a wait.
body:
### Situation
You have line and a hook or a bent pin. This card is how the gear works, not a food verdict. Last-resort when you can know the law. Not a camping hobby.

### Do
1. Materials: 20–50 ft (6–15 m) of line you trust, a hook or a pin bent into a J and wrapped so it cannot pull out, a small weight (split shot, a pebble in a wrap, a nut), bait that stays on the hook, gloves if the line can cut.
2. Tie the hook with a knot that cinches on the shank. Test-pull. Add the weight 12–18 in (30–45 cm) above the hook so the hook can still move.
3. Bait so the point is not fully buried in a wad. The point has to be able to catch.
4. Lower or swing into a seam: the slower edge of a current, a pool tail, a shaded undercut. Do not stand on the only undercut and collapse it.
5. Hold a loop in the fingers. When the line ticks or runs, wait a beat, then pull firm, not a yank that snaps the knot.
6. If the line loads, keep tension, walk it to a shallow, and land with a wet hand or a scoop, not a dry squeeze that tears the hook out. Unhook with the point away from you.
7. If nothing takes it, change depth or seam once, then stop. Hours of this while shelter is unfinished is the wrong rank. See priorities.

### Cautions
- This is how the gear works, not a food verdict. It does not make a meal plan.
- Hooks in a pocket without a cork are a later wound. See bleeding if that happens.
- Know the law when you can. Closed water, gear bans, and seasons exist. This is last-resort survival, not a hobby.
- **Rockies**: snowmelt creeks run fast and cold. A pool behind a boulder is the usual seam. Do not wade a pushy Front Range creek for a maybe.
summary: Hook, weight, baited point, seam in the current, tension then land. Gear technique, not a food verdict. Law first.

title: A baited sliver that turns sideways.
body:
### Situation
You have line and no hook. A gorge is a short stiff sliver tied at the middle. This is how the device works, not a food verdict. Last-resort. Know the law when you can. Not a hobby.

### Do
1. Materials: a sliver of hardwood, bone, or a trimmed thorn, 1–1.5 in (2.5–4 cm), pointed at both ends; line; bait that will hide the sliver; a small weight optional.
2. Notch or wrap the middle of the sliver so the line cannot slide to one end. Tie hard. Test-pull both points.
3. Bait with the sliver in line with the line, points covered but not buried in a ball that will not pack down. The idea is it swallows straight, then a pull turns it across.
4. Lower into a quiet pool or the slow seam, same as a handline. Hold the line. Do not leave a set line and walk off if the law you know forbids it.
5. When the line moves and stays heavy, give a firm pull and keep tension so the sliver stays turned. Slack is how it dumps.
6. Land in the shallows. Back the sliver out the way it went in, points away from your palm. A gorge is as sharp as a hook.
7. Timebox. If the device does not work, stop. Shelter, water, signal still rank first.

### Cautions
- This is how the device works, not a food verdict.
- A gorge left in a throat and yanked wild is a torn mess and a lost sliver. Tension, then slow.
- Last-resort survival. Know the law when you can. This is not a camping hobby.
- **Rockies**: clear high creeks show a standing person. Sit low, keep shadow off the pool, or you are practicing for nothing.
summary: Middle-tied sliver, baited in line, pull turns it across. Device technique, not a food verdict. Law, last-resort, not a hobby.

title: A fence in the water that funnels.
body:
### Situation
Shallow, slow water and a handful of stakes. A weir is a fence that narrows to a pocket. This is how the structure works, not a food verdict. Last-resort. Know the law when you can. Not a hobby.

### Do
1. Materials: wrist-thick stakes, thinner lattice, a few rocks, a gap you can close with a basket or a second fence, gloves.
2. Pick a shallow run or a side channel you can work without swimming. Not a full river. Not a public ditch you will wreck.
3. Drive a fence of stakes a hand apart — 4–6 in (10–15 cm) — from one bank toward the current, angled, not a wall that dams the whole creek. Leave most of the flow a way around.
4. Lattice the gaps with twigs so the fence is a screen, not a dam. Water must still pass or you blow the banks and lose the pocket.
5. The funnel ends in a small pocket or a second V. The pocket is shallow enough that you can see and scoop with a basket or hands, not a deep hole you fall in.
6. Work it in daylight. Check often. Do not leave a blocking fence overnight in a creek other people use.
7. When you are done, pull every stake. Restore the channel. A left-behind weir is trash and a legal problem.

### Cautions
- This is how the structure works, not a food verdict. It is not a meal plan.
- Last-resort survival. Know the law when you can. Blocking a stream is often illegal. This is not a camping hobby.
- A dam in a slot canyon is a flood trap for you, not a clever fence.
- **Rockies**: snowmelt jumps overnight. A weir you built at 16:00 can be under a dirty push at 10:00. Pull it before the rise.
summary: Angled stake fence, lattice, funnel to a shallow pocket, restore the channel. Structure technique, not a food verdict. Law first.

title: Heat in a pot. Dirt stays out.
body:
### Situation
You have a pot and a heat source. You need a rolling boil and a pour that does not put dirt in the vessel. This is technique, not a food verdict.

### Do
1. Materials: a pot of 1–2 qt (1–2 L) with a lid if you have one, a stable grate or three rocks of even height, a coal bed or stove, a clean pour vessel, a cloth, a glove or sleeve for the bail.
2. Site on mineral soil, same rules as a fire pad. Pot must sit level. A tip into the dirt is the whole failure.
3. Prefilter grit if the contents are a liquid. Grit scorches and wastes fuel.
4. Lid on. Bring to a rolling boil — bubbles across the surface, not a side simmer. At Front Range and higher, hold the roll about a minute if this batch is a water treat. Time it.
5. Keep tools out of the dirt. One spoon stays the pot spoon. It does not go on the ground and back in.
6. Off the heat. Lid stays until the steam is not a face burn. Pour to the clean vessel. Do not set the hot pot in duff.
7. Cool, cover, hang or cache away from sleep if it smells. See hang card. Drown the fire if you are done.

### Cautions
- This is technique, not a food verdict. Heat and a clean pot do not decide what belongs in a mouth.
- A grab of a wire bail out of flame is a burn. See wound if you do it.
- Fuel sheen and unknown ditch water are still a treat problem. Boil is not a filter for everything.
- **Rockies**: thin air and wind steal heat. Lid and a wind screen, or you empty the wood store on a pot that never rolls.
summary: Level pot on mineral soil, lid on, rolling boil, dirt stays off the spoon. Technique, not a food verdict.

title: Over coals, turning, off the dirt.
body:
### Situation
You have a heat bed and a stick. You need the load off the dirt and out of the flame. This is technique, not a food verdict.

### Do
1. Materials: a green or wet-sappy stick that will not torch in the first ten minutes, two forked supports or two rock notches, a coal bed (not a high flame), a clean lift (another stick or a pot lid) so nothing hits the ground.
2. Let the fire run down to coals. Flame blacks the outside and leaves the inside cold. Coals are the heat.
3. Skewer on the spit. Supports at both ends so the load hangs above the coals with a fist of air under it — 4–5 in (10–13 cm). Not in the ash.
4. Turn on a clock: a quarter turn every few minutes. If one face hardens and the other is raw to the eye, you are too close or you stopped turning.
5. Fat or drip that hits coals will flare. Lift, let the flare die, then return. Do not chase a grease fire with a sleeve.
6. When you take it off, it lands on bark, a lid, or the pot — not on the duff. Dirt on the surface is the thing this skill exists to stop.
7. Put the spit out of the walkway. A sharp stick at shin height is a wound. Drown or bank the bed when the job is done.

### Cautions
- This is technique, not a food verdict. A browned outside is not a safety statement.
- A dry dead stick as a spit is a torch. If it chars through, the load dumps in the ash. That is the dirt problem again.
- **Rockies**: wind drives flame sideways into the load. A low ring of rocks or a reflector wall on the windward side. See reflector.
summary: Green spit over coals, turn, keep the load off dirt and out of flame. Technique, not a food verdict.

title: Move, stop, look. Last resort.
body:
### Situation
Last-resort survival, when you can know the law. This is a movement technique: slow travel with long pauses. It is not a camping hobby and not a meal plan.

### Do
1. Materials: quiet clothes, the wind on your face, a line of travel you can reverse, a sit pad or a stump, binoculars if you have them, a watch so you timebox.
2. Rank first: people, shelter, water, signal. Only then this. If those are undone, sit down and do those.
3. Wind in the face or on a cheek, not at your back. If the breeze flips, stop and re-pick the line.
4. Walk 4–8 quiet steps, about 10–20 ft (3–6 m). Stop longer than you walked. Look at edges, shade, and motion, not just the open park.
5. Freeze on a snap you did not make. Wait. Then look with the eyes before the feet.
6. Sit a stand: a place with a view and a back, for a timed watch. Then move. Endless wandering is not still-hunting.
7. End it. Mark the time you spent. Return on your own line. This skill does not outrank dark, a cell, or a signal duty.

### Cautions
- Last-resort survival. Know the law when you can. Seasons, land status, and methods are not optional because you are hungry.
- This is not a camping hobby. Do not practice it on a weekend trail as sport from this card.
- Do not name a wild animal as a meal. Technique only.
- **Rockies**: timber and blowdown hide a lot and snap under a boot. Parks at first and last light are where you can actually see. Midday talus is a noise machine.
summary: Wind in the face, few steps, longer stop, look at edges, timebox. Last-resort, know the law, not a hobby, not a food verdict.

title: Read the ground. Do not invent a chase.
body:
### Situation
You can see a print, a scrape, or a drop of sign. The skill is to read what is there, not to invent a story and walk into the next drainage. Last-resort context. Know the law when you can.

### Do
1. Materials: the print in decent light, a stick for scale (mark 6 in / 15 cm beside it), a notebook or a photo if the phone still has battery, the wind direction, your own boot for a size check.
2. Stop short of the print. Do not stand in it. Crouch to the side.
3. Shape: outline sharp or melted, toe count if it is clear, claw marks or not, stride length between two prints you can actually pair.
4. Freshness is a guess you must label as a guess: sharp edges and no debris in the well is newer than a print with needles in it or rain-pits on the floor. Snow melt rounds everything by noon.
5. Direction: the way the toes point, plus a second print. One print is not a line.
6. Decide whether this changes your next hour. Usually it does not. Shelter, water, signal still rank. Following a line of sign until dark is how people get lost twice.
7. If you needed this for last-resort movement, still-hunt into the wind along a feature you can reverse. Timebox. Write what you saw so you do not upgrade a maybe at 21:00.

### Cautions
- Do not invent a chase. A print is not a promise. This is technique, not a food verdict.
- Last-resort survival. Know the law when you can. This is not a camping hobby.
- Do not name a wild animal as a meal from a print. Technique only.
- **Rockies**: freeze-thaw wrecks snow sign by late morning. Mud at a seep holds shape longer. Your own party’s boots will fake a story if you do not check the tread.
summary: Do not step in it. Outline, direction, freshness as a labeled guess. Do not invent a chase. Last-resort, law, not a hobby.

title: A loop that closes. Law first.
body:
### Situation
Last-resort survival when you can know the law. A snare is a running loop on a constriction. This card is how the device is built, not a food verdict. Not a camping hobby.

### Do
1. Materials: smooth cord or wire that can slide, a small lock (a wrapped eye or a washer), an anchor that will not pull out, optional spring pole, gloves.
2. Make a loop that runs: the working end through an eye so a pull shrinks the loop and the eye does not spill. Test on your fist, then take it off. The loop should close easy and not cut your own kit.
3. Pick a constriction on a small trail you did not invent — a gap under a log, a fence of sticks you added to narrow an existing run, not a random park.
4. Hang the loop so the bottom sits a fist off the ground — about 4 in (10 cm) — on that small run, or at the height of the trail you actually see. Anchor solid to a stake or stem on the side, not a dead twig.
5. Optional spring: a bent sapling tied so a dislodge lifts. If you cannot control it, skip it. A wild spring is a face injury.
6. Check on a short clock. A set device you forget is cruel and often illegal. If the law you know bans this method, do not set it.
7. When you leave the site, pull every loop. Disable. A left-behind snare is a problem for everything that walks, including a person.

### Cautions
- Last-resort survival. Know the law when you can. Snares are illegal in many places and seasons. This is not a camping hobby.
- This is how the device is built, not a food verdict. Do not name a wild animal as a meal.
- Wire on a neck or a wrist is a wound. See bleeding. Keep the unused loop in a tin, not a pocket.
- **Rockies**: public land and park rules are not a rumor. If you cannot know the law, do not set this. Walk-out and signal still win most days.
summary: Running loop, constriction, solid anchor, check often, pull when you leave. Last-resort, know the law, not a hobby, not a food verdict.

title: Three sticks, one weight. Last resort.
body:
### Situation
Last-resort survival when you can know the law. A figure-4 is a three-stick trigger that holds a weight. This card is how the device is built, not a food verdict. Not a camping hobby.

### Do
1. Materials: three wrist-to-thumb sticks you can notch, 8–12 in (20–30 cm), a weight (flat rock or log) heavy enough that you would not want it on a hand, a work site away from the bed, gloves.
2. Cut a vertical upright with a square notch near the top. Cut a diagonal lock-stick with a notch that seats in that square, and a blunt heel. Cut a trigger stick with a shallow notch that holds the heel and a long arm.
3. Assemble off to the side first: upright, diagonal, trigger, so you can see the lock without the weight. The trigger arm should dump with a light bump, not a kick.
4. Set the weight so it rests on the diagonal, balanced, with a clear fall path onto a small box of sticks — a catch space, not an open trail. You should be able to pull the trigger from the side with a long stick.
5. Test from the side, never with a hand under the weight. If it will not dump, recut the notches shallower. If it dumps in the wind, the notches are too shallow or the weight is cocked wrong.
6. If the law you know bans deadfalls, do not set it. If you cannot know the law, do not set it. This is last-resort, not practice behind the tent.
7. Check on a short clock. Knock it down and scatter the sticks when you leave. A cocked weight is a later injury for the next boot.

### Cautions
- Last-resort survival. Know the law when you can. Deadfalls are illegal in many places. This is not a camping hobby.
- This is how the device is built, not a food verdict. Do not name a wild animal as a meal.
- Hands under a cocked rock are a fracture problem. See wound. Set and unset from the side.
- **Rockies**: a rock on a slope can slide instead of fall. Flat mineral pad, or skip the device. Do not cock this in a camp path.
summary: Upright, diagonal, trigger; weight tested from the side; pull when you leave. Last-resort, know the law, not a hobby, not a food verdict.

title: Swelling, sting, cannot breathe. Treat as if.
body:
### Situation
A sting, a known trigger, or a sudden swell of lips, tongue, or throat. They itch, wheeze, or say their throat is closing. You are not naming a diagnosis. You are keeping air in and getting to care.

### Do
1. Scene. Get away from bees, ants, the plant, the smoke. Do not stand in the swarm.
2. Ask: do they carry their own injector, and can they use it. If they have one and they want it used, help them use THEIR device in the outer thigh as THAT device’s label shows. You are not issuing medicine.
3. Sit them up if they are struggling to breathe. If they are faint and pale, lie them down and raise the legs unless that wrecks breathing. If they vomit, roll.
4. Loosen collars. Nothing in the mouth. No mystery pills from the group kit.
5. Watch the airway. If they stop answering, see the unresponsive card. Airway first.
6. Messenger and signal now. This is a get-to-care problem even if they “feel a bit better.” A second wave can land after the first.
7. Write the time, the trigger if known, what they used of their own, and what changed.

### Cautions
- Treat as if. Do not wait for a perfect textbook picture.
- Do not put ice, a tourniquet, or a cut on a sting and call it done.
- Do not give a stranger’s injector, leftover pills, or a “Benadryl and hike it off” plan as care.
- **Rockies**: a first sting on a 14er with no injector still gets descent and a messenger, not a summit push.
summary: Get off the trigger, help them use only their own injector if they have it, keep the airway, get to care.

title: Chest pain, pressure, or cannot get air.
body:
### Situation
Pressure, squeezing, or pain in the chest, jaw, neck, or one arm. Short of breath, pale, sweaty, or a sudden dread they cannot joke off. You are not calling it a heart attack. You are stopping work and getting to care.

### Do
1. Stop the group. Pack off. No more climbing, no “one more switchback.”
2. Sit them. Loosen straps and collar. Still air is better than a marching chest.
3. If they have their own prescribed chest medicine and they ask to take it the way they were taught, that is theirs. Do not hand out group aspirin, caffeine, or a mystery tablet.
4. Ask: did this start with a sting, a known allergy, a fall, or a climb in heat. Branch: allergy card, heat card, or stay on this one.
5. If they fade, slump, or will not answer: unresponsive card. Airway and compressions beat a debate.
6. Signal and messenger now. Someone stays. Write time of onset and what you see.
7. Keep them warm from the ground up. Do not feed a big meal. Sips only if they can swallow and want water.

### Cautions
- Altitude, panic, and heart trouble can look alike. You do not have to pick. Get to care.
- Do not stretch, burp, or hike it out because it “might be gas.”
- Do not leave them alone to “catch their breath” on a slope.
- **Rockies**: a hard push above treeline plus a heavy pack is a common setup. Descent is part of the plan once they can move, not a summit.
summary: Stop work, sit them, keep the airway, get to care. Do not diagnose. Do not hand out mystery pills.

title: I broke my leg. Weight first.
body:
### Situation
They say the leg is broken, or they went down and will not stand. Ask weight before you invent a plan.

### Do
1. Ask: can they take weight on it. That question first. Watch their face, not their pride.
2. If they cannot take weight, or the limb looks wrong: do not walk them. Open the fracture card. Splint, pad, signal, carry or wait.
3. If they can take some weight and the limb looks straight: open the sprain card. Still stop the day if 100 yd (90 m) will wreck it.
4. Scene. Stop the group. Same rock does not take a second person.
5. Warmth and a written time. Bleeding first if there is any.
6. Messenger. A broken-leg story above treeline is an overnight unless you already have a carry.

### Cautions
- Walk it off after a snap or a give-way is how it becomes two patients.
- Do not copy the whole fracture procedure here. This id exists so the ask hits. Then use the child cards.
- **Rockies**: a femur story at 11,000 ft (3350 m) is stay-and-signal, not a hero carry down scree.
summary: Ask weight first. No weight: fracture card. Weight with a straight limb: sprain card.

title: Too hot. Use the heat card.
body:
### Situation
Hot, dizzy, nauseated, or not making sense on a climb. This id is the heat tree so the ask hits.

### Do
1. Open the heat card. Shade, strip the pack, sip, cool the pits.
2. If they are confused, collapsing, or hot and dry: cool hard and get to care. Do not rest it off.
3. If this started as a sting or a closing throat, switch to the allergy card.
4. Hold the group. One more short push is how you carry someone.

### Cautions
- This is a pointer, not a second heat manual. The steps live on the heat card.
- **Rockies**: black rock and noon sun stack. Descend when they can walk.
summary: Standards id heat. Hands off to the heat card.

title: Bite. Use the snake card.
body:
### Situation
A strike on a foot or hand. You will not ID venom by folklore. This id is the snake tree so the ask hits.

### Do
1. Open the snake card. Move away. Sit. Limb still. Rings off.
2. Get to care. No cutting, no suction, no ice-and-hope.
3. Photo from far away only if it costs you nothing.
4. Time the strike. Watch swelling and how they feel.

### Cautions
- This id exists so the ask hits. The steps live on the snake card.
- **Rockies**: prairie and western rattlesnakes. Still a get-to-care problem with or without a rattle.
summary: Standards id snake. Hands off to the snake card.

title: You are not sure where you are.
body:
### Situation
The trail vanished or the junction did not match. This id is the lost tree so the ask hits.

### Do
1. Open the lost card. Stop. Last sure point. Reverse once if cheap.
2. Otherwise stay put and signal. Do not invent a drainage march in the last hour of light.
3. If it is still daylight and you have a named catching feature, use that card, not a wander.

### Cautions
- This is a pointer. The lost card has the steps.
- **Rockies**: beetle-kill braids drainages. A creek is a handrail only if you chose it.
summary: Standards id lost. Hands off to the lost card.

title: Bleeding. Use the bleed card.
body:
### Situation
Blood is leaving. You need pressure, not a story. This id is the bleed tree so the ask hits.

### Do
1. Open the bleed card. Direct pressure. Pack if it soaks. Do not peek.
2. Scene first if rock or water is still winning.
3. If they fade, shock-position and a messenger.
4. Write the time you started pressure. The next helper needs that.

### Cautions
- This id is the matcher hook. The pressure steps live on the bleed card.
- A soaked shirt is not a dressing. Pack the hole, then wrap.
summary: Standards id bleed. Hands off to the bleed card.

title: Losing heat. Use the cold cards.
body:
### Situation
They are cold in the middle, or the group is losing heat faster than it makes it. This id is the cold tree.

### Do
1. Ask: still shivering and making sense, or quiet and clumsy.
2. Open the hypothermia card for the person. Open the cold situation card for the group plan (shelter, wind, packed food).
3. Wet clothes off. Wind off. Pad under them. Fire only if it does not delay the bag.

### Cautions
- This id is the hook. Do not treat cold hands as the whole problem.
- **Rockies**: 50 F (10 C) rain plus wind is enough.
summary: Standards id cold. Hands off to hypothermia and the cold situation card.

title: Burned. Use the burn card.
body:
### Situation
Flame, steam, or hot metal just hit skin. This id is the burn tree so the ask hits.

### Do
1. Open the burn card. Cool with water you can spare. Then cover.
2. Scene: the stove, the fire, the fuel bottle. Do not add a second burn.
3. If the area is large, or the face or hands, get to care.
4. Blisters later. Airway and cooling first if the face was in it.

### Cautions
- This id is the hook. Grease, toothpaste, and leaf-paste are not the plan.
- Do not pop the whole blister field to “have a look.”
summary: Standards id burn. Hands off to the burn card.

title: Behind on water. Use the water card.
body:
### Situation
Bottles are low or empty and the day is still working. This id is the water tree so the ask hits.

### Do
1. Open the water situation card. Stop wasting sweat. Count what you have. Move to a named source. Treat before you drink.
2. If they are already crashing, that card plus the dehydration signs card.
3. Snow is not a ration until it is melted. Eating cold snow drops core temp.

### Cautions
- This id is the hook. The find-and-treat steps live on the water cards.
- Clear is not clean. Do not chug ditch water because you are scared.
summary: Standards id water. Hands off to the water situation card.
